agaricus-bernardii.hymenium: Gills crowded; grey-pinkish when young, becoming brown with maturity
agaricus-bernardii.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat or slightly depressed; cream, beige to brownish; smooth when young, with brownish scales; margin initially inrolled
agaricus-bernardii.stipe: Short, very stout, solid, cylindrical to slightly tapering toward base; whitish, often browning below; thick sheathing ring
agaricus-bernardii.spore-print: Spore print chocolate-brown to dark brown
agaricus-bernardii.ecology: Saprobic in grasslands, coastal dunes, sandy and saline soils, parks, roadsides and other disturbed urban habitats, notably where winter road salt accumulates; solitary or gregariously; summer to late autumn
agaricus-bernardii.edibility: Edible but generally not highly valued
agaricus-bernardii.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~4–8 cm long and ~2–5 cm thick
agaricus-bernardii.flesh: White, thick and firm, turning pinkish-red to reddish-orange when cut or bruised, sometimes slowly
agaricus-bernardii.odour: Variable; mild mushroomy or faintly anise-like when young, often becoming briny, iodine-like or fishy with age
agaricus-bernardii.taste: Mild when young, sometimes unpleasant or iodine-like in mature specimens
agaricus-bernardii.microscopy: Spores broadly ovoid to subglobose, smooth, thick-walled, dark brown, ~5.5–7.5 × 5–6 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant, clavate to cylindrical

agaricus-bitorquis.hymenium: Gills free, close to crowded; pale pink when young, becoming reddish-brown to dark chocolate-brown at maturity
agaricus-bitorquis.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; white to whitish, smooth or finely flaky/scaly, often dirty with soil; thick and firm
agaricus-bitorquis.stipe: Short, stout, solid, cylindrical to slightly tapering or enlarged below; whitish, smooth to finely scaly near apex; with a thick sheathing double ring
agaricus-bitorquis.description: Saprobic on compacted or disturbed soil, roadsides, paths, gardens, parks, verges, cracks in paving and sometimes pushing through asphalt; late spring to autumn
agaricus-bitorquis.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~2–10 cm long, ~1–4 cm thick
agaricus-bitorquis.flesh: Flesh white, thick, firm, usually unchanging when cut, very rarely slightly pinkish in wet/old specimens
agaricus-bitorquis.chemical-reactions: KOH negative on cap surface, no yellowing
agaricus-bitorquis.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, thick-walled, ~5–7 × 4–5.5 µm; basidia mostly 2- to 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia inconspicuous or basidiole-like; pleurocystidia absent

agaricus-subperonatus.hymenium: Crowded; whitish when very young, becoming greyish-pink to pink and finally dark chocolate-brown as spores mature
agaricus-subperonatus.cap: Initially hemispherical to convex, later broadly convex or almost flat; pale cream beneath appressed brown fibrils or scales, often darkest toward the centre; margin may retain veil fragments when young
agaricus-subperonatus.hymenium-attachment: Free — gills do not reach the stipe
agaricus-subperonatus.stipe: Robust, whitish, cylindrical to slightly clavate or tapering and often rooting deeply; substantial superior to median ring, with whitish to brownish veil zones or a characteristic boot-like sheath below the ring
agaricus-subperonatus.spore-print: Spore print chocolate-brown to dark brown
agaricus-subperonatus.ecology: Saprobic on humus-rich, disturbed or grassy ground (parks, gardens and roadside verges); often reported sharing soil with other Agaric species (A. bitorquis, A. bisporus, A. campestris); gregarious; summer to late autumn
agaricus-subperonatus.edibility: Edible but of indifferent or poor culinary quality
agaricus-subperonatus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~5–12 cm long and ~1.5–3 cm thick
agaricus-subperonatus.flesh: Flesh whitish, firm; may remain unchanged or slowly stain pale pink to reddish when cut, particularly toward the stipe base; never characteristically yellow-staining
agaricus-subperonatus.odour: Mild, mushroomy, sometimes becoming liquorice-like in old specimens
agaricus-subperonatus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, thick-walled, brown in KOH, ~6–8 × 4–5.5 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia abundant, clavate to subclavate, ~20–30 × 6–8 µm; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis

agaricus-sylvicola.hymenium: Gills crowded, whitish when very young, becoming greyish-pink to pink and finally chocolate-brown as spores mature
agaricus-sylvicola.cap: Ovoid to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; white to cream, smooth to finely silky-fibrillose; slowly bruising yellow to ochre-yellow, particularly near the margin
agaricus-sylvicola.stipe: Slender, white, cylindrical, usually with a distinctly bulbous base; yellowing when handled; large, thin, pendulous white ring, often with yellowish floccose scales or a cogwheel-like pattern beneath
agaricus-sylvicola.ecology: Saprobic in coniferous, deciduous and mixed woodland; alone, scattered or gregariously, often among leaf or needle litter; summer to late autumn
agaricus-sylvicola.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~5–10 cm long and ~1–2 cm thick
agaricus-sylvicola.flesh: White, firm, sometimes faintly yellowing when cut; bruised outer surfaces gradually yellow to ochre
agaricus-sylvicola.chemical-reactions: Schaeffer reaction positive, orange-red on cap surface; KOH yellow
agaricus-sylvicola.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, ~5–6.5 × 3.5–4.5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant, subglobose to ellipsoid or clavate

agaricus-xanthodermus.hymenium: Crowded; whitish when very young, becoming pinkish and finally dark chocolate-brown as spores mature
agaricus-xanthodermus.cap: Convex to broadly convex or nearly flat; whitish to cream or pale grey-brown, smooth to finely fibrillose, often somewhat squared or flattened at the centre; bruises rapidly bright chrome-yellow, especially along the margin
agaricus-xanthodermus.hymenium-attachment: Free — gills do not reach the stipe
agaricus-xanthodermus.stipe: Cylindrical, whitish, slightly enlarged or bulbous at base; rapidly stains bright yellow when rubbed or cut, particularly at the base; with a large, persistent, flaring double ring with a thickened outer margin
agaricus-xanthodermus.spore-print: Spore print very dark brown to chocolate-brown
agaricus-xanthodermus.ecology: Saprobic on nutrient-rich and disturbed soils (lawns, gardens, parks, roadside verges, hedgerows); solitary to clustered or forming arcs; summer to autumn
agaricus-xanthodermus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~4–15 cm long and ~1–3 cm thick
agaricus-xanthodermus.flesh: Flesh white, sometimes weakly yellowing elsewhere but turning conspicuously bright chrome-yellow in the stipe base when cut or bruised, yellow colour may later fade or become brownish
agaricus-xanthodermus.odour: Strongly phenolic, ink-like, iodine-like or carbolic, intensified by cooking
agaricus-xanthodermus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, brownish in KOH, ~4.5–5 × 3–4 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia clavate to subcylindrical, ~20–30 × 4–8 µm; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis

agrocybe-molesta.hymenium: Gills close to crowded, whitish at first, becoming dull greyish-brown to clay-brown as spores mature
agrocybe-molesta.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat; whitish, cream to dull yellowish, slightly tacky when fresh but soon dry; often cracking with age and retaining pale veil fragments around the margin
agrocybe-molesta.stipe: Rigid, cylindrical, whitish, sometimes browning toward the base; with a thin, fragile and often short-lived whitish ring
agrocybe-molesta.ecology: Saprobic in lawns, meadows, fields, grassy roadside verges and gardens; solitary, scattered, gregarious or occasionally in fairy rings; late spring to summer
agrocybe-molesta.edibility: Reported as edible after thorough cooking but bitter and of poor quality
agrocybe-molesta.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~5–10 cm long, ~0.3–1.5 cm thick
agrocybe-molesta.flesh: Flesh white, firm, unchanging when cut
agrocybe-molesta.chemical-reactions: KOH negative to yellowish on the cap surface
agrocybe-molesta.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, 11–16(–19) × 6–9(–10) µm, with a conspicuous germ pore; basidia clavate, 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia and pleurocystidia broadly utriform to clavate

agrocybe-pediades.hymenium: Gills close to moderately spaced; creamy-beige to pale yellow-brown when young, becoming grey-brown to rust-brown with maturity; edges often paler
agrocybe-pediades.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat; smooth, sometimes slightly greasy or sticky when fresh; honey-yellow, ochre-yellow to pale brownish-yellow, fading when dry; young margin may retain ephemeral white veil fragments
agrocybe-pediades.hymenium-attachment: Adnexed to narrowly adnate, sometimes with a slight decurrent tooth
agrocybe-pediades.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, whitish to pale ochre-yellow or cap-coloured; finely pruinose to fibrillose, solid when young and becoming hollow; ring absent, with white basal mycelium or fine rhizomorphs
agrocybe-pediades.spore-print: Spore print dark brown to dull cinnamon-brown
agrocybe-pediades.description: Saprobic in lawns, meadows, pastures, grassy parkland, roadside verges and dune grasslands; occasionally on compost, manure or woodchips; alone or gregariously; spring to autumn
agrocybe-pediades.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2–8 cm long and ~0.2–0.6 cm thick
agrocybe-pediades.chemical-reactions: KOH red to pink on cap surface
agrocybe-pediades.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, ~9.5–15(–18) × 7–10 µm, with a conspicuous germ pore; basidia 4-spored with basal clamps; cheilocystidia lageniform to ventricose, often capitate; pleurocystidia sparse or absent

albatrellopsis-confluens.hymenium: Pores very small, round to angular, white to cream when fresh, sometimes faintly yellowish or greenish when bruised; ~3–5 pores per mm
albatrellopsis-confluens.cap: Irregularly rounded, convex to flattened or centrally depressed; often strongly fused with neighbouring caps; cream, apricot, salmon-orange to pinkish-buff or ochre, dry and smooth, sometimes cracking with age
albatrellopsis-confluens.stipe: Short, stout, central to eccentric or lateral; whitish to cream or pinkish-buff, smooth, frequently fused with adjacent stipes in clustered fruit bodies
albatrellopsis-confluens.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers (spruce, boreal conifers); terrestrial on forest soil, gregarious and commonly forming large fused clusters; late summer to autumn
albatrellopsis-confluens.edibility: Edible when young but generally considered mediocre; older specimens become tough and the taste may be bitter or cabbage-like
albatrellopsis-confluens.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to very large when clustered; individual stipes ~3–8 cm long and ~1–3 cm thick; fused masses may reach ~30–50 cm across
albatrellopsis-confluens.flesh: Flesh cream to whitish, thick and fairly soft when fresh, becoming firm or hard when dry; often developing pale pink, salmon or brick-red tones on drying
albatrellopsis-confluens.chemical-reactions: KOH Purple on cap, pore surface and flesh
albatrellopsis-confluens.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, weakly amyloid, ~4–5.5 × 2.5–4 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate; cystidia absent; hyphal system monomitic with frequent clamp connections and scattered gloeoplerous hyphae

albatrellus-ovinus.hymenium: Pores, small and round (≈2–5/mm), white to creamy or pale yellow; pores may become slightly angular near stipe
albatrellus-ovinus.cap: Convex to flat or shallowly depressed, surface smooth when young, often developing areolate pattern in maturity; color white to off-white, buff with age
albatrellus-ovinus.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent pores (pores extend down the stipe)
albatrellus-ovinus.stipe: Central or slightly off-center, color whitish to tan; smooth to faintly velvety; may be stout or thick
albatrellus-ovinus.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers, terrestrial, occurs in clusters, august to october
albatrellus-ovinus.edibility: Edible (young, properly cooked), slimy or laxative effect reported
albatrellus-ovinus.fruit-body: Fruit body large, stipe 3–10 cm long, 1–4 cm thick
albatrellus-ovinus.flesh: Cut surface slowly turns yellowish, then greenish, then turns gray
albatrellus-ovinus.chemical-reactions: Flesh turns dirty golden yellow with KOH application
albatrellus-ovinus.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, ~4.0–5.0×2.5–3.5µm, inamyloid, often with a germ pore, no clamp connections

amanita-citrina.hymenium: Gills white to faintly cream or citrine-tinged, crowded, with numerous shorter lamellulae
amanita-citrina.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to almost flat; pale lemon-yellow, citrine, straw-yellow to nearly white; usually carrying irregular whitish to ochraceous universal-veil patches or warts; margin generally non-striate
amanita-citrina.stipe: White to pale yellowish, cylindrical and tapering upward; prominent abruptly marginate basal bulb surrounded by an adherent circumscissile volva forming a gutter-like rim; large persistent, pendulous pale ring
amanita-citrina.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods or conifers; alone, scattered, or gregariously; in forests and woodland edges; neutral to alkaline soils; summer and autumn
amanita-citrina.edibility: Inedible, potential confusion with toxic species and mild toxicity
amanita-citrina.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~5–8(–13) cm long and ~0.6–2.5 cm thick
amanita-citrina.flesh: White, sometimes faintly citrine immediately beneath the cap surface; fairly firm and unchanging when cut
amanita-citrina.microscopy: Spores globose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, approximately ~6.5–10 × 6–9 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; lamellar trama bilateral

amanita-excelsa.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, broad, with shorter lamellulae
amanita-excelsa.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to almost flat; grey-brown, olive-brown to dark brown; usually covered with irregular whitish-grey to grey universal-veil patches or warts; margin generally non-striate
amanita-excelsa.stipe: White to greyish, robust, cylindrical and tapering upward from a swollen base; smooth or striate above the ring and finely scaly below; ring broad, membranous, persistent and distinctly striate above; volva fragmented and inconspicuous, without a distinct gutter-like rim
amanita-excelsa.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; alone, scattered or gregariously; in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests and woodland edges; summer to autumn
amanita-excelsa.edibility: Edible after thorough cooking but not recommended; toxic raw and easily confused
amanita-excelsa.uses-compounds: Thermolabile hemolysins present in raw fruit bodies
amanita-excelsa.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~8–15 cm long and ~1.5–3 cm thick
amanita-excelsa.flesh: White, firm, usually unchanging when cut; occasionally faintly pinkish or reddish toward the stipe base
amanita-excelsa.odour: Faint radish-like to slightly unpleasant, sometimes indistinct
amanita-excelsa.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~8–11 × 6–8.5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; clamp connections absent at basidia

amanita-fulva.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, with shorter lamellulae
amanita-fulva.cap: Ovoid to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat with a small central umbo; tawny-orange, reddish-brown to orange-brown, usually without veil remnants; margin prominently striate
amanita-fulva.stipe: Slender, fragile, hollow, white to pale tawny, tapering upward and often finely fibrillose; ring absent; base enclosed in a large loose, sack-like white volva that may become stained tawny-brown
amanita-fulva.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers, especially birch, oak, chestnut, pine and spruce; alone, scattered or gregariously; forests and woodland paths; particularly acidic soils; summer to late autumn
amanita-fulva.edibility: Edible only after thorough cooking, but not recommended due to possible toxicity when raw and dangerous confusion
amanita-fulva.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~7–16 cm long and ~0.5–1.5 cm thick
amanita-fulva.flesh: White, soft and relatively thin; unchanging when cut
amanita-fulva.microscopy: Spores globose to subglobose, smooth, hyaline, non-amyloid, ~9–12.5 × 9–12.5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; clamp connections absent at basidia; lamellar trama bilateral

amanita-muscaria.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, with numerous shorter lamellulae
amanita-muscaria.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; bright scarlet-red; covered with loose white universal-veil warts that may wash away; margin increasingly striate at maturity
amanita-muscaria.stipe: White, cylindrical to clavate, tapering upward; basal bulb surrounded by concentric rings or scales of volval remnants; large membranous, pendulous white ring, sometimes with a yellowish margin
amanita-muscaria.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers (birch, pine and spruce); alone, scattered or gregariously; sandy or peaty soils; summer to autumn
amanita-muscaria.uses-compounds:
Used as microdosing nootrop and as folk medicine
Ibotenic acid, muscimol, muscarine
amanita-muscaria.fruit-body: Fruit body large; stipe ~8–25 cm long and ~1–2.5 cm thick
amanita-muscaria.flesh: White, with yellow to orange-yellow tissue immediately beneath the cap skin; unchanging when cut or bruised
amanita-muscaria.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8–10.5 × 6–8 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored

amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, with numerous shorter lamellulae
amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; yellow, golden-yellow to orange-yellow or tawny-orange, sometimes darker centrally; covered with yellowish to whitish universal-veil warts that may wash away; margin increasingly striate at maturity
amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.stipe: White to faintly yellowish, cylindrical to clavate, tapering upward; basal bulb surrounded by concentric rings or scales of yellowish volval remnants; large membranous, pendulous pale ring
amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers, especially beech, birch, spruce and pine; alone, scattered or gregariously; deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests; often acidic to siliceous soils; summer to autumn
amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.edibility: Poisonous and psychoactive; causes variable neurological intoxication and gastrointestinal symptoms
amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.uses-compounds:
Historically used in folk and ethnomycological practices
Ibotenic acid, muscimol, muscarine
amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~8–20 cm long and ~1–2.5 cm thick
amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.flesh: White, sometimes yellowish immediately beneath the cap skin; unchanging when cut or bruised
amanita-muscaria-var-formosa.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8–10.5 × 6–8 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; gill trama bilateral

amanita-pantherina.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, broad, with numerous shorter lamellulae
amanita-pantherina.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; ochre-brown, hazel-brown to dark brown; covered with numerous pure white to cream universal-veil warts that may wash away; margin distinctly striate at maturity
amanita-pantherina.stipe: White, cylindrical and tapering upward; base distinctly bulbous, with an adherent volva forming a characteristic collar or gutter-like rim and often one or more concentric rings above; membranous, pendulous white ring, usually smooth on its upper surface
amanita-pantherina.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with hardwoods; alone, scattered or gregariously; deciduous, mixed forests and woodland edges; summer to autumn
amanita-pantherina.edibility: Poisonous and psychoactive; severe neurological intoxication with agitation, confusion, hallucinations, ataxia, CNS depression and gastrointestinal symptoms
amanita-pantherina.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~5–15 cm long and ~0.6–3 cm thick
amanita-pantherina.flesh: White, firm, unchanging when cut or bruised; does not redden
amanita-pantherina.odour: Mild to indistinct, sometimes slightly radish-like or raw-potato-like when bruised
amanita-pantherina.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8–12 × 6–8 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; clamp connections absent at basidial bases

amanita-rubescens.hymenium: Gills white to creamy-white, crowded, with numerous shorter lamellulae; developing pinkish to reddish stains when bruised or with age
amanita-rubescens.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; highly variable, pale pinkish-brown, grey-brown, reddish-brown to dark brown; usually covered with irregular greyish-white, pinkish-grey to brownish universal-veil warts; margin generally non-striate
amanita-rubescens.stipe: White to pale pinkish, cylindrical, often slightly enlarged or bulbous at base; progressively staining pink to wine-red when damaged; volva poorly developed and usually disappearing with age; membranous, pendulous ring distinctly striate on upper surface
amanita-rubescens.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; alone, scattered or gregariously; deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests; especially frequent on acidic, nutrient-poor soils; summer to autumn
amanita-rubescens.edibility: Edible only after thorough cooking; poisonous raw, easily confused
amanita-rubescens.uses-compounds: Rubescenslysin, a thermolabile haemolytic/cytolytic protein toxin
amanita-rubescens.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~7–15 cm long and ~1–2(–3) cm thick
amanita-rubescens.flesh: White, slowly turning pale pink, wine-red to reddish when cut, bruised or damaged, especially in the stipe base and around insect tunnels
amanita-rubescens.odour: Mild, indistinct, mushroomy; sometimes unpleasant in old specimens
amanita-rubescens.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~8–10 × 5–7 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; clamp connections absent at basidial bases; lamellar trama bilateral

ampulloclitocybe-clavipes.hymenium: Gills close to moderately spaced, with frequent lamellulae; white to cream when young, becoming pale ochre to brownish with age
ampulloclitocybe-clavipes.cap: Convex to nearly flat when young, later centrally depressed to funnel-shaped; smooth to slightly rugged centrally; grey-brown, yellow-brown to dark brown, usually darker at centre and paler toward margin
ampulloclitocybe-clavipes.stipe: Short, robust, buff to pale brownish; characteristically club-shaped or bulbous at base, though sometimes nearly equal with age; base often spongy with white mycelium; ring absent
ampulloclitocybe-clavipes.ecology: Ecology uncertain, reported as saprobic or possibly mycorrhizal; primarily under conifers, sometimes hardwoods; alone, scattered or gregariously; forests, mainly heathland; summer to late autumn
ampulloclitocybe-clavipes.edibility: Edible, not recommended; alcohol may trigger a disulfiram-like reaction
ampulloclitocybe-clavipes.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~2.5–8 cm long and ~0.5–3 cm thick
ampulloclitocybe-clavipes.flesh: White, soft to spongy, unchanging when cut
ampulloclitocybe-clavipes.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid or elongated-ellipsoid, smooth to minutely ornamented, hyaline, inamyloid, ~6–10 × 3–5 µm; basidia 4-spored; occasional clavate pseudocystidia; pileipellis a cutis; clamp connections present

antherospora-scillae.hymenium: hymenium is not applicable due to the nature of the organism, which is a rust fungus
antherospora-scillae.cap: cap is not applicable, as rust fungi do not form traditional mushroom caps
antherospora-scillae.spore-print: spore print is not typically obtained, but the spores are often orangish or rust-colored
antherospora-scillae.ecology: ecology is parasitic, typically found on the leaves, stems, and bulbs of Scilla species and other host plants
antherospora-scillae.edibility: not applicable, as rust fungi are not typically considered for consumption
antherospora-scillae.fruit-body: size varies, but the fungal structures visible on the host plant are typically very small

antrodiella-serpula.hymenium: Irregular, maze-like or labyrinthine pores with a whitish to cream coloration.
antrodiella-serpula.cap: Absent or indistinct, as this species primarily forms resupinate fruiting bodies directly on the substrate.
antrodiella-serpula.hymenium-attachment: Resupinate, forming a thin, crust-like layer directly on the substrate.
antrodiella-serpula.ecology: Saprobic, primarily found on dead or decaying hardwoods, often on fallen branches or logs in forested habitats.
antrodiella-serpula.fruit-body: The fruiting bodies can vary widely in size and shape, ranging from small patches to extensive crust-like formations.
antrodiella-serpula.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoidal to cylindrical, smooth, 4-6 x 2-3 µm.

apioperdon-pyriforme.hymenium: Internal gleba is white and firm when young, turning olive-brown and powdery as it matures, filled with spores
apioperdon-pyriforme.cap: Pear-shaped to round, covered with small, fine spines or granules that wear off with age, giving the surface a smooth, pale brown to tan appearance
apioperdon-pyriforme.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Gasteroid fungi, spore mass is internal)
apioperdon-pyriforme.stipe: Pseudostipe, shorter and less defined, often off-center or absent, typically blends with the cap, leading to its pear-like shape
apioperdon-pyriforme.spore-print: Spore print olive-brown to dark brown
apioperdon-pyriforme.ecology: Saprobic, growing in dense clusters on decaying wood, especially stumps and logs of both deciduous and coniferous trees, late summer to autumn
apioperdon-pyriforme.edibility: Edible when young, but only before the gleba turns dark and powdery, not highly regarded, though safe to eat when firm and white inside
apioperdon-pyriforme.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium-sized, up to 3–5 cm tall
apioperdon-pyriforme.microscopy: Spores round, 3.5–4.5 µm, covered with fine spines or warts, produced inside gleba

armillaria-mellea.hymenium: Gills, white when young, yellow-to-cream tinged with age, spacing moderate to somewhat distant
armillaria-mellea.cap: Convex when young, flattening with age, honey-yellow to red-brown, often darker toward the center, surface smooth or slightly scaly-toward center, sticky when wet, margin may become striate or wavy
armillaria-mellea.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, tapering at base, upper portion paler, whitish, lower portion yellow-brown to reddish, has a prominent ring, base with dark black rhizomorphs and connected clumps
armillaria-mellea.ecology: Parasitic (causes root rot) and saprotrophic on dead wood, found at the base of living or dead trees, on stumps, especially hardwoods, in dense clusters
armillaria-mellea.edibility: Edible and choice, young specimens preferred, ring and caps more palatable
armillaria-mellea.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large clusters, stipe 5–17 cm long, 0.5–3 cm thick
armillaria-mellea.chemical-reactions: No widely documented dramatic color chemical reactions
armillaria-mellea.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, with a prominent apiculus, 6–9 × 4–6 µm; hyaline in KOH; basidia 2- and 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia present (25–40 × 2.5–10 µm), thin-walled, pleurocystidia absent

arrhenia-acerosa.hymenium: Gills, arising from cap margin, moderate spacing, slightly darker than cap surface.
arrhenia-acerosa.cap: Fan- or kidney-shaped, thin and sessile; smooth surface, medium grey-brown, margin incurved when young, later lobed; base attached by a fuzzy tomentum.
arrhenia-acerosa.ecology: Saprobic and bryophilous, growing on dead wood fragments, on mossy soil among twigs and debris along forest paths
arrhenia-acerosa.fruit-body: Fruit body small, up to ~15 mm across
arrhenia-acerosa.microscopy: Spores narrowly elliptical to lacrymoid, smooth, hyaline, average ~7.4×3.8µm, basidia 4-spored, 21–25×6–7µm, cystidia absent, clamps present

arrhenia-gerardiana.hymenium: Gills, smooth, typically pale gray-brown, decurrent to slightly decurrent, moderately spaced
arrhenia-gerardiana.cap: Convex to shallowly umbilicate or funnel-shaped, smooth to finely tomentose, gray to brownish-gray, often scaly at the center when fresh
arrhenia-gerardiana.stipe: Thin, cylindrical, smooth or slightly pruinose, pale gray to brownish, sometimes with whitish basal mycelium
arrhenia-gerardiana.ecology: Sphagnicolous—grows in association with Sphagnum mosses, found in bogs, wet heaths, and moss-rich coniferous substrates
arrhenia-gerardiana.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe generally 3–6 cm long, thin
arrhenia-gerardiana.microscopy: Spores subglobose to ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid, 6.8–12.4 × 3.4–5.1 µm, basidia 4-spored, ~24 × 7 µm

artomyces-pyxidatus.hymenium: Smooth, covering the outer surfaces of the branches; whitish to pale yellowish, becoming tan or faintly pinkish with age
artomyces-pyxidatus.fruit-body:
Repeatedly branched, coral- to candelabra-shaped; branch tips characteristically crown-shaped, each ending in a shallow cup surrounded by 3–6 pointed teeth
Fruit body medium; ~4–13 cm tall and ~2–10 cm wide
artomyces-pyxidatus.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the branches
artomyces-pyxidatus.stipe: Short basal trunk, whitish to pinkish-brown, finely fuzzy, repeatedly dividing into upright branches
artomyces-pyxidatus.ecology: Saprobic on well-decayed hardwood logs and fallen trunks, especially aspen, poplar, ash; solitary to clustered; summer to autumn
artomyces-pyxidatus.edibility: Young specimens reported edible, but often tough, peppery or bitter
artomyces-pyxidatus.flesh: Whitish, tough and pliable, sometimes slowly browning when bruised
artomyces-pyxidatus.chemical-reactions: FeSO₄ negative to greyish or brownish on branches and base
artomyces-pyxidatus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, minutely pitted, hyaline, amyloid, ~4–5 × 2–3 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia variably fusoid, cylindrical or clavate; gloeoplerous hyphae present; clamp connections abundant

ascocoryne-sarcoides.hymenium: Apothecial disc surface smooth, gelatinous, violet-pink to purple, underside sometimes finely fuzzy or lighter in tone
ascocoryne-sarcoides.apothecium: Begins as irregular, brain-like gelatinous lobes (anamorphic form), then becomes more cup- or disc-shaped, lobed margin
ascocoryne-sarcoides.ecology: Saprobic, growing on heavily decayed hardwood, autumn to winter, in clustered patches
ascocoryne-sarcoides.fruit-body: Apothecium size up to ~5–15 cm when clustered (discs merging)
ascocoryne-sarcoides.dimensions: Individual apothecia few mm to ~1–2 cm in diameter
ascocoryne-sarcoides.flesh: Flesh gelatinous, fleshy, violet-pink unchanging color
ascocoryne-sarcoides.microscopy: Spores fusiform/ellipsoid, hyaline, smooth, ~13–21×3.5–5 µm; biguttulate early, asci 8-spored cylinders (~115–130×8–10 µm), paraphyses filiform (~1–2 µm width)

asterophora-lycoperdoides.hymenium: Gills—thick, distant, often reduced or poorly formed, sometimes vein-like rather than clearly gilled, whitish to pale grey
asterophora-lycoperdoides.cap: Convex to nearly round, dry, initially whitish and a bit lumpy or roughened, quickly becoming covered by a dense orangish-brown chlamydospores powder
asterophora-lycoperdoides.stipe: Slender, more or less equal, surface dry, initially whitish or pale, becoming powdery orangish-brown, basal mycelium white
asterophora-lycoperdoides.ecology: Parasitic on decaying mushrooms (Russula, Lactarius spp.), appears when the host has begun to blacken and decay, singly, groups in mixed, hardwood, coniferous forests, summer through autumn
asterophora-lycoperdoides.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 4–30 mm long, ~2–5 mm thick
asterophora-lycoperdoides.chemical-reactions: No significant staining reactions noted, flesh unchanging when cut
asterophora-lycoperdoides.odour: Rotten and foul to decaying fungi substrate
asterophora-lycoperdoides.microscopy: Basidiospores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline in KOH, ~5–6 × 4–5 µm, 4-sterigmate, chlamydospores globose to subglobose, ornamented, 16–20 × 14–17 µm, hyaline to faintly yellowish

auriscalpium-vulgare.hymenium: Teeth densely crowded, cylindrical and pointed, ~1–3 mm long; whitish when young, becoming pale brown to grey-brown with age
auriscalpium-vulgare.cap: Kidney- to semicircular, broadly convex to flat; dry, finely bristly or hairy, sometimes smoother with age; reddish-brown, chestnut to nearly black, usually with a paler margin
auriscalpium-vulgare.hymenium-attachment: Fertile teeth cover the underside of the cap
auriscalpium-vulgare.stipe: Slender, tough, lateral to strongly eccentric; reddish-brown to dark brown, densely hairy; often arising directly from a buried cone
auriscalpium-vulgare.ecology: Saprobic primarily on fallen and often partly buried pine cones, occasionally other conifer cones and litter; solitary or scattered; coniferous and mixed forests; summer to late autumn
auriscalpium-vulgare.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2–7 cm long and up to ~0.3 cm thick
auriscalpium-vulgare.flesh: Whitish to brownish, thin, fibrous and tough, unchanging when cut
auriscalpium-vulgare.chemical-reactions: KOH instantly black on cap and stipe
auriscalpium-vulgare.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, finely warted to minutely spiny at maturity, hyaline, amyloid, ~4–6 × 3.5–5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia fusoid, clamp connections present

badhamia-utricularis.plasmodium-color: Often yellowish, turning brown with age
badhamia-utricularis.ecology: Habitat: Decaying wood, leaves, and organic material
badhamia-utricularis.description: Lifecycle stages: Amoeba → multicellular slug → sporulating fruit body

baeospora-myosura.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, white to pale cream when young, becoming yellowish or slightly brownish with age
baeospora-myosura.cap: Initially convex, flattening with age, surface smooth and dry, pale tan to light brown, sometimes slightly translucent-striate near the edges
baeospora-myosura.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, usually with a finely fibrillose surface, cream to pale tan, slightly darker towards the base, no ring or veil
baeospora-myosura.description: Saprobic, primarily on decaying conifer cones, especially those of pine and spruce, found in clusters or groups, late autumn
baeospora-myosura.edibility: Inedible, due to small size and insubstantial flesh
baeospora-myosura.fruit-body: Fruit body small, delicate structure, stipe 1.5-5 cm long and 1-2 mm thick
baeospora-myosura.chemical-reactions: KOH negative or faintly olive on cap surface
baeospora-myosura.microscopy: Spores elliptical to nearly cylindric, smooth, amyloid, 3-4.5 x 1.5-2 µm, basidia 4-spored

bjerkandera-adusta.hymenium: Pores, small and angular (≈5–7 / mm), initially greyish, aging to dark grey or black, forming the undersurface of the bracket
bjerkandera-adusta.cap: Bracket- or shelf-like, sometimes effused-reflexed, upper surface velvety, pale buff, tan to greyish, often zoned, margin whitish when young
bjerkandera-adusta.ecology:
Saprobic (weakly parasitic) on dead hardwoods, causing white-rot of fallen logs, stumps, autumn to winter (year-round)
Inedible - tough, leathery
bjerkandera-adusta.flesh: Flesh whitish to buff, leathery-corky, no color change
bjerkandera-adusta.microscopy: Spores roughly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, ~4–6×2.5–3.5 µm, clamp-connections, no cystidia

bjerkandera-fumosa.hymenium: Pores, angular to slightly irregular, ≈2–5/mm, color buff to pale smoky-gray when young, later darker, surface clearly separated from tissue by a darker line
bjerkandera-fumosa.bracket: Sessile, often effused-reflexed, buff to pale ochre or smoky-buff above, surface finely tomentose, zoned, margin thin
bjerkandera-fumosa.ecology:
Saprobic, causing white rot in hardwoods, dead or decaying broadleaf wood (logs, stump), year-round
Inedible - tough, leathery
bjerkandera-fumosa.flesh: Flesh buff to pale, tough, cork-like
bjerkandera-fumosa.microscopy: Spores smooth, short-cylindrical to ellipsoid, hyaline, ~5.5–7×2.5–3.5 µm, basidia club-shaped, ~20–22 µm long

boletus-edulis.hymenium: Pores—small, rounded, whitish when young, aging to greenish-yellow or olive tones
boletus-edulis.cap: Convex when young, flattening with age, smooth to slightly velvety or slightly sticky when moist, color ranges from light tan to reddish-brown
boletus-edulis.stipe: Solid, robust, cylindrical to slightly clubbed, whitish to pale cream with a fine reticulate pattern, especially near the apex
boletus-edulis.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers and deciduous trees (pines, spruces, oaks, beeches) in forest or mixed settings, fruits in summer to autumn
boletus-edulis.edibility: Choice edible, highly prized for flavor and texture
boletus-edulis.fruit-body: Fruit body large, stipe 8–20 x ~10 cm
boletus-edulis.flesh: Flesh is white and unchanging when cut, no blue staining
boletus-edulis.chemical-reactions: KOH reaction: dull orange color change on the flesh, cap surface remains negative
boletus-edulis.microscopy: Spores subfusiform (ellipsoid to spindle-shaped), smooth, ~14–17×5–7µm, basidia predominantly 4-sterigmate.

boletus-pinophilus.cap: 8-25 cm in diameter. Convex to broadly convex, sometimes flat in older specimens. The surface is velvety to slightly sticky, deep brown to reddish-brown.
boletus-pinophilus.hymenium: Tubular or poroid. Pores are initially small and red but become yellowish and larger with age, often staining blue when bruised.
boletus-pinophilus.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly descending on the stipe.
boletus-pinophilus.stipe: Stout and cylindrical, often swollen or bulbous. Yellowish at the top, reddening downwards, and covered with a fine, mesh-like network (reticulate).
boletus-pinophilus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, mainly associated with pine (Pinus) but can also be found with spruce (Picea) and other conifers.

botryobasidium-candicans.hymenium: Smooth, waxy, thin layer that forms a continuous, web-like surface over the substrate, white to cream-colored when fresh to pale yellow
botryobasidium-candicans.cap: (Forms a resupinate, crust-like layer directly on substrate)
botryobasidium-candicans.hymenium-attachment: (The hymenium forms directly on the surface of the substrate without a cap)
botryobasidium-candicans.ecology: Saprobic, decomposing dead wood and plant material, found on birch branches, fallen logs, in all seasons
botryobasidium-candicans.edibility: Inedible, lacking substantial flesh and considered insignificant for culinary use
botryobasidium-candicans.fruit-body: Fruit body crust-like, spreading irregularly, forming patches up to 1–20 cm across, with a thickness of only 0.1–0.5 mm
botryobasidium-candicans.chemical-reactions: Yellowish tint and occuring on birch (Betula sp) dead wood
botryobasidium-candicans.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thin-walled, 6–10 x 2.5–4 µm, hyaline in KOH, basidia 4-spored and clavate

britzelmayria-multipedata.hymenium: Gills, initially pale grey-brown with white edges, later darkening to deep brown
britzelmayria-multipedata.cap: Conical to convex, later bell-shaped but not completely flat, smooth, silky when moist, hygrophanous, colors from reddish-clay-brown when wet to pale ochre when dry, darker center
britzelmayria-multipedata.stipe: Slender and hollow; white to pale, often fused at the base in clusters; stems may be wavy, tapering slightly upward
britzelmayria-multipedata.ecology: Saprobic, growing in dense tufts on soil, leaf litter, buried or decayed hardwoodin grassy, woodland or edge habitats, from summer to autumn
britzelmayria-multipedata.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stems 7–12 cm long, many stems clustered together
britzelmayria-multipedata.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, with a germ pore, ~6.5–10×3.5–4 µm, basidia 4-sterigmate, with clamp connections

butyriboletus-fechtneri.hymenium: Pores, pale yellow to lemon-yellow when young, turning olive-yellow as mature, pores bruise blue when handled
butyriboletus-fechtneri.cap: Initially convex, becoming broadly convex to nearly flat with age, surface is smooth and slightly sticky when moist, typically silvery-grey to pale greyish-brown
butyriboletus-fechtneri.stipe: Cylindrical to clavate, pale yellow, often with a reddish flush near the base, surface is typically smooth, sometimes exhibit slight reticulation near the apex
butyriboletus-fechtneri.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with oak and beech, grows in calcareous soils, in mixed forests, appearing from late spring to autumn
butyriboletus-fechtneri.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 12 cm tall
butyriboletus-fechtneri.odour: Odour: Mild, pleasant with a slight nutty aroma
butyriboletus-fechtneri.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, 12–16 x 5–6.5 µm, smooth, inamyloid, basidia four-spored

caloboletus-radicans.hymenium: Pores small, rounded, lemon-yellow when young, later to olive-yellow, rapidly bruising blue when touched
caloboletus-radicans.cap: Hemispherical to convex, later broadly convex; pale buff, ivory, greyish-whitish-brown; dry, finely downy when young, cracked or uneven with age
caloboletus-radicans.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to adnexed, sometimes slightly depressed around the stipe
caloboletus-radicans.stipe: Stout, swollen to barrel-shaped when young, later elongated and rooting/tapering at base; yellow near apex, paler to brownish below; fine pale reticulation near the upper part
caloboletus-radicans.spore-print: Spore print: Olive-brown to olivaceous walnut-brown
caloboletus-radicans.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with broadleaved trees: oak, beech, hornbeam, chestnut and lime; woodland, parks and calcareous or base-rich soils; summer to early autumn
caloboletus-radicans.edibility: Strongly inedible, extremely bitter, causes severe gastrointestinal symptoms
caloboletus-radicans.fruit-body: Fruit body: Large and robust; stipe ~5–10 cm long, ~3–5 cm thick
caloboletus-radicans.flesh: Flesh pale yellow to whitish, rapidly turning blue when cut or bruised
caloboletus-radicans.chemical-reactions: KOH orange on flesh; red-brown on cap
caloboletus-radicans.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, smooth, ~11.5–14 × 4–5.5 µm; pileipellis a trichodermium of interwoven septate, finely incrusted hyphae

calocera-viscosa.cap: 0.5-2 cm across. Initially convex, becoming more irregular and lobed, often elongated, bright yellow to orange-yellow, gelatinous in texture, sometimes forked at the tip.
calocera-viscosa.hymenium: No true gills or pores, but a smooth, gelatinous surface.
calocera-viscosa.stipe: Tapered, gelatinous, bright yellow, and often forked or branched.
calocera-viscosa.ecology: Saprobic; growing on coniferous wood, especially on fallen logs and stumps.
calocera-viscosa.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical, smooth, 9-11 x 3-3.5 µm.

calocybe-gambosa.cap: convex to flat with age, smooth surface, color ranging from white to yellowish or pale ochre, margin often inrolled when young
calocybe-gambosa.stipe: Stout, white to yellowish, sometimes slightly bulbous at the base, surface smooth, lacking a ring
calocybe-gambosa.ecology: Ecology saprotrophic, occasionally mycorrhizal, grasslands, meadows, roadside verges, woodlands, calcareous soils, fairy rings, may till june
calocybe-gambosa.edibility: Choice edible, highly prized in various European cuisines, traditionally consumed sautéed or in omelettes
calocybe-gambosa.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe 3–10 cm long and 1–4 cm thick
calocybe-gambosa.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 4–7 × 2–3.5 µm, inamyloid

calvatia-gigantea.hymenium: Internal, forming the gleba, initially white and firm, becoming yellowish-green to olive-brown as spores mature
calvatia-gigantea.cap: No distinct cap, the fruiting body is a large, smooth, rounded, or irregularly shaped puffball, with a leathery outer skin that cracks and flakes as it ages
calvatia-gigantea.stipe: Lacking, the fruiting body is sessile or attached to the ground by a small base of mycelial threads
calvatia-gigantea.description: Saprobic found in nutrient-rich soils, meadows, fields, and open woodlands, often in grass or alongside paths, late summer to autumn
calvatia-gigantea.edibility: Edible only when the gleba is firm and pure white, mature specimens are inedible
calvatia-gigantea.fruit-body: Fruit body large, typically 10–50 cm in diameter, may exceed 70 cm
calvatia-gigantea.odour: Odour mild and pleasant when young, unpleasant and musty when mature
calvatia-gigantea.taste: Taste mild when young, unpleasant when mature
calvatia-gigantea.microscopy: Spores subglobose to globose, 2.5–4 µm, with or without a short pedicel, smooth, thick-walled, hyaline to yellowish in KOH

calycina-citrina.hymenium: Smooth, forms the inner surface of the apothecium, bright yellow to lemon-yellow
calycina-citrina.cap: Cup- or disc-shaped, often shallow, lemon-yellow, smooth, and slightly translucent when fresh
calycina-citrina.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Hymenium forms the internal surface of the cup)
calycina-citrina.stipe: With or without a tiny, tapering pseudostem;
calycina-citrina.ecology: Saprobic, grows on decaying wood, twigs, in moist, shaded environments, found in large groups, during autumn
calycina-citrina.edibility: Inedible due to its tiny size and insubstantial flesh
calycina-citrina.fruit-body: Fruit body very small, with or without a tiny, tapering pseudostem
calycina-citrina.microscopy: Spores elongated-ellipsoid, smooth, sometimes becoming 1–2-septate, often biguttulate, hyaline in KOH, 12–16 x 3.5–5 µm, asci 120–175 x 5–8 µm, 8-spored

candolleomyces-candolleanus.hymenium: Gills are initially pale but become purplish-brown to almost black as the spores mature. They are crowded and often have a slightly jagged edge.
candolleomyces-candolleanus.cap: conic to convex or flat, often with a slightly upturned, ragged edge when mature. It's thin-fleshed, hygrophanous, and can be pale brown when moist, drying to a lighter color, almost straw-yellow or pale grayish.
candolleomyces-candolleanus.stipe: Slender, pale at the top, becoming brownish towards the base, with a annulus which can be lost in age.
candolleomyces-candolleanus.ecology: Saprobic/ Sometimes growing in groups or clusters, especially in places where wood chippings have been applied.
candolleomyces-candolleanus.edibility: Edible, but not highly regarded due to its insubstantial nature.
candolleomyces-candolleanus.fruit-body: Fruit body: Up to 8 cm tall.

cantharellopsis-prescotii.hymenium: Folded, irregular gill-like ridges—intermediate between chanterelles and typical gills
cantharellopsis-prescotii.cap: No distinct cap, tan to whitish, surface resembling an omphalinoid or chanterelle form
cantharellopsis-prescotii.stipe: Present but slender, not prominently differentiated from cap-like structure
cantharellopsis-prescotii.ecology: Ecology, bryophilous—grows among mosses on calcareous soils, summer-autumn
cantharellopsis-prescotii.description:
Rare and too small to eat
Red list fungi
cantharellopsis-prescotii.fruit-body: Fruit body small, 0.7-1.5 cm, stipe 1.0 x 0.1-0.2 cm
cantharellopsis-prescotii.microscopy: Spores smooth, inamyloid, 4.5-6(-6.5) x 2.5-4 µm, no cystidia

cantharellula-umbonata.hymenium: Gills, frequently forked, white when young
cantharellula-umbonata.cap: Convex to flat with a small bump, surface grayish, minutely tomentose, radially wrinkled or slightly striate, margin incurved when young and becoming wavy
cantharellula-umbonata.stipe: Slender, often equal or slightly tapering, color similar to cap, sometimes moist, base with moss/mycelial attachment
cantharellula-umbonata.ecology: Saprotrophic, bryophilous (Polytrichum and other mosses), under conifers, heathlands, acidic soils, summer and autumn
cantharellula-umbonata.edibility: Edible (especially when young), not highly prized
cantharellula-umbonata.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 2.5–12.5 cm long, 0.3–0.7 cm thick
cantharellula-umbonata.flesh: Flesh is white, when bruised, flesh and gills may stain reddish
cantharellula-umbonata.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid-to-elongate, smooth, ~6–10×3–5µm, amyloid in iodine, absence of cystidia is typical, no cheilocystidia or pleurocystidia

cantharellus-cibarius.hymenium: False gills / thick forked ridges, not true lamellae; blunt, wrinkled, strongly decurrent, yellow to pale yellow
cantharellus-cibarius.cap: Convex to flat, later shallowly funnel-shaped; margin wavy and irregular; smooth, egg-yolk yellow to golden-yellow
cantharellus-cibarius.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent — ridges run down the stipe
cantharellus-cibarius.stipe: Solid, smooth, fleshy, same colour as or slightly paler than cap, merging gradually into the cap
cantharellus-cibarius.spore-print: Spore print pale yellow to creamy white, sometimes faintly pinkish
cantharellus-cibarius.ecology: Ecology ectomycorrhizal with broadleaved and coniferous trees, especially oak, chestnut, hazel and conifers; woodland soils, often acid; summer to autumn
cantharellus-cibarius.edibility: Edibility choice edible, highly prized for flavour and texture
cantharellus-cibarius.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; usually ~3–10 cm tall
cantharellus-cibarius.flesh: Flesh firm, pale yellowish-white, fibrous, unchanging when cut
cantharellus-cibarius.chemical-reactions: No distinctive macroscopic reaction; spores hyaline in KOH
cantharellus-cibarius.odour: Odour fruity, apricot-like, sometimes faint when fresh
cantharellus-cibarius.taste: Taste mild, pleasant, not strongly distinctive raw
cantharellus-cibarius.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~7–11 × 4–6 µm; basidia typically 4–6-spored, hymenium formed on blunt ridges rather than true gills

ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.plasmodium-phase: Watery, translucent to whitish, sometimes faintly yellowish or pinkish
ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.fruiting-bodies: Dense colonies of erect, simple to repeatedly branched, finger- or coral-shaped columns; gelatinous and translucent at first, later white, cream or pale yellow
ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.peridium: The spores are produced openly on the outer surface rather than enclosed within a sporangium
ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.attachment: Macroscopic columns sessile on a confluent, mucilaginous hypothallus; each individual spore supported by a delicate microscopic pedicel
ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.description:
Spore mass white to pale yellow
Amoeboflagellate cells → multinucleate plasmodium → coral-like sporophores bearing external stalked spores → spores germinate to release amoeboid or flagellated cells
ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.ecology: On moist, heavily decayed logs, stumps, branches and other plant debris, often appearing in extensive clustered sheets after rain; late spring to autumn
ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.edibility: Tiny, gelatinous slime mould with no culinary value
ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.fruit-body: Individual columns approximately 1–10 mm tall and ~0.2–1 mm wide; colonies may spread across many centimetres of decaying wood
ceratiomyxa-fruticulosa.microscopy: Spores smooth, thin-walled, hyaline to very pale yellow, globose, ovoid or ellipsoid, approximately 6–8 × 10–13 µm; borne individually on slender pedicels about 7–20 µm long; true capillitium absent

cerioporus-squamosus.hymenium: hymenium is poroid, cream to yellowish in color
cerioporus-squamosus.cap: cap is semicircular or fan-shaped, with dark brown scales on a lighter background, becoming more convex with age
cerioporus-squamosus.hymenium-attachment: hymenium attachment is not applicable as it grows directly out of the wood
cerioporus-squamosus.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic or parasitic, found on deciduous trees, especially willows and poplars
cerioporus-squamosus.edibility: edibility: edible when young, but older specimens can be tough and have a strong flavor

cerioporus-varius.hymenium: Pores angular, whitish to pale grey when young, becoming dingy brownish with age; sometimes bruising faintly brown; approximately 3–5 pores per mm
cerioporus-varius.cap: Plane-convex to flat, later centrally depressed with an uplifted margin; round to kidney-shaped; dry, smooth or finely radially fibrillose; dull yellow to pale tan, often radially streaked
cerioporus-varius.stipe: Central, eccentric or lateral, short and tough; pale near apex, becoming dark brown to black and finely velvety from the base upward
cerioporus-varius.ecology:
Saprobic, causing white rot on decaying hardwood sticks, fallen branches and small barkless logs; solitary or scattered; late spring to autumn
Inedible, too tough, leathery and woody
cerioporus-varius.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~1–3 cm long and ~0.2–0.7 cm thick
cerioporus-varius.flesh: Flesh whitish to dull yellowish, thin, very tough
cerioporus-varius.chemical-reactions: KOH brownish-orange on cap surface and flesh
cerioporus-varius.microscopy: Spores cylindrical, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~6–10 × 2–3 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate; true cystidia absent, lageniform cystidioles present; hyphal system dimitic with clamped generative hyphae and thick-walled skeletal hyphae

chamaemyces-fracidus.hymenium: A membranous, gill-like palisade of hyphae (~20 × 3–5 µm), lacking a true subhymenium
chamaemyces-fracidus.cap: Convex to flattened, thin and delicate, smooth, pale yellowish straw-colored, developing dark spots when dry
chamaemyces-fracidus.hymenium-attachment: Marginal (forms the underside edge of the cap)
chamaemyces-fracidus.stipe: Cylindrical, smooth to slightly fibrillose, paler than cap, tapering slightly toward base; basal white mycelium present
chamaemyces-fracidus.ecology: Ecology humus saprotrophic, nutrient-rich or calcareous soils, forests, woodlands, and pastures, along forest tracks and grassy margins, early summer to autumn
chamaemyces-fracidus.description:
Rare red list mushroom!!
Covered in dew-like orange droplets
chamaemyces-fracidus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium stipe 3–4 cm long, 7–10 mm thick
chamaemyces-fracidus.microscopy: Spores ovoid, smooth, 4–5 × 4 µm; binucleate, inamyloid; basidia 18–26 × 5–7.5 µm, 4-spored

chlorociboria-aeruginascens.hymenium: Smooth, exposed on the inner surface of the apothecium, bright blue-green to turquoise in color
chlorociboria-aeruginascens.cap: Small, cup-shaped to disc-like, thin and delicate, typically bright blue-green
chlorociboria-aeruginascens.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Forms the inner surface of the cup)
chlorociboria-aeruginascens.stipe: Short, slender, bluish-green, sometimes absent or very reduced
chlorociboria-aeruginascens.spore-print: Spore print white (microscopic spore mass on the substrate)
chlorociboria-aeruginascens.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood, especially hardwoods, causing a characteristic blue-green stain in the wood, found throughout the year
chlorociboria-aeruginascens.edibility: Inedible due to its small size and insignificant flesh
chlorociboria-aeruginascens.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe up to 1-2 mm long when present
chlorociboria-aeruginascens.microscopy: Spores subfusiform to nearly cylindric, smooth, 6-8 x 1-2 µ, biguttulate with a small oil droplet near each end

chroogomphus-rutilus.hymenium: Gills widely spaced, and have a waxy texture. Initially, the gills are pale greyish, becoming darker with age and developing dark brown to blackish spots
chroogomphus-rutilus.cap: convex when young, later flattening, and sometimes developing a central depression, surface is smooth, slimy when wet, and shiny when dry, with a coppery color, with purplish tinges
chroogomphus-rutilus.stipe: cylindrical, often slightly tapering towards the base, and concolorous with the cap, solid at first but becomes hollow with age, with a sticky surface when moist
chroogomphus-rutilus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines, found in sandy, acidic soils in pine forests, late summer to autumn
chroogomphus-rutilus.edibility: Edible but not highly regarded due to its slimy texture and somewhat bland taste
chroogomphus-rutilus.fruit-body: Fruit Body: 6–12 cm tall, stipe 4–12 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
chroogomphus-rutilus.microscopy: Spores smooth, elongated, fusiform, 17–22 x 6–7 µm, basidia tetrasporic, cystidia present on the gill edges, hyphal system monomitic

ciboria-amentacea.hymenium: Cup-shaped, often irregular, with a smooth or finely wrinkled inner surface. Typically orange to reddish-brown in color.
ciboria-amentacea.cap: Cup-shaped, with a smooth or finely hairy surface. Colors vary from orange to brown.
ciboria-amentacea.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable, as this species forms cup-shaped fruiting bodies.
ciboria-amentacea.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, not distinct from the cap.
ciboria-amentacea.description: Saprobic, commonly found on catkins (amenta) of various deciduous trees, particularly alders.
ciboria-amentacea.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to oblong, smooth, 7-10 x 4-6 µm.

ciboria-amentacea-f-alba.hymenium: Cup-shaped, often irregular, with a smooth or finely wrinkled inner surface. Typically orange to reddish-brown in color.
ciboria-amentacea-f-alba.cap: Cup-shaped, with a smooth or finely hairy surface. Colors vary from orange to brown.
ciboria-amentacea-f-alba.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable, as this species forms cup-shaped fruiting bodies.
ciboria-amentacea-f-alba.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, not distinct from the cap.
ciboria-amentacea-f-alba.description: Saprobic, commonly found on catkins (amenta) of various deciduous trees, particularly alders.
ciboria-amentacea-f-alba.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to oblong, smooth, 7-10 x 4-6 µm.

clavaria-fragilis.hymenium: Smooth, covering most of the outer club surface; short basal portion sterile
clavaria-fragilis.fruit-body:
Slender, cylindrical to narrowly club-shaped, usually unbranched, straight to wavy and sometimes slightly flattened or longitudinally grooved; pure white to cream, tips becoming pale yellow then brownish with age
Fruit body small to medium; individual clubs ~2–12(–15) cm tall and ~3–5(–7) mm thick
clavaria-fragilis.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the club
clavaria-fragilis.stipe: Indistinct; short, slightly narrowed, often translucent sterile basal zone
clavaria-fragilis.description:
Saprobic on soil in unimproved grasslands, meadows, mossy lawns, woodland edges and clearings, occasionally leaf litter; usually densely tufted; summer to late autumn
Insubstantial for food
clavaria-fragilis.flesh: White, very thin, soft and extremely brittle
clavaria-fragilis.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to pip-shaped, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–7 × 3–4 µm; basidia clavate, 4-spored, ~30–50 × 6–8 µm; cystidia absent; hyphae monomitic, thin-walled, without clamp connections

clavariadelphus-ligula.hymenium: Club-shaped fruit bodies, with a smooth, even hymenium covering the entire exterior surface.
clavariadelphus-ligula.cap: Absent, as the mushroom is club-shaped and lacks a distinctive cap.
clavariadelphus-ligula.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable due to the club-shaped structure of the fruit body.
clavariadelphus-ligula.stipe: Typically not differentiated from the main club-like structure, although the base may be somewhat tapered.
clavariadelphus-ligula.ecology: Saprobic, decaying coniferous wood debris in forested areas.
clavariadelphus-ligula.edibility: Edible, but not highly sought after for culinary use due to its slightly bitter flavor.
clavariadelphus-ligula.fruit-body: Up to 10 cm tall and 1-2 cm in diameter.
clavariadelphus-ligula.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid,  7-10 x 4-6 µm, smooth, and hyaline.

claviceps-purpurea.hymenium: (Ascomycete fungi with perithecia embedded in the stroma)
claviceps-purpurea.cap: Forms sclerotia instead of a cap)
claviceps-purpurea.description:
Ascospores produced in perithecia; conidia produced in honeydew stage.
Odour not applicable
claviceps-purpurea.ecology: Parasitic on grasses, particularly rye and other cereals; produces sclerotia that replace grains.
claviceps-purpurea.microscopy: Ascospores are filiform (thread-like), 50-70 x 1-2 μm; conidia produced in the honeydew stage are ellipsoid to cylindrical.

clavulina-cinerea.hymenium: Smooth, covering the entire surface of the upright, amphigenous branches
clavulina-cinerea.cap: No distinct cap; fruit body consists of intricately branched, upright coral structures, tips blunt or pointed, surface is smooth to slightly wrinkled, dull lilac‑grey to pale or dark grey, sometimes with brownish tones
clavulina-cinerea.stipe: Absent or very rudimentary; branches arise from a short base
clavulina-cinerea.ecology: Ecology ectomycorrhizal, found on soil under mixed woodlands—deciduous trees, summer to autumn
clavulina-cinerea.edibility: Occasionally consumed raw or preserved in oil
clavulina-cinerea.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, 2–8 cm tall, 2–6 cm wide
clavulina-cinerea.chemical-reactions: May turn green with FeSO₄ on branch surface, KOH reaction negative
clavulina-cinerea.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, thin-walled, non-amyloid, 7–10.5 × 5.5–9 µm; basidia 2-spored

clavulina-coralloides.hymenium: Smooth, covering most of the outer branch surface; white to cream
clavulina-coralloides.fruit-body:
Coral-like, repeatedly branched; white to cream, sometimes faintly grey, buff or pinkish; branch tips characteristically flattened and divided into several sharp, comb-like or crown-like points
Fruit body small to medium; ~2–8 cm tall and up to ~3–8 cm wide
clavulina-coralloides.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the branches
clavulina-coralloides.stipe: Short basal trunk, whitish to greyish, sometimes indistinct; branches often fused near base
clavulina-coralloides.spore-print: Spore print white to pale yellowish
clavulina-coralloides.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; on soil among litter and humus, occasionally appearing from strongly decayed wood; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
clavulina-coralloides.edibility: Edible but poor culinary value; thin, brittle and insubstantial
clavulina-coralloides.flesh: Whitish, brittle to slightly tough, unchanging when cut
clavulina-coralloides.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, ~7–11 × 6–10 µm; basidia predominantly 2-spored; cystidia absent; clamp connections present

clavulinopsis-laeticolor.hymenium: Smooth, covering most of the outer club surface; yellow-orange to orange
clavulinopsis-laeticolor.fruit-body:
Slender, cylindrical to narrowly club-shaped, unbranched; straight to slightly curved, sometimes flattened or grooved; apex rounded, spatulate or occasionally pointed; yellow-orange to orange, paler toward base
Fruit body small; ~2–5(–6) cm tall and ~1.5–4 mm thick
clavulinopsis-laeticolor.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the club
clavulinopsis-laeticolor.stipe: Indistinct; base narrowed, whitish to pale yellow, sometimes with white basal mycelium
clavulinopsis-laeticolor.description:
Saprobic on soil, moss, humus and leaf litter; unimproved grasslands, meadows, heathland, woodland edges; solitary, scattered or in small clusters; summer to late autumn
Insubstantial
clavulinopsis-laeticolor.flesh: Pale yellow to orange, thin and pliant, unchanging when cut
clavulinopsis-laeticolor.chemical-reactions: KOH yellow-green to green on flesh; FeSO₄ dingy greenish on hymenium
clavulinopsis-laeticolor.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose or pyriform, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–8 × 3.5–5.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent; clamp connections present

climacodon-septentrionalis.hymenium: Spines, densely packed, up to 10 mm long, initially white, becoming cream to yellowish as they age
climacodon-septentrionalis.cap: Overlapping, shelf-like to semicircular, with a rough, warty, or lumpy surface, color ranges from white to cream, becoming yellowish with age, margin is wavy and irregular
climacodon-septentrionalis.hymenium-attachment: N/A (spines on the underside of the cap)
climacodon-septentrionalis.ecology:
Parasitic and saprobic, found on living or dead hardwood trees, particularly beech and maple, causes a white rot in the heartwood of its host trees, fruits from late summer to autumn
Inedible, the fruit bodies are tough and woody
climacodon-septentrionalis.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 40 cm in diameter
climacodon-septentrionalis.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, 5–7 x 4–5 µm, smooth, inamyloid.

clitocybe-fragrans.hymenium: Gills moderately crowded, cream to pale beige or faintly pinkish
clitocybe-fragrans.cap: Convex when young, later flat to shallowly depressed or funnel-shaped; smooth, hygrophanous; beige to pale buff when moist, almost white when dry; margin translucently striate
clitocybe-fragrans.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, smooth to slightly fibrillose; cream, pale buff; base with white mycelial tomentum; ring absent
clitocybe-fragrans.spore-print: Spore print pale cream, sometimes faintly orange-cream
clitocybe-fragrans.ecology: Saprobic among leaf litter, moss and humus in deciduous, mixed and coniferous forests, hedgerows, parkland and grasslands; solitary or in small groups; late summer to autumn
clitocybe-fragrans.edibility: Not recommended; edibility disputed and easily confused with toxic species
clitocybe-fragrans.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2.5–6.5 cm long and ~0.2–0.5 cm thick
clitocybe-fragrans.flesh: Whitish to pale cream, thin and fragile, unchanging when cut
clitocybe-fragrans.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~6.5–9 × 3.5–5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis; clamp connections present

clitocybe-nebularis.hymenium: Gills, crowded, pale cream to light grayish-buff
clitocybe-nebularis.cap: Convex when young, becoming broadly convex to flat with a slight depression in the center, surface smooth, moist to greasy, grayish-brown to smoky-gray, with a frosted or nebulous appearance
clitocybe-nebularis.stipe: Stout, cylindrical, slightly bulbous at the base, smooth or slightly fibrillose, whitish to pale gray, with a mealy coating near the apex
clitocybe-nebularis.spore-print: Spore print whitish in a thin print, but pale yellowish in thick prints
clitocybe-nebularis.ecology: Saprobic, growing in leaf litter in deciduous and coniferous woodlands, often in dense clusters, late summer to late autumn
clitocybe-nebularis.edibility: Edible when cooked, but causes digestive upset in some individuals
clitocybe-nebularis.fruit-body: Fruit body large, stipe 5–12 cm long, 1–3 cm thick
clitocybe-nebularis.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, 5–7 × 3.5–4.5 µm, basidia 4-spored, 30–40 × 5–7 µm

clitocybe-phyllophila.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially white to cream, ageing to ochre-buff or faint buff tones
clitocybe-phyllophila.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming shallowly funnel-shaped; surface smooth, whitish with a fine frosted bloom when young, developing buff spots with age
clitocybe-phyllophila.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly tapering, smooth, whitish, no ring, base often with white mycelial tomentum
clitocybe-phyllophila.spore-print: Spore print pale pink-ish ochraceous or white to very pale buff
clitocybe-phyllophila.ecology: Saprobic on leaf- and needle-litter and soil in coniferous woodland, under trees, novemeber - december
clitocybe-phyllophila.flesh: Flesh white to pale, firmish; unchanging when cut
clitocybe-phyllophila.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, ~4–5.5×3–4µm, basidia 4-spored; hyphae with clamp connections

clitocybe-rivulosa.hymenium: Gills are closely spaced, white to cream, becoming buff-colored with age.
clitocybe-rivulosa.cap: 3-6 cm in diameter. Convex, later becoming flat or slightly depressed; creamy-white to buff, often with darker center.
clitocybe-rivulosa.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to emarginate or slightly decurrent.
clitocybe-rivulosa.stipe: Cylindrical, smooth, and white, often with a somewhat swollen base.
clitocybe-rivulosa.description: Saprobic; often found in grassy areas, parks, and gardens; occasionally in woodlands.
clitocybe-rivulosa.edibility: Toxic; contains muscarine, which can cause severe poisoning.
clitocybe-rivulosa.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, and non-amyloid.

clitopilus-prunulus.hymenium: Gills, white when young, turning pinkish with age as spores mature, gills are decurrent and crowded
clitopilus-prunulus.cap: Convex to flat or slightly depressed in the center, often irregularly shaped, surface is smooth, dry, and finely velvety, color ranges from white to pale grey or greyish-brown
clitopilus-prunulus.stipe: Cylindrical or slightly tapered towards the base, white, smooth, and often curved, stipe is firm but may become hollow with age
clitopilus-prunulus.description: Saprobic; found growing alone or in groups on leaf litter or moss in deciduous and mixed forests, often under beech, oak
clitopilus-prunulus.odour: Odour is distinctive mealy or flour-like smell
clitopilus-prunulus.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid to cylindrical, 9–12 × 5–6.5 μm, with characteristic longitudinal ridges. The basidia are four-spored and clavate. Pileipellis consists of cutis with thin-walled, hyaline hyphae

collybia-cirrhata.hymenium: Gills, relatively crowded, white to cream in color, becoming slightly yellowish or brownish with age
collybia-cirrhata.cap: convex to flat when mature, sometimes with a small central depression, surface is smooth, often translucent-striate, colored white to cream, margin is initially incurved, becoming wavy with age
collybia-cirrhata.stipe: thin, and thread-like, color is white to pale yellow, surface is smooth, slightly translucent
collybia-cirrhata.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decayed remains of old fruit bodies of Russula or Lactarius spp, damp, decaying litter in deciduous and coniferous forests, late summer to autumn
collybia-cirrhata.edibility: Inedible, insubstantial to be of culinary interest
collybia-cirrhata.fruit-body: Fruit Body: 1–4 cm tall, stipe 1–3 cm long, 0.5–1 mm thick
collybia-cirrhata.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth,  non-amyloid, 4–6 x 2.5–3.5 µm, basidia mostly two- to four-spored, pileipellis is composed of filamentous hyphae

collybiopsis-confluens.hymenium: Lamellar, white to cream, becoming pale brown with age.
collybiopsis-confluens.cap: Convex when young, expanding to almost flat, smooth, ranging from reddish-brown to ochre.
collybiopsis-confluens.stipe: Slender, fibrous, whitish to brownish at the base, and darker towards the top.
collybiopsis-confluens.spore-print: spore print: Pale brown to tan.
collybiopsis-confluens.ecology: Saprobic; growing in deciduous and coniferous forests, particularly on decaying wood or among leaf litter.
collybiopsis-confluens.edibility: Inedible due to its small size and tough texture.

coltricia-perennis.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, with small, angular pores.
coltricia-perennis.cap: 3-8 cm in diameter. Convex to flat, becoming slightly depressed at maturity; with a zonate pattern, orange-brown to dark brown.
coltricia-perennis.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, extending slightly down the stipe.
coltricia-perennis.stipe: Cylindrical, central, and somewhat fibrous; the same color or paler than the cap, sometimes with a zonate pattern.
coltricia-perennis.ecology: Saprobic, typically found growing on the ground in coniferous or mixed woods, particularly on well-decayed wood or woody debris.
coltricia-perennis.edibility: Not considered edible due to its tough texture.
coltricia-perennis.fruit-body: Up to 8 cm in diameter for the cap, stipe up to 5 cm tall.
coltricia-perennis.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical to allantoid, 7-9 x 3-4 µm.

coniophora-puteana.hymenium: Smooth, spread across the surface of the substrate, brown to dark brown in color, with a waxy or velvety texture
coniophora-puteana.cap: N/A (Resupinate, crust-like fungi without a true cap)
coniophora-puteana.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Directly attached to substrate, covering surfaces in a crust-like layer)
coniophora-puteana.stipe: N/A (Lacks a stipe, growing directly on wood)
coniophora-puteana.ecology:
Saprobic and wood-decaying, commonly found on damp, decaying wood in buildings and forested environments; known as a significant cause of brown rot in timber structures, persisting year-round
Inedible and potentially hazardous due to its role in structural wood decay
coniophora-puteana.fruit-body: Fruit body forms crust-like patches, 1–4 mm thick, can cover extensive areas on wood surfaces
coniophora-puteana.dimensions: Spread patches can vary greatly in size, up to several meters in favorable conditions
coniophora-puteana.odour: Odour often described as musty or unpleasantly earthy, especially in confined, damp spaces
coniophora-puteana.microscopy: Ellipsoidal, smooth, 6–8 x 4–5 µm, brownish, inamyloid, produced on a smooth hymenial layer

connopus-acervatus.hymenium: Gills, close, cream-buff, young ones whitish
connopus-acervatus.cap: Convex when young with incurved margin, at maturity broadly convex to nearly flat, surface smooth, glabrous, moist/subviscid when fresh, color dingy reddish-brown, fading when dry to buff-brown
connopus-acervatus.hymenium-attachment: Adnate or narrowly attached to appearing nearly free
connopus-acervatus.stipe: Slender, hollow, cartilaginous, equal, cylindrical, surface smooth or faintly fibrillose in lower part, apex paler vinaceous-brown, base fused or clustered with other stipes, base with mycelium
connopus-acervatus.ecology: Saprobic, in dense clusters on decaying coniferous wood, summer-autumn
connopus-acervatus.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, stipe length about 4–10 cm; thickness ~2–3 mm
connopus-acervatus.chemical-reactions: No known color changes to reagents
connopus-acervatus.microscopy: Spores 5.0–7.0 × 2.0–2.5 µm, smooth, narrowly tear-shaped or ellipsoid to nearly cylindrical, inamyloid, pleurocystidia absent, cheilocystidia up to ~40 µm long

conocybe-apala.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially whitish to pale, becoming cinnamon-brown to rust-colored as spores mature
conocybe-apala.cap: Conical to bell-shaped when young, becoming broadly convex to almost flat with age, delicate, pale cream to whitish, a slight brownish tint in the center, smooth in texture
conocybe-apala.stipe: Slender, fragile, hollow, pale whitish, covered in fine fibrils, lacking a ring, and often bruising easily
conocybe-apala.description: Saprobic, commonly found on lawns, pastures, and grassy areas, after rain, late spring to early autumn
conocybe-apala.edibility: Inedible, due to its fragile nature and potential confusion with toxic species
conocybe-apala.fruit-body: Fruit body small and delicate, 7–10 cm long, 1–3 mm thick
conocybe-apala.chemical-reactions: KOH gray to lilac gray on cap surface
conocybe-apala.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, large pore, smooth, 10–15 x 6–8 µm, walls 0.5–1 µm thick, orangish brown in KOH, orangish in Melzer's, basidia 20 x 12 µm, abruptly clavate, 4-spored

conocybe-tenera.hymenium: Gills crowded; pale ochre when young, becoming cinnamon to rust-brown with maturity; edges distinctly paler
conocybe-tenera.cap: Conical when young, later bell-shaped; smooth, dry, hygrophanous; ochre-brown, cinnamon to rust-brown, fading yellowish-beige when dry; margin faintly striate
conocybe-tenera.stipe: Slender, straight, whitish to pale ochre-brown with rusty tones; finely pruinose or granular, hollow and very fragile; base sometimes slightly swollen; ring absent
conocybe-tenera.description: Saprobic in lawns, meadows, pastures, parks, gardens; disturbed nutrient-rich soil; occasionally on leaf litter or woodchips; solitary or scattered; spring to autumn
conocybe-tenera.edibility: Not recommended; insubstantial, difficult to identify
conocybe-tenera.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~3–9 cm long and ~0.1–0.4 cm thick
conocybe-tenera.flesh: Cream to pale ochre, very thin and fragile, unchanging when cut
conocybe-tenera.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, ~9–14 × 5–8 µm, with a conspicuous germ pore; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia and caulocystidia lecythiform; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis hymeniform

coprinellus-disseminatus.hymenium: Gills close to moderately spaced; white when young, becoming grey then blackish with maturity
coprinellus-disseminatus.cap: Ovoid when young, later bell-shaped to broadly convex; whitish to pale grey when young, becoming grey-brown with a darker brown centre; deeply radially grooved almost to the centre; finely granular or hairy when young
coprinellus-disseminatus.stipe: Very slender, cylindrical, hollow, smooth, white and extremely fragile; often slightly curved; ring absent
coprinellus-disseminatus.ecology: Saprobic on decaying wood, especially stumps, buried roots and woody debris; typically in dense troops of dozens to hundreds; spring to late autumn
coprinellus-disseminatus.fruit-body: Fruit body very small; stipe ~1.5–4 cm long and ~0.1–0.2 cm thick
coprinellus-disseminatus.flesh: Whitish, extremely thin and fragile, do not deliquesce into black ink
coprinellus-disseminatus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, ~6.5–10 × 4–6 µm, with a central germ pore; basidia 4-spored, surrounded by brachybasidia; cheilocystidia cylindrical; pleurocystidia absent; pileocystidia lageniform to subcapitate; clamp connections absent

coprinellus-micaceus.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially white, turning black then deliquescing as spores mature
coprinellus-micaceus.cap: Starts bell-shaped, expanding to flat, ochre‑brown to gray‑brown, hygrophanous, covered in shiny, mica-like veil granules when young
coprinellus-micaceus.stipe: Slender, hollow, white to pale tan, smooth to finely pruinose, with potential basal veil remnants
coprinellus-micaceus.spore-print: Spore print very dark brown to black
coprinellus-micaceus.ecology: Ecology saprobic, clustering on decaying wood and stumps (buried or exposed), in spring through autumn
coprinellus-micaceus.edibility: Edible when young but delicate, not recommended with alcohol (coprine)
coprinellus-micaceus.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, stipe 3–10 cm long, 2–6 mm thick
coprinellus-micaceus.microscopy: Ellipsoid to mitriform, smooth, 7–10 × 4.5–6 µm, with central germ pore, basidia 10–15 × 4–7 µm, 4-spored

coprinopsis-atramentaria.hymenium: Gills, free and very crowded; white when young, turning gray, then black and liquefying
coprinopsis-atramentaria.cap: Starts egg-shaped or bell-shaped, then becomes convex or flat; smooth; gray to gray-brown; margin often splits before deliquescing
coprinopsis-atramentaria.stipe: Slender, hollow, smooth or slightly fibrous; whitish above, darker or grayer below; no persistent ring (veil is ephemeral)
coprinopsis-atramentaria.spore-print: Spore print very dark brown to black
coprinopsis-atramentaria.ecology: Saprobic, on buried or decayed wood, root systems, stumps, or mixed with soil in lawns, gardens, and disturbed sites, spring through autumn
coprinopsis-atramentaria.edibility: Edible when young, poisonous with alcohol (coprine, causing a disulfiram-like reaction)
coprinopsis-atramentaria.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe ~8–15 cm length, 0.6–2 cm thick
coprinopsis-atramentaria.description: Inky deliquescence tied to autolysis of gills
