coprinopsis-atramentaria.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to almond-shaped, smooth, ~7.5–11×4.5–6 μm, with a distinct apical germ pore, 4-spored basidia

coprinopsis-lagopus.hymenium: Gills crowded; white when young, becoming faintly reddish-grey, then grey-black
coprinopsis-lagopus.cap: Ovoid when young, later conical, bell-shaped to flattened with upturned margin; grey-brown to dark grey; densely covered in ephemeral silvery-white woolly hairs when young, becoming smooth; strongly striate
coprinopsis-lagopus.stipe: Slender, hollow and very fragile; white, initially covered with ephemeral white hairs, becoming smooth; ring absent
coprinopsis-lagopus.ecology: Saprobic on humus-rich soil, leaf litter, decaying woody debris and woodchip mulch; solitary to densely gregarious; forests, woodland tracks and disturbed habitats; spring to late autumn
coprinopsis-lagopus.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~4–10 cm long and ~0.3–0.6 cm thick
coprinopsis-lagopus.flesh: Whitish to greyish, extremely thin and fragile, rapidly collapsing as the gills deliquesce
coprinopsis-lagopus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, dark, non-amyloid, ~10–14 × 6–8.5 µm, with acentral germ pore; basidia 4-spored with brachybasidia; pleurocystidia and cheilocystidia large

coprinus-comatus.hymenium: Gills, free and extremely crowded; start white, then turn pinkish with maturing spores, then rapidly become black and undergo deliquescence
coprinus-comatus.cap: Initially cylindrical or egg-shaped, later bell-shaped to broadly conical, surface white, shaggy with fibrous scales, becoming smooth near the top
coprinus-comatus.stipe: Tall, hollow, smooth; white to creamy; bears a movable ring (veil remnant) that may slip with spore drop
coprinus-comatus.ecology: Saprobic, growing on soil, lawns, roadsides, compost, grassy patches, in disturbed locations, late spring through autumn
coprinus-comatus.edibility: Choice edible when young (before deliquescence), shortly after harvesting
coprinus-comatus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe length ~10–25 cm, 1–2 cm thick
coprinus-comatus.description: Deliquescence of gills into black ink
coprinus-comatus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, ~10–13×6.5–8 µm, with germ pore, pleurocystidia absent, cheilocystidia present

cordyceps-militaris.cap: 1-2.5 cm in length. Typically small and club-shaped, bright orange or reddish-orange. The surface can be smooth to slightly granular.
cordyceps-militaris.hymenium: Not applicable in the traditional sense; Cordyceps species produce spores from the surface of the fruiting body.
cordyceps-militaris.stipe: Long, slender, and cylindrical, similar in color to the cap or slightly paler.
cordyceps-militaris.spore-print: Spore Print: Whitish to pale orange.
cordyceps-militaris.description: Parasitic on underground pupae and larvae of various insects, particularly caterpillars. When the fungus matures, it bursts forth from the host body.
cordyceps-militaris.uses-compounds: Traditionally used in Chinese medicine for various health benefits, including boosting the immune system.
cordyceps-militaris.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical, hyaline, 3-5 x 1-1.5 µm.

cortinarius.hymenium: Gills crowded to fairly crowded, relatively narrow; pale beige-grey to clay-cinnamon; edges slightly paler
cortinarius.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to almost plane, sometimes irregular or wavy; dry-looking, finely radial-fibrillose; sand-brown to ochre-tan with a darker centre and paler whitish margin
cortinarius.stipe: Robust, cylindrical to smoothly clavate; cream-white below, pale ochre-brown above; longitudinally fibrillose; base enlarged but not clearly marginate-bulbous; abundant white cobwebby cortina when young
cortinarius.ecology: Presumably mycorrhizal; gregarious in a rich wooded meadow among aspen, birch, pine, hazel, oak and apple trees; Nedrema, Estonia; autumn
cortinarius.edibility: Do not consume; exact species unresolved within a difficult Cortinarius–Phlegmacium complex
cortinarius.fruit-body: Fruit bodies medium to large and robust

cortinarius-alboviolaceus.hymenium: Gills, initially pale lilac, becoming brown as spores mature, moderately spaced
cortinarius-alboviolaceus.cap: Conical to umbonate when young, flattening with age, surface dry, silky, and smooth, color silvery-violet, often fading to pale ochre with age
cortinarius-alboviolaceus.stipe: clavate, with a slightly bulbous base, silvery-violet, with remnants of a white universal veil, partial veil is white and cobwebby ​
cortinarius-alboviolaceus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with hardwood trees (beech and birch), deciduous and mixed forests, summer and autumn
cortinarius-alboviolaceus.edibility: Not recommended due to conflicting reports
cortinarius-alboviolaceus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 4–10 cm long and 0.5–1.5 cm thick
cortinarius-alboviolaceus.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, finely warty, measuring 7.5–9 × 4.5–6 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-spored

cortinarius-bolaris.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, initially light with a pinkish tinge that gradually darken to a brownish hue
cortinarius-bolaris.cap: Convex when young, becoming broadly convex to flat with age, surface smooth/viscid, reddish-brown with a slightly paler margin, developing subtle striations
cortinarius-bolaris.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, somewhat bulbous base, surface smooth to faintly fibrillose, reddish-brown color, retaining vestigial cortina remnants
cortinarius-bolaris.ecology: Mycorrhizal with both deciduous and coniferous trees (frequently found under birch, oak, or pine) in mixed or coniferous woodlands, late summer to autumn
cortinarius-bolaris.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 5–12 cm long and 1–2.5 cm thick
cortinarius-bolaris.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, roughened to finely verrucose, 8–12 × 5–7 µm, inamyloid, basidia are usually 4-spored

cortinarius-croceus.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, bright yellow when young, becoming rusty-brown as spores mature
cortinarius-croceus.cap: Convex to broadly convex, often with a slight umbo, bright saffron-yellow to orange-yellow, slimy or sticky when wet, fading slightly with age
cortinarius-croceus.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, yellowish to orange-yellow, often with rusty-brown fibrils from the veil, slightly swollen at the base
cortinarius-croceus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with conifer trees, growing alone or scattered, in mossy forest floors, late summer to autumn
cortinarius-croceus.edibility: Inedible, not recommended for consumption due to potential confusion with toxic species
cortinarius-croceus.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium-sized, 3-7 cm long, up to 1 cm thick
cortinarius-croceus.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface red, then dark red to black
cortinarius-croceus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, slightly to moderately roughened, 6.5-9 x 4.5-6 µ, basidia 4-spored

cortinarius-delibutus.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced to distant, at first bluish, becoming buff tinged with violet as the spores mature
cortinarius-delibutus.cap: Initially convex, becoming broadly convex to flat with age, smooth and viscid when wet, pale yellow, slight brown tint in the center
cortinarius-delibutus.stipe: Finely fibrillose, clavate at base, surface sticky, covered with yellowish veil remnants that stain rust-brown once spores begin to fall
cortinarius-delibutus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with birch, beech and spruce, found in damp mixed woodlands, autumn
cortinarius-delibutus.edibility: Inedible, not recommended for consumption due to potential confusion with toxic species
cortinarius-delibutus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 5-9 cm long and 3-6 mm thick
cortinarius-delibutus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subspherical, coarsely verrucose, 7-9.5 x 6-7µm, basidia 4-spored

cortinarius-flexipes.hymenium: Gills moderately crowded; grey-buff to brown when young, rusty to dark brown with maturity; edges usually paler
cortinarius-flexipes.cap: Conical to bell-shaped when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat; hygrophanous; dark brown to violet-brown when moist, fading grey-brown to pale fawn when dry; densely covered with fine whitish veil scales
cortinarius-flexipes.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, often curved; grey-brown with a violet flush near apex; conspicuous white fibrillose veil remnants forming incomplete bands or zones; cortina ephemeral
cortinarius-flexipes.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce and pine; moist coniferous and mixed forests, among mosses and Sphagnum; scattered to gregariously; summer to autumn
cortinarius-flexipes.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~4–8 cm long and ~0.3–0.7 cm thick
cortinarius-flexipes.flesh: Pale brown to ochraceous, thin, unchanging when cut
cortinarius-flexipes.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, finely to moderately verrucose, yellow-ochre to rusty-brown, ~7–9 × 4.5–6 µm; basidia 4-spored; pileipellis filamentous with clamp connections

cortinarius-infractus.hymenium: Gills, initially pale gray to olive-brown, becoming dark brown as the spores mature
cortinarius-infractus.cap: Convex to plano-convex, with a slight central depression when mature, surface is dry, matte, and finely fibrillose to somewhat scaly, with a color ranging from dark olive-brown to almost blackish, margin is usually inrolled when young, later becoming wavy or irregular
cortinarius-infractus.stipe: 5–10 cm long and 1–2.5 cm thick, cylindrical or slightly tapering toward the base, with a dry, fibrillose surface, base of the stipe may be slightly bulbous
cortinarius-infractus.ecology: Mycorrhizal primarily with deciduous trees beech, oak, found in mixed forests on well-drained soils, from late summer to autumn
cortinarius-infractus.edibility: Inedible, has a very bitter taste
cortinarius-infractus.fruit-body: Fruit body up to 15 cm tall
cortinarius-infractus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, 8–10 x 5–6 µm, finely warted, with a distinct plage, basidia 4-spored

cortinarius-mucosus.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, initially pale brownish, becoming rusty-brown with age as spores mature
cortinarius-mucosus.cap: Convex, becoming broadly convex or nearly flat with age, slimy and sticky when wet, reddish-brown to yellowish-brown, darker at the center
cortinarius-mucosus.stipe: Cylindrical, sticky, whitish to pale yellow, often covered in a slimy veil when young, slightly clavate at the base
cortinarius-mucosus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines and with other conifers, growing alone, scattered, or gregariously, late summer and fall
cortinarius-mucosus.edibility: No nutritional value and considered inedible, tends to accumulate heavy metals in large quantities
cortinarius-mucosus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large-sized, stipe 4-10 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
cortinarius-mucosus.chemical-reactions: KOH blackish red on cap surface
cortinarius-mucosus.microscopy: Spores amygdaliform, moderately to strongly verrucose, 11-17 x 5-7.5 µ, basidia 4-spored

cortinarius-rubellus.hymenium: Gills, starting as yellowish to rusty-brown, eventually becoming darker brown with age
cortinarius-rubellus.cap: Initially conical to bell-shaped, later expanding to become broadly umbonate, surface is dry, with a fibrous texture and a reddish-orange to brick-red color
cortinarius-rubellus.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, often with a bulbous base, surface is orange to reddish and may feature some fibrous veils forming a cortina
cortinarius-rubellus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pine and spruce, commonly found in mixed forests, grows solitary or in small groups on mossy forest floors during late summer to autumn
cortinarius-rubellus.edibility: Deadly poisonous, contains orellanine, which can cause severe kidney damage or failure, with symptoms often delayed for days
cortinarius-rubellus.microscopy: Spores are almond-shaped, warty, 9-12 x 6.5-8.5µm, the basidia are four-spored, cystidia are rare or absent

cortinarius-sanguineus.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; bright carmine to blood-red when young, becoming rusty red-brown with maturity
cortinarius-sanguineus.cap: Convex to broadly convex, later plane, often with a broad umbo; hygrophanous, finely silky-fibrillose; rich blood-red, dark red to dull reddish-brown
cortinarius-sanguineus.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, blood-red to dark red; orange-yellow to reddish-yellow basal mycelium; cortina red and ephemeral; ring absent
cortinarius-sanguineus.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce; mesic to damp mossy coniferous forests, often among Sphagnum and bilberry on nutrient-rich ground; scattered or gregariously; late summer to autumn
cortinarius-sanguineus.uses-compounds: Anthraquinone pigments including emodin, dermocybin, dermolutein and dermorubin
cortinarius-sanguineus.description: Dye fungus, yields red and reddish-brown shades
cortinarius-sanguineus.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–8.5 cm long and ~0.3–0.7 cm thick
cortinarius-sanguineus.flesh: Dark red to blood-red, with orange tints toward the stipe base; unchanging when cut
cortinarius-sanguineus.chemical-reactions: KOH distinctly aniline-red on cap surface
cortinarius-sanguineus.microscopy: Spores amygdaloid to ellipsoid, moderately verrucose, weakly dextrinoid, ~5.6–7.3 × 3.1–4.6 µm; basidia 4-spored; pileipellis hyphae lacking or with only slight encrustation; clamp connections present

cortinarius-semisanguineus.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, color of the gills is initially light yellow to olive-yellow, eventually darkening with a reddish tinge
cortinarius-semisanguineus.cap: conical to bell-shaped when young, becoming convex or nearly flat in maturity, with a small umbo, surface is smooth, dry, fibrillose, colors rom olive-brown to yellow-brown
cortinarius-semisanguineus.stipe: cylindrical and sometimes tapering toward the base, color is pale yellow, surface is dry, silky-fibrillose, may develop longitudinal streaks of rust near the top
cortinarius-semisanguineus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines and spruces, on acidic, nutrient-poor soils in coniferous forests, in mossy or grassy areas, late summer to autumn
cortinarius-semisanguineus.edibility: Inedible, consumption is not recommended due to its potential toxicity
cortinarius-semisanguineus.fruit-body: Fruit body 3–10 cm in height, stipe 4–10 cm long, 0.5–1.5 cm thick
cortinarius-semisanguineus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to almond-shaped, 9–12 x 6–7 µm, with a rough, warty surface, basidia four-spored, gill trama has a parallel structure

cortinarius-traganus.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, adnate to slightly decurrent, pale violet when young, becoming later rusty-brown
cortinarius-traganus.cap: Convex to flat with a pronounced central umbo, surface is dry and covered with fine, fibrous scales, color ranges from pale lilac to purplish-brown, fading with age
cortinarius-traganus.stipe: Club-shaped, thick, solid, and covered with a fibrous, pale lilac to violet veil when young
cortinarius-traganus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in coniferous and mixed forests, forming symbiotic associations with pine and spruce trees, grows usually in acidic soils
cortinarius-traganus.edibility: Inedible due to unpleasant odor and toxicity
cortinarius-traganus.odour: Odour is strong, foetid and goat-like
cortinarius-traganus.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to almond-shaped, 8–9 x 5–5.5 μm, with fine dots, basidia are typically four-spored, 30–35 x 6.5–7.5 μm.

cortinarius-violaceus.hymenium: Gills that are close together, violet in color.
cortinarius-violaceus.cap: Convex to broadly convex, occasionally nearly flat when mature; deep violet, often with a slightly campanulate or bell-shaped center.
cortinarius-violaceus.stipe: Cylindrical, sometimes slightly swollen in the middle, with a violet hue throughout; often fibrillose or covered in fine, velvety scales.
cortinarius-violaceus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, primarily associating with deciduous trees in mixed and coniferous forests, especially with birches and pines.
cortinarius-violaceus.edibility: Not recommended for consumption due to potential confusion with toxic species.
cortinarius-violaceus.fruit-body: Cap 6-10 cm in diameter, stipe up to 15 cm tall.
cortinarius-violaceus.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid, 9-11 x 5-6.5 µm, with a rough surface.

cosmospora-annulohypoxyli.ascomata: Non-stromatic or weakly stromatic perithecia, superficial on host surface, bright reddish-orange when fresh, turning dark red or reddish-brown with age
cosmospora-annulohypoxyli.body: Teleomorph appearing as clusters of tiny perithecia immersed or superficial on the decaying stromata of a host fungus (not on wood directly)
cosmospora-annulohypoxyli.ecology: Fungicolous (mycoparasitic), growing on the dead stromata of fungi in the genus Annulohypoxylon
cosmospora-annulohypoxyli.microscopy:
Inedible, microscopic
Ascospores ellipsoid, verrucose, 8.5-9.5(–10) × 3.8-4.2 µm, 1-septate, hyaline becoming pale yellow-brown at maturity, asci unitunicate cylindrical, ~70–75 × 4–5 µm, 8-spored
cosmospora-annulohypoxyli.fruit-body: Fruit body microscopic, perithecial clusters < 1 mm in height

craterellus-lutescens.hymenium: Smooth to slightly wrinkled, pale yellow to orange-yellow, with the hymenium running down the stem, surface appear almost vein-like
craterellus-lutescens.cap: Funnel-shaped to tubular, thin and fragile, often with wavy edges. The cap surface is typically yellowish to orange or brownish
craterellus-lutescens.hymenium-attachment: The hymenium is decurrent and runs down the stipe
craterellus-lutescens.stipe: Slender, hollow, and often somewhat twisted, with a color that matches the cap or is slightly paler
craterellus-lutescens.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
craterellus-lutescens.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pine and spruce, mossy and damp areas of coniferous forests, in groups or small clusters
craterellus-lutescens.edibility: Edible and highly regarded, with a fruity aroma and a mild, slightly peppery taste
craterellus-lutescens.microscopy: Spores elliptical to slightly ovoid, 8–12 x 6–8 µm, smooth surface, basidia four-spored, hyphae in the flesh are interwoven

crepidotus-calolepis.hymenium: Gills, radiating from the point of attachment, close, whitish when young, later dull brown
crepidotus-calolepis.cap: Semicircular or fan-shaped, cap surface with fine brown scales, pallid cream/yellowish under the fibrils, slightly rubbery texture when moist due to a gelatinized zone under pileipellis
crepidotus-calolepis.hymenium-attachment: N/A (no cap-stem structure; gills attach at the lateral or basal point of the cap)
crepidotus-calolepis.ecology: Saprobic on dead hardwood (oak and aspen), sometimes bark of living trees, solitary to gregarious, in moist conditions, autumn to early winter
crepidotus-calolepis.edibility: Edibility unknown, unsubstantial for culinary use
crepidotus-calolepis.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface dull-reddish, on gills red
crepidotus-calolepis.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subamygdaliform, smooth, 6–9 × 4.5–6.0 µm, basidia 4-sterigmate, 18–25 × 4–6 µm, cheilocystidia present (30-60 × 3-5 µm)

crucibulum-laeve.hymenium: Internal, smooth, forms the inner surface of the peridium, pale to dark brown when mature
crucibulum-laeve.cap: Cup-shaped peridium that is initially covered by a thin, yellowish to brown membrane; once the membrane breaks, inner surface reveals white to grey, lens-shaped peridioles resembling eggs inside nest
crucibulum-laeve.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Hymenium forms the inner surface of the peridium)
crucibulum-laeve.spore-print: Spore print white (peridioles contain microscopic spores)
crucibulum-laeve.ecology: Saprobic, decomposing organic matter, found on dead wood, twigs, woody debris, and plant stems; grows in clusters in damp, shaded environments, summer to autumn
crucibulum-laeve.fruit-body: Fruit body small, peridium (nest) 4–10 mm tall and 3–8 mm in diameter
crucibulum-laeve.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, colorless, 6–8 x 3–4 µm, produced within the peridioles (1–2 mm wide)

cudonia-circinans.cap: 0.5-1.5 cm in diameter. Initially convex, becoming flatter or slightly depressed, tan to ochre-brown, smooth to slightly wrinkled, edges typically turned down and inrolled.
cudonia-circinans.hymenium: Smooth surface, no true gills or pores, pale brown to ochre.
cudonia-circinans.stipe: Same color as cap, but paler and often more translucent, slightly tapered, and with a smooth surface.
cudonia-circinans.spore-print: Spore Print: Pale ochre to light brown.
cudonia-circinans.ecology: Saprobic; found on soil among mosses, leaf litter, and decaying organic matter in mixed and coniferous forests.
cudonia-circinans.edibility: Not recommended for consumption due to its small size and unknown edibility.
cudonia-circinans.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, 16-20 x 6-8 µm.

cuphophyllus-virgineus.hymenium: Gills, decurrent, waxy in texture; whitish to pale, sometimes tinged cream
cuphophyllus-virgineus.cap: Convex to flat or slightly depressed with age; smooth, dry to somewhat greasy when damp; white to ivory, sometimes with brownish tints centrally
cuphophyllus-virgineus.stipe: smooth, cylindrical or tapering at base; white to ivory, sometimes discolored near base
cuphophyllus-virgineus.description: Occurs in old, unimproved grassland, in woodland on mossy substrates elsewhere, neither strictly saprotrophic nor mycorrhizal, but form associations with mosses or act as biotrophic endophytes
cuphophyllus-virgineus.edibility: Edible and regarded as good (though not highly prized)
cuphophyllus-virgineus.fruit-body: Fruit body variable size, stipe up to ~7 cm long
cuphophyllus-virgineus.dimensions: Cap ~1–5 cm up to ~7.5 cm in larger specimens
cuphophyllus-virgineus.chemical-reactions: KOH reaction on cap surface is yellowish.
cuphophyllus-virgineus.odour: Very mild smell of coconut cookies
cuphophyllus-virgineus.microscopy: Spores: Ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid; about 7.0–8.5 × 4.5–5.0 µm

cyathus-striatus.hymenium: Gleba lining inner surfaces of peridium, peridioles are attached by funiculi cords and dispersed by splash mechanism
cyathus-striatus.peridium: Small cup- or urn-shaped nest, inner surface with distinct vertical striations, outer surface hairy or tomentose
cyathus-striatus.peridioles: Disc-shaped, ~1–1.5 mm wide, occasionally up to 2 mm, sometimes encased in thin tunica membrane
cyathus-striatus.funiculus: A structural hyphal cord with ballooned purse, coiled cord, basal and middle portions.
cyathus-striatus.ecology: Saprobic on woody debris, mulch, forest litter, woodchips, tends to cluster, summer to early winter
cyathus-striatus.fruit-body: Fruit body size ~7–10 mm tall, ~6–8 mm wide
cyathus-striatus.microscopy: Spores ~15–20×8–12 µm, ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, with a notch, basidia clavate and sessile, 4-spored

cystoderma-amianthinum.hymenium: Gills, moderately crowded, whitish becoming pale yellowish
cystoderma-amianthinum.cap: Convex to broadly convex, often flattening with age, covered with a granular surface, light yellow to yellowish-brown, margin scalloped
cystoderma-amianthinum.stipe: Cylindrical, with a distinct, powdery to fibrous surface, pale yellow to brownish, adorned with a small, fragile ring near the top
cystoderma-amianthinum.ecology: Saprobic, growing in grasslands, heathlands, and woodland edges, in moss under conifers, late summer to autumn
cystoderma-amianthinum.edibility: Edible but not recommended due to confusion with toxic species
cystoderma-amianthinum.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium-sized, stipe 3-7 cm long, 3-8 mm thick
cystoderma-amianthinum.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface rusty red
cystoderma-amianthinum.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 4-7 x 3-4 µm, weakly amyloid, basidia 4-spored, cystidia absent

dacrymyces-stillatus.hymenium: N/A in the usual sense (gelatinous basidiocarp without typical gills or pores)
dacrymyces-stillatus.cap: Absent in typical format — fruit bodies are small, cushion-shaped or blob-like, gelatinous orange-yellow turning brown/red with age
dacrymyces-stillatus.ecology: Saprobic on decaying wood of both hardwoods and conifers, fruiting whenever damp
dacrymyces-stillatus.edibility: Too small and gelatinous to be of culinary value
dacrymyces-stillatus.fruit-body: Fruit bodyv Very small, can appear larger when merged
dacrymyces-stillatus.flesh: Flesh gelatinous, translucent to orange-yellow, unchanging when cut
dacrymyces-stillatus.microscopy: Spores sausage-shaped or elongated (14–17×~5–6µm); 3-septate at maturity, basidia Y-shaped and chains of arthrospores present

daedalea-quercina.hymenium: Pores large, elongated, winding and labyrinthine, sometimes gill-like; thick blunt walls ~1–3 mm wide; whitish to pale cream when young, becoming ochre-buff; not bruising
daedalea-quercina.cap: Semicircular to fan- or shelf-shaped, broadly attached; surface uneven, sometimes concentrically zoned, smooth to finely velvety; whitish, greyish-buff, ochre-brown to dark brown with age; margin thick, rounded and often paler
daedalea-quercina.hymenium-attachment: Maze-like pore surface covers the underside of the bracket
daedalea-quercina.stipe: Absent; fruit body sessile, broadly attached to wood
daedalea-quercina.ecology:
Saprobic, causing brown rot on dead hardwood (Quercus); fallen branches, trunks, stumps and standing dead wood; solitary or in overlapping groups; perennial, visible year-round
Inedible; extremely tough, corky and woody
daedalea-quercina.flesh: Whitish to pale ochre-brown, thick, corky to woody, unchanging when cut
daedalea-quercina.chemical-reactions: KOH dark grey to black on cap, hymenium and flesh
daedalea-quercina.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–7 × 2–4 µm; basidia 4-spored

diatrype-undulata.fruit-body:
Thin, flat to slightly raised carbonaceous stromata forming crust-like patches on bark of dead branches, stromata are blackish, with a whitish entostromal layer underneath
Dimensions: Stromatal patches can cover branch surfaces; perithecia ostioles about 5–7 µm wide by 75–95 µm long in stalk length
diatrype-undulata.perithecia: Perithecia immersed to erumpent, arranged singly, often with black sulcate ostioles visible on surface of stromata
diatrype-undulata.description:
Spores dispersed from perithecia
Asci: Long-stalked, 8-spored.
Ascospores: Allantoid, pale olivaceous, ~ 5–8 × ~1 µm
diatrype-undulata.ecology: Parasite, pathogen, saprobe on birch (monophagous on Betula spp.) branches, especially dead or dying bark
diatrype-undulata.dimensions: Crust width: Extent variable depending on branch area

diplomitoporus-flavescens.hymenium: Pores, round to angular, small (4–5 per mm), bright yellow to pale cream when fresh, becoming duller with age
diplomitoporus-flavescens.cap: Resupinate, spreading flat on the substrate, soft and spongy when fresh, drying to a brittle texture, surface smooth to finely cracked, bright yellow to pale ochre
diplomitoporus-flavescens.hymenium-attachment: Poroid, directly attached to the substrate without a stipe or cap margin
diplomitoporus-flavescens.stipe: Lacking, as it is a crust fungus
diplomitoporus-flavescens.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
diplomitoporus-flavescens.ecology:
Saprobic, growing on dead conifer wood, including fallen logs, branches, and stumps, in moist environments, spring to autumn
Inedible due to tough texture and insubstantial flesh.
diplomitoporus-flavescens.fruit-body: Fruit body poroid crust, spreading up to 10–30 cm across and 0.1–3 cm thick.
diplomitoporus-flavescens.chemical-reactions: Yellowish on the surface and hymenium
diplomitoporus-flavescens.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, 6–8 × 2.5–3.5 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-sterigmate, 20–30 × 5–7 µm

discina-ancilis.hymenium: Smooth to slightly wrinkled fertile surface lining the upper side of the apothecium; reddish-chestnut-dark-brown
discina-ancilis.apothecium: Irregularly cup-, ear- or saddle-shaped, often lobed and folded; margin wavy or contorted; outer surface paler, finely tomentose to smooth
discina-ancilis.hymenium-attachment: Apothecial, fertile surface exposed on the upper inner folds
discina-ancilis.stipe: Short, thick, ribbed or folded, often partially buried, whitish to pale brown
discina-ancilis.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
discina-ancilis.ecology: Saprobic on decaying conifer wood, buried timber, wood debris, after snowy winter, spring to early summer
discina-ancilis.edibility: Uncertain to mildly toxic; sometimes consumed after thorough cooking, gyromitrin-related toxins
discina-ancilis.flesh: Fragile, fleshy to brittle, unchanging when cut
discina-ancilis.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, smooth, hyaline, ~30–38 × 12–15 µm with oil droplets and apiculi; asci cylindrical, 8-spored; paraphyses slender, septate, slightly enlarged apically

drepanopeziza-ribis.hymenium: Pale to medium grey fertile discs within minute dark apothecia, emerging through the epidermis of overwintered fallen leaves
drepanopeziza-ribis.body: Tiny cup- to disc-shaped apothecia, initially immersed, later erumpent; asexual stage forming small greyish acervuli within dark brown, circular to irregular leaf spots, often surrounded by yellowing tissue
drepanopeziza-ribis.description:
Spore mass hyaline to whitish
Parasitic on living leaves of Ribes species; causes anthracnose, leaf spotting and premature defoliation; overwinters saprobically on fallen leaves; airborne ascospores in spring, rain-splashed conidia during summer to autumn
drepanopeziza-ribis.fruit-body: Microscopic; infected leaf spots usually ~1–2 mm across, sometimes merging into larger necrotic patches
drepanopeziza-ribis.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, hyaline, aseptate, ~16–22 × 7–9.5 µm; asci clavate, 4–8-spored, ~65–105 × 18–21 µm, with iodine-blue apical ring; paraphyses filiform, slightly enlarged apically; macroconidia falcate, aseptate, ~17.5–24 × 5.5–7 µm; microconidia cylindrical, ~4–6.5 × 2–3 µm

encoelia-furfuracea.hymenium: Smooth or minutely hairy, typically pale brown to tan in color.
encoelia-furfuracea.cap: Cup-shaped to irregularly shaped, with a fuzzy or tomentose surface. Colors vary from tan to brown.
encoelia-furfuracea.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable, as this species forms cup-shaped fruiting bodies.
encoelia-furfuracea.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, not distinct from the cap.
encoelia-furfuracea.ecology: Saprobic, commonly found on decaying wood, particularly on fallen branches and twigs in forested habitats.
encoelia-furfuracea.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to oblong, smooth, 10-15 x 5-8 µm.

entoloma-chalybeum.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced, rather thick; whitish to pale grey when young, sometimes faintly bluish, becoming dirty salmon-pink with maturity
entoloma-chalybeum.cap: Convex to broadly convex, often shallowly umbilicate; finely velvety to minutely squamulose; dark steel-blue, blue-black to purplish-brown, sometimes becoming browner with age
entoloma-chalybeum.stipe: Slender, cylindrical to slightly flattened or longitudinally grooved; steel-blue to blue-black with longitudinal fibres, often paler toward apex; white tomentum at base; ring absent
entoloma-chalybeum.spore-print: Spore print pale pink to salmon-pink
entoloma-chalybeum.ecology: Ecology saprotrophic(?); unimproved nutrient-poor grasslands, moist meadows, heathland and deciduous woodland; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to autumn
entoloma-chalybeum.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.2–0.5 cm thick
entoloma-chalybeum.flesh: Grey-blue to pale bluish, thin, unchanging when cut
entoloma-chalybeum.microscopy: Spores heterodiametrical, angular with 5–9 facets, ~8.5–12.5 × 6–8.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia cylindrical to slender-clavate; pileipellis transitional between cutis and trichoderm; clamp connections absent

entoloma-sericellum.hymenium: Gills moderately distant; pure white when young, becoming pale pink with maturity; edges concolorous
entoloma-sericellum.cap: Hemispherical to convex, later expanding; white, progressively yellow-ochre from centre; finely felted to minutely squamulose; non-hygrophanous, margin not translucently striate
entoloma-sericellum.hymenium-attachment: Adnate with a slight decurrent tooth
entoloma-sericellum.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, white to yellowish-ochre; pruinose near apex, smooth and polished below; hollow and fragile; ring absent
entoloma-sericellum.description: Saprobic mainly in semi-natural grasslands, meadows and grassy woodland edges, also parkland and deciduous woodland; scattered or in small groups, occasionally arcs; summer to late autumn
entoloma-sericellum.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2–4 cm long and ~0.1–0.2 cm thick
entoloma-sericellum.flesh: White, thin and brittle, unchanging when cut
entoloma-sericellum.microscopy: Spores heterodiametrical, distinctly 5–7-angled, ~9.5–14 × 7–9.5 µm; basidia 4-spored with clamps; cheilocystidia scattered, cylindrical, fusiform to lageniform, ~35–50 × 7–11.5 µm; pileipellis transitional between cutis and trichoderm

entoloma-vernum.description: gills adhering to the stem almost or freely from it, quite frequent, in young mushrooms are white, brownish or grayish, turning pink with age
entoloma-vernum.cap: cap is sharply conical at a young age, opening to flat-convex, with a tubercle in the center, hygrophanous, brown in color, darker in the central part than closer to the edge, smooth, silky, fibrous
entoloma-vernum.fruit-body: fruit body to 2-9 cm, leg 0.2-1 cm thick

eutypella-quaternata.stroma-fruit-body: Black, carbonaceous stromata, either crust-like patches or erumpent areas on bark of dead wood; often with a thin whitish entostroma below the surface.
eutypella-quaternata.perithecia-ostioles: Perithecia immersed to slightly erumpent, with small black ostioles breaking through the stromal surface.
eutypella-quaternata.ecology: Saprobic, primarily on dead or decaying hardwood branches, especially birch, alder, acer, occurs on dead bark
eutypella-quaternata.fruit-body: Dimensions stromatal patches variable, perithecial ostioles ~ tens to hundreds of micrometers in diameter
eutypella-quaternata.description:
Asci: 8-spored asci
Ascospores: Allantoid (curved) spores, hyaline, ~ 3 × 15-18 µm
Stromatal structure: Stromata composed of ectostroma and entostroma, perithecia embedded within these layers

exidia-nigricans.hymenium: Smooth, located on the outer surface, forming a gelatinous mass, dark brown to black in color
exidia-nigricans.cap: Irregular, lobed or ear-shaped, gelatinous, dark brown to black, becoming darker and more opaque as it matures, surface wrinkled when dry
exidia-nigricans.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Hymenium forms the external surface of the gelatinous body)
exidia-nigricans.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying hardwoods, in damp, shaded environments, individually or in overlapping clusters, autumn to winter and early spring
exidia-nigricans.edibility: Inedible, due to its tough, gelatinous texture
exidia-nigricans.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, directly attached to substrate, often forming overlapping lobes
exidia-nigricans.dimensions: Composite blobs, typically 2 to 15 cm across
exidia-nigricans.microscopy: Spores allantoid, smooth, 14-19 x 4.5-5.5 µm, inamyloid.

exidia-saccharina.hymenium: Smooth, gelatinous, forming the outer surface of the fruiting body, initially pale amber or yellowish, becoming dark brown to blackish with age
exidia-saccharina.cap: Lacks a distinct cap, fruiting body is irregularly lobed or brain-like, with a gelatinous, rubbery texture, surface is shiny and somewhat translucent when moist
exidia-saccharina.stipe: Lacking; the fruiting body is sessile and directly attached to the substrate
exidia-saccharina.ecology: Saprobic, growing on dead coniferous wood, particularly on logs and branches, in damp conditions, late autumn to winter
exidia-saccharina.edibility: Inedible due to gelatinous texture and insubstantial flesh
exidia-saccharina.fruit-body: Fruit body small, up to 2–5 cm across and 1–3 cm tall
exidia-saccharina.microscopy: Spores allantoid, smooth, hyaline in KOH, 10–15 x 4–6 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate, 14–18 x 8–10 µm

exobasidium-juelianum.hymenium: Smooth, forms on the undersides of infected leaves, pinkish to pale red in color, covering the affected area
exobasidium-juelianum.cap: N/A (Not applicable, as it is a parasitic fungus that grows on leaves)
exobasidium-juelianum.hymenium-attachment: N/A (The hymenium forms directly on the host tissue, no attachment to a cap)
exobasidium-juelianum.stipe: N/A (Does not have a stipe, parasitic on leaves)
exobasidium-juelianum.spore-print: Spore print white (microscopic spore mass on the affected leaf)
exobasidium-juelianum.description: Parasitic, infects specific plants, particularly Vaccinium species, causing leaf and shoot deformations, spring to summer
exobasidium-juelianum.fruit-body: Infection symptoms: Causes swellings or galls on shoot or flower, sometimes whole plant is infected
exobasidium-juelianum.microscopy: Spores elliptical to cylindrical, smooth, 12–16 x 4–5 µm, hyaline, produced in basidia on the infected plant surface

exobasidium-vaccinii.description:
Spores are produced in specialized cells on the surface of the infected plant tissue
Parasitic, infects species in the genus Vaccinium, including cranberries, blueberries, and lingonberries, found in temperate and boreal regions
exobasidium-vaccinii.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly fusiform and smooth, 12–16 × 3–5 µm, basidia are elongated and produce spores on the plant surface

fistulina-hepatica.hymenium: Pores initially whitish to straw-yellow, becoming pinkish-red to reddish-brown with age; tubes cylindrical and separate from one another
fistulina-hepatica.cap: Tongue-, fan- to kidney-shaped; upper surface pinkish-red when young, becoming dark red-brown; finely papillate when young, later smoother
fistulina-hepatica.spore-print: Spore print white to pale pinkish-yellow
fistulina-hepatica.ecology: Weakly parasitic and saprobic, causing brown rot primarily on old oaks and sweet chestnut; usually low on trunks, root bases and stumps, also on fallen wood; solitary or overlapping; summer to autumn
fistulina-hepatica.edibility: Edible when young (sour), becoming tough with age
fistulina-hepatica.fruit-body: Fruit body large, thick and fleshy; ~3–6 cm thick
fistulina-hepatica.flesh: Reddish-pink, marbled with paler fibres, soft and juicy
fistulina-hepatica.description: Exudes conspicuous blood-red liquid when cut
fistulina-hepatica.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~4–6 × 3–4 µm; basidia 4-spored; hyphal system monomitic with clamp connections; laticiferous hyphae with brownish contents present

flammulina-velutipes.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, pale cream to white when young, becoming pale ochre with age.
flammulina-velutipes.cap: Convex to broadly convex, flattened with age, surface smooth and sticky when moist, orange to reddish-brown, often paler at the margin.
flammulina-velutipes.stipe: Cylindrical, slender, velvety to the touch, dark brown to nearly black at the base, transitioning to yellowish or pale near the cap, hollow
flammulina-velutipes.ecology: Saprobic, found growing in clusters on decaying hardwoods, elm, willow, and poplar, late autumn through winter, appearing during freezing conditions
flammulina-velutipes.edibility: Edible and highly prized, with a pleasant taste, especially in cultivated forms (enoki)
flammulina-velutipes.fruit-body: Fruit body cap 2–10 cm in diameter, stipe 3–10 cm long and 2–6 mm thick
flammulina-velutipes.chemical-reactions: KOH red to brownish red on cap surface
flammulina-velutipes.microscopy: Spores subcylindric to elongated-ellipsoid, smooth, 5–10 x 2.5–3.5 µm, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, basidia 25–28 x 3–4 µm, subclavate, 4-sterigmate

fomes-fomentarius.hymenium:
pores on hymenium, small and round, white to grayish
hymenium is tubular (composed of tubes instead of gills)
fomes-fomentarius.cap: cap is hoof-shaped or semicircular, with a hard, woody texture, and typically has concentric zones of different colors ranging from gray to brown
fomes-fomentarius.stipe: stipe is not present, as this fungus grows directly from the wood in a bracket-like manner
fomes-fomentarius.spore-print: spore print is pale brown to cinnamon
fomes-fomentarius.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic and sometimes parasitic, typically found on the wood of deciduous trees, especially beech and birch
fomes-fomentarius.edibility: inedible due to its tough, woody texture
fomes-fomentarius.fruit-body: individual brackets can be 5-45 cm across

fomitopsis-pinicola.hymenium: Pores round, whitish to pale yellowish, not strongly bruising; usually ~3–4 pores per mm, with distinct annual tube layers
fomitopsis-pinicola.cap: Perennial bracket or hoof-shaped conk; hard, woody, semicircular to fan-shaped; zoned dark blackish near attachment, with orange-red varnished bands and a thick pale growing margin
fomitopsis-pinicola.ecology:
Saprobic, sometimes weakly parasitic, causing brown cubical rot on dead or living conifers and hardwoods; perennial, year-round
Woody and inedible
fomitopsis-pinicola.fruit-body: Fruit body large, up to ~15 cm thick
fomitopsis-pinicola.flesh: Flesh whitish to cream, leathery to woody, unchanging when cut
fomitopsis-pinicola.chemical-reactions: KOH flesh turns red to reddish-brown
fomitopsis-pinicola.microscopy: Spores subellipsoid to oval, smooth, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, ~6–9 × 3–4.5 µm; basidia 4-sterigmate; cystidia absent; hyphal system trimitic with clamped generative hyphae, skeletal hyphae and binding hyphae

fuscoporia-ferruginosa.hymenium: Pores, small (often ~4–7 per mm), angular to hexagonal, initially pale but turning rusty-brown to cinnamon as spores mature
fuscoporia-ferruginosa.cap: Bracket or crust form (resupinate or effused-reflexed), surface smooth to slightly tomentose, cinnamon to rusty brown, zonate in places
fuscoporia-ferruginosa.hymenium-attachment: Poroid (underside of bracket), sometimes flush with substrate (crust)
fuscoporia-ferruginosa.stipe: Absent (fungus grows directly attached to wood substrate)
fuscoporia-ferruginosa.spore-print: Spore print pale, slightly pinkish to white
fuscoporia-ferruginosa.ecology:
Saprotrophic (and wood-decay) fungus, causes white rot on dead hardwoods, occurs on branches, stumps, logs, often in shaded, moist environments.
Inedible (hard, woody, no flesh)
fuscoporia-ferruginosa.fruit-body: Fruit body size medium to large, thickness up to ~1.5 cm
fuscoporia-ferruginosa.description:
Spores globose to subglobose, smooth, hyaline, non-amyloid
Hyphal system: dimitic (generative + skeletal)
Hymenial setae: dark brown setae often present in pore surface

fuscopostia-fragilis.hymenium: Pores, round, 3–5 per mm, cream to pale yellow when young, becoming ochre to light brown with age, bruising reddish brown
fuscopostia-fragilis.cap: Shelflike, semicircular to kidney-shaped, surface velvety to finely hairy when young, becoming smooth with age, pale cream to light brown, often darker towards the attachment point
fuscopostia-fragilis.ecology:
Saprobic on the deadwood of spruces and pines, causing a brown rot, growing alone or gregariously, annual, spring through fall
Inedible due to tough, corky texture
fuscopostia-fragilis.fruit-body: Fruit body size cap 5–15 cm wide, 1–3 cm thick
fuscopostia-fragilis.chemical-reactions: KOH negative on the cap surface and flesh
fuscopostia-fragilis.microscopy: Spores 4–5 x 2–2.5 µm, allantoid to cylindric, smooth, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, basidia 15–18 x 4–5 µm, clavate, 4-sterigmate

fuscopostia-lateritia.hymenium: Pores, cream to pale brown, pores circular to angular, densely packed
fuscopostia-lateritia.cap: Semicircular to fan-shaped, rough and velvety when young, becoming smoother with age, light brown to reddish-brown, darker toward the center, with a margin that becomes paler with age
fuscopostia-lateritia.ecology: Saprobic, found on dead conifer wood, decomposing fallen logs, and stumps, visible year-round, prominent in late autumn
fuscopostia-lateritia.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, sessile, up to 10 cm wide, with a thickness of 1–3 cm
fuscopostia-lateritia.dimensions: Cap 5–15 cm in diameter, often layered when older
fuscopostia-lateritia.chemical-reactions: Cottony and soft when dry, not fragile
fuscopostia-lateritia.microscopy: Spores smooth, elliptical, hyaline, 4–5 x 1.5–2 µm, non-amyloid

galerina-calyptrata.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, initially pale yellow to light brown, becoming dark brown with age
galerina-calyptrata.cap: Convex to bell-shaped when young, often flattening with age, smooth, sticky when moist, yellowish-brown to tawny, often with a slightly darker center
galerina-calyptrata.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, yellowish to light brown, often darker towards the base
galerina-calyptrata.ecology:
Saprobic, typically found on decaying wood or in mossy forest floors, in mixed or coniferous forests, from late summer to autumn
Inedible, toxic, contains amatoxins similar to Amanita species
galerina-calyptrata.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 3–6 cm long, 2–5 mm thick
galerina-calyptrata.microscopy: Spores almond shaped, with small calyptrates, mottled 9-12 x 5-7 µm

gamundia-striatula.hymenium: Gills, fairly close, cream-to-buff when young, aging to light brown
gamundia-striatula.cap: Conical to broadly convex, smooth or faintly fibrillose, brown to tan with distinctive radial striations near the margin
gamundia-striatula.stipe: Slender, whitish to pale brown, smooth, with no prominent ring
gamundia-striatula.description: Saprobic, on decomposed-litter nitrogen rich soil, under woodland trees, forests, parks, heathland, late spring to autumn
gamundia-striatula.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe ~1–3 cm long
gamundia-striatula.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 6-8.5x4-6 µm, cheilocystidia mixed with basidia, sinous, 35-100 µm

ganoderma-applanatum.hymenium: Pores, small and round (~4–6 per mm), underside white to pale, staining brown
ganoderma-applanatum.cap: Shelf- or bracket-shaped, semicircular to hooflike, sessile, surface dull, brownish to gray-brown, often zonate, texture rough, firm and woody
ganoderma-applanatum.stipe: Absent, generally comes off dead or live wood directly
ganoderma-applanatum.ecology:
Saprotrophic wood-decay fungus, causing white rot in both dead and living hardwoods, weak parasite, perennial fruiting bodies
Inedible, tough/woody
ganoderma-applanatum.fruit-body: Fruit body size large, thickness of bracket 1–10 cm
ganoderma-applanatum.dimensions: Bracket ~10–30 cm across, depth up to ~8–14 cm
ganoderma-applanatum.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface, flesh, and tubes black
ganoderma-applanatum.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, ~6–9 × 4–5 µm, finely stippled ornamentation, inamyloid, brown in KOH, hyphal system trimitic, clamp connections present

geastrum-fimbriatum.hymenium: Internal, forming a gleba that is brownish and powdery at maturity, containing the spores
geastrum-fimbriatum.cap: No distinct cap, fruiting body begins as a round, smooth, and pale tan to brownish peridium, splitting into star-like rays that curve downward, exposing the spore sac in the center
geastrum-fimbriatum.stipe: Absent, the spore sac sits on a small, sessile base formed by the rays
geastrum-fimbriatum.ecology: Saprobic, grows in leaf litter, mossy areas, and nutrient-rich soils, often in deciduous or mixed forests, late summer to autumn
geastrum-fimbriatum.fruit-body: Fruit Body small to medium, rays extend to 2–5 cm wide when fully open, spore sac 1–2 cm in diameter
geastrum-fimbriatum.microscopy: Spores globose, warted, brown, 3.5–5 µm in diameter, with a hyaline perisporium, basidia not well-developed

gloeophyllum-sepiarium.hymenium: Gills—irregular, somewhat maze-like (gilled polypore), closely spaced, initially pale to orange-brown, darkening with age
gloeophyllum-sepiarium.cap: Fan-shaped to semicircular brackets, often irregular lobed, surface velvety when young, later smooth or slightly rugged, concentric zones of brown-yellow-orange tones, margin often lighter
gloeophyllum-sepiarium.description: Saprobic (wood-decay fungus) causing brown rot on dead conifer wood (logs, stumps, beams, posts)
gloeophyllum-sepiarium.fruit-body: Fruit body depth variable, up to several cm
gloeophyllum-sepiarium.flesh: Flesh is brownish, no color change when cut
gloeophyllum-sepiarium.chemical-reactions: Flesh and tissues turn black with KOH
gloeophyllum-sepiarium.microscopy: Spores cylindrical, smooth, ~9–13 × 3–5 µm, inamyloid, hyaline in KOH, basidia elongated, cylindric cystidia, up to ~100 × 10 µm.

gomphidius-glutinosus.hymenium: Gills that are decurrent, rather spaced, yellowish turning olive-brown with age.
gomphidius-glutinosus.cap: Initially convex, later becoming flattened or slightly depressed in the center, slimy and sticky when wet, yellowish to orange-brown, often with a darker center.
gomphidius-glutinosus.stipe: Cylindrical, often tapered towards the base, white at the top and yellowish to reddish-brown downwards, covered in a gelatinous veil when young.
gomphidius-glutinosus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, particularly associated with conifers such as spruces and pines.
gomphidius-glutinosus.edibility: Edible, though not highly regarded due to its slimy texture.
gomphidius-glutinosus.microscopy: Spores 17-22 x 5-6.5 µm, elliptical and smooth.

gomphidius-roseus.hymenium: Gills, thick, decurrent, initially white or pale pink, becoming grayish to blackish as the spores mature
gomphidius-roseus.cap: Convex to broadly convex, often slightly depressed in the center, rosy pink to reddish in color, sticky and slimy when wet
gomphidius-roseus.stipe: Cylindrical, tapering towards the base, pale yellow to whitish, with faint fibrils and a sticky surface
gomphidius-roseus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, associated with pine trees, parasitic on Suillus bovinus mycelium, growing in mossy coniferous forests, late summer to autumn
gomphidius-roseus.edibility: Edible but not highly prized, often used in combination with other mushrooms
gomphidius-roseus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 5–10 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
gomphidius-roseus.odour: Odour mild, slightly fruity or mushroomy
gomphidius-roseus.microscopy: Smooth, spindle-shaped to ellipsoid, 18–22 x 5–6 µm, dark brown to black, basidia 2-spored

grifola-frondosa.hymenium: Pores, small and rounded when young (≈1–3/mm), becoming angular with maturity, tubes shallow (2–3 mm)
grifola-frondosa.fronds: Composed of many overlapping fan-shaped fronds, forming a rosette, wavy margins, color zones of tan, olive, gray, cream, surface tomentose to smooth
grifola-frondosa.hymenium-attachment: Poroid, decurrent across the undersides of fronds onto basal structure
grifola-frondosa.base: Short, branching, stout base from which all fronds emerge, white, compact, toughing with maturity
grifola-frondosa.ecology: Weakly parasitic and saprobic on oaks roots and stumps, fruits repeatedly at same base year after year, autumn
grifola-frondosa.description:
Red List (CR) I
Up to > 20 kg
grifola-frondosa.fruit-body: Fruit body size clusters 10–60 cm or more across
grifola-frondosa.flesh: Flesh white, firm when young, unchanging when cut, more fibrous with age
grifola-frondosa.taste: Rich, nutty, older parts acrid or bland flavor
grifola-frondosa.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid, 5–7×3.5–5 µm

gymnopilus-penetrans.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially pale yellow to ochre, becoming rusty orange to cinnamon-brown
gymnopilus-penetrans.cap: Convex to broadly convex, flattening with age, surface dry to slightly fibrillose, yellowish-orange to reddish-brown, often paler toward the margin
gymnopilus-penetrans.stipe: Cylindrical, slender, yellow to orange-brown, fibrillose, often darker toward the base, without a ring or veil remnants
gymnopilus-penetrans.spore-print: Spore print rusty orange to cinnamon-brown
gymnopilus-penetrans.ecology: Saprobic, typically on decaying conifer wood (pine chips), in groups, summer to late autumn
gymnopilus-penetrans.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 3–6 cm long, 0.3–0.8 cm thick
gymnopilus-penetrans.chemical-reactions: KOH reddish-orange on cap surface, flesh unchanging in ammonia
gymnopilus-penetrans.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, roughened to verrucose, 7–9 × 4–5 µm, rusty orange in KOH, dextrinoid, basidia 4-spored, cheilocystidia clavate to lageniform

gymnopilus-picreus.hymenium: Gills, crowded to moderately spaced, pale yellow to golden-yellow, becoming rust-brown with spore maturation
gymnopilus-picreus.cap: Convex to flat, surface smooth, orange-brown to reddish-brown, fading to a paler shade with age, margin initially inrolled, later straight
gymnopilus-picreus.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, orange to reddish-brown, darker towards the base, surface smooth or faintly fibrillose
gymnopilus-picreus.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood, logs, or stumps of deciduous and coniferous trees, solitary or in small clusters, late summer to autumn
gymnopilus-picreus.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium-sized, stipe 3–8 cm long, 0.3–0.8 cm thick
gymnopilus-picreus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, roughened, dextrinoid, 7–9 x 4–5 µm, rusty orange-brown in KOH, basidia clavate, 4-spored

gymnopus-dryophilus.hymenium: Gills that are broad, close to moderately spaced, and pale pinkish to creamy-brown, becoming darker with age.
gymnopus-dryophilus.cap: initially convex, later flat or slightly upturned; smooth, moist but not sticky, tan to brownish or occasionally reddish-brown.
gymnopus-dryophilus.stipe: 3-10 cm tall, 0.1-0.5 cm thick; smooth to slightly hairy; pale to brownish, often darker at the base.
gymnopus-dryophilus.spore-print: Spore Print: White to pale cream.
gymnopus-dryophilus.ecology: Saprobic; found in leaf litter, rotting wood, and grassy areas, particularly under oaks and other hardwoods.
gymnopus-dryophilus.edibility: Edible but not of high culinary value.
gymnopus-dryophilus.microscopy: Spores 6-9 x 2.5-4 µm, ellipsoid, smooth, and hyaline.

gyrodon-lividus.hymenium: Pores, large, angular to irregular, yellowish when young, becoming olive to brownish with age
gyrodon-lividus.cap: Convex to flat or slightly depressed with age, velvety when young, later smooth, dull yellow to olive-brown or tawny, margin initially inrolled, becoming wavy
gyrodon-lividus.stipe: Short, thick, cylindrical or slightly tapering, often curved, pale yellow to brownish, smooth or slightly fibrillose, no ring or veil
gyrodon-lividus.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with alder (Alnus spp.), found in moist, swampy areas, riparian zones, or near wet woodlands, late summer to autumn
gyrodon-lividus.edibility: Edible but not highly valued, consume only when young
gyrodon-lividus.fruit-body: Fruit body size medium-sized, cap 5–15 cm in diameter, stipe 3–7 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
gyrodon-lividus.chemical-reactions: Flesh slowly stains blue when cut, especially in the stipe base
gyrodon-lividus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, yellowish-brown in KOH, 10–13 × 4–5 µm, basidia 4-spored

hebeloma-crustuliniforme.hymenium: Gills crowded; whitish to pale cream when young, becoming clay- to cinnamon-brown with maturity; edges whitish
hebeloma-crustuliniforme.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to flat, sometimes obtusely umbonate; smooth, viscid when moist; whitish-buff, pale tan, usually darker centrally and paler toward margin
hebeloma-crustuliniforme.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly clavate, white to pale cream; pruinose or floccose-granular near apex, fibrillose below; base sometimes enlarged with white mycelial threads; ring absent
hebeloma-crustuliniforme.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; forests, woodland edges, dunes and grassy places beneath trees; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
hebeloma-crustuliniforme.edibility: Poisonous; causes gastrointestinal upset, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea
hebeloma-crustuliniforme.description: Gills often exuding clear droplets in moist weather that dry as rusty-brown spots
hebeloma-crustuliniforme.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~4–13 cm long and ~0.5–2 cm thick
hebeloma-crustuliniforme.flesh: White, thick and firm, unchanging when cut
hebeloma-crustuliniforme.microscopy: Spores amygdaloid, verrucose, yellow-brown, weakly dextrinoid, ~9–12 × 5–6.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant, clavate- to spathulate-stipitate; pleurocystidia absent; clamp connections present

hebeloma-mesophaeum.hymenium: Gills close to crowded; cream to pale clay-brown when young, becoming brown; edges often paler
hebeloma-mesophaeum.cap: Convex to broadly convex or nearly flat; smooth, distinctly sticky when moist; pinkish-brown centrally, contrasting with a pale buff to nearly whitish margin; young margin often with whitish veil remnants
hebeloma-mesophaeum.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to notched, sometimes with a slight decurrent tooth
hebeloma-mesophaeum.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, whitish to pale buff, gradually browning from base; silky-fibrillose; partial veil ephemeral to persistent, leaving fibrils
hebeloma-mesophaeum.ecology: Mycorrhizal, especially with pine; scattered to gregariously; forests, woodland edges, sandy and often acidic soils; late summer to autumn
hebeloma-mesophaeum.edibility: Might be poisonous and result in severe gastrointestinal upset; in Mexico this species is eaten and widely marketed
hebeloma-mesophaeum.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2–9 cm long and up to ~1 cm thick
hebeloma-mesophaeum.flesh: Whitish, moderately firm, unchanging when cut
hebeloma-mesophaeum.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, very finely verrucose to nearly smooth, ~8.5–11 × 5–7 µm, non-dextrinoid; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant; pileipellis an ixocutis

hebeloma-sinapizans.hymenium: Gills, crowded, adnate to sinuate, cream to pale clay-brown when young, turning darker with age, and often with a white, jagged edge
hebeloma-sinapizans.cap: Convex to flat, often with a slight umbo, becoming slightly depressed with age, surface is smooth and sticky when wet, with colors ranging from pale beige to ochre-brown
hebeloma-sinapizans.stipe: Stout, cylindrical, often tapering slightly towards the base, with a bulbous bas, white to pale beige and covered with silky fibrils
hebeloma-sinapizans.ecology: Mycorrhizal with oaks, beeches, and birches, found in deciduous and mixed woodlands, in well-drained soils, sometimes in large groups
hebeloma-sinapizans.edibility: Inedible due to its bitter taste and toxicity
hebeloma-sinapizans.microscopy: Spores elliptical to almond-shaped, 10–14 x 6–8 µm, finely roughened surface, basidia four-spored

helvella-acetabulum.cap: no distinct cap, but rather a lobed, cup-shaped structure, grayish-brown to dark brown, smooth or slightly wrinkled
helvella-acetabulum.stipe: stipe is hollow, cylindrical, furrowed, whitish to pale grayish-brown
helvella-acetabulum.edibility: edibility: not recommended, as some Helvella species contain the toxin gyromitrin

helvella-crispa.hymenium: Smooth to wrinkled or irregularly folded, covering the exposed upper surface of the saddle-shaped apothecium; ivory-white to cream or pale buff
helvella-crispa.apothecium: Irregularly saddle-, mitre- to lobed-shaped, usually with 2–4 strongly folded or curled lobes; whitish, ivory to pale cream; margin wavy
helvella-crispa.hymenium-attachment: Ffertile surface exposed over the upper lobes
helvella-crispa.stipe: Robust, white to cream, hollow and strongly longitudinally ribbed, fluted and chambered; ribs often branch and reconnect
helvella-crispa.ecology: Mycorrhizal, mainly with hardwoods such as beech and oak, occasionally with conifers; woodland, path edges and disturbed forest soil; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
helvella-crispa.edibility: Poisonous (hydrazine toxins); historically eaten after cooking
helvella-crispa.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~4–10 cm long and ~0.8–3 cm thick
helvella-crispa.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, usually with one large central oil droplet, ~17–21 × 10–13 µm; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~220–300 × 12–18 µm, inamyloid;

helvella-lacunosa.cap: 2-6 cm across. Saddle-shaped, often with irregular lobes. The surface is smooth, dark gray to almost black, and appears somewhat wrinkled or veined.
helvella-lacunosa.hymenium: Smooth, covering the undersurface of the cap's lobes.
helvella-lacunosa.stipe: Tall and distinctive, with deep, irregular pits and ridges. It is hollow, with a similarly dark color as the cap but can be somewhat paler.
helvella-lacunosa.spore-print: Spore Print: White to pale cream.
helvella-lacunosa.ecology: Saprobic, found on the ground in mixed woods, particularly under hardwood trees.

hemitrichia-decipiens.plasmodium-color-stage: In active phase, plasmodium is white or pale, later may show orange or salmon tints toward maturity
hemitrichia-decipiens.fruiting-bodies: Sporocarps borne on slender stalks, typically egg-shaped or conical; the sporangia are often clustered and brightly colored in development
hemitrichia-decipiens.peridium: Thin peridium, often shining, ranging from orange-yellow to more olive or brown with age; peridium may persist as a calyculus when spores dehisce
hemitrichia-decipiens.description:
Stalk is part of the sporocarp
Spore mass olive to olive-yellow spore mass inside sporangium
Amoeboflagellate cells → multinucleate → sporulation producing stalked sporangia with internal spores → spores released and germinating back to amoeboflagellates
Spores: Globose to subglobose, ~10–13 µm in diameter, reticulate or warty
Stalk: Tissue may contain pseudocclusions in some populations
hemitrichia-decipiens.ecology: Habitat: On decaying wood (logs, branches) in conifer and mixed forests, present in clusters on rotten wood surfaces in humid conditions
hemitrichia-decipiens.fruit-body: Sporangia dimensions: Sporangia up to ~0.6–0.8 mm in diameter, stalked up to ~3 mm tall (or less) in many populations
hemitrichia-decipiens.spore-print: Capillitia: net-like network of threads that often take on the spore color

hortiboletus-rubellus.hymenium: Pores angular, yellow at first, becoming dull olive-yellow with age, bruising blue
hortiboletus-rubellus.cap: Convex to broadly convex or nearly flat; dry, smooth to finely velvety when young; bright ruby-red, cherry-red to pinkish-red, often fading and cracking with age
hortiboletus-rubellus.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly depressed around the stipe
hortiboletus-rubellus.stipe: Slender, yellow at apex, pinkish-red to red below, often with red dots or points, not reticulate
hortiboletus-rubellus.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with broadleaved trees, especially oaks; in woodland edges, parks, gardens, lawns, meadows and disturbed roadsides; summer to autumn
hortiboletus-rubellus.edibility: Edible but poor quality, often maggot-infested and sometimes described as soapy
hortiboletus-rubellus.fruit-body: Fruit body: Small to medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long, ~0.4–1 cm thick
hortiboletus-rubellus.flesh: Flesh: whitish to yellowish, slowly and slightly blueing when cut
hortiboletus-rubellus.chemical-reactions: KOH: Dull orange on cap surface and flesh
hortiboletus-rubellus.microscopy: Spores subfusoid, smooth, ~10–13 × 4–5 µm; golden in KOH; hymenial cystidia lageniform; pileipellis a palisadoderm of septate, encrusted elements

humaria-hemisphaerica.hymenium: Smooth, hymenial surface exposed in mature specimens.
humaria-hemisphaerica.cap: Hemispherical, initially covered in a layer of white mycelium, later revealing orange-brown to dark brown surface.
humaria-hemisphaerica.spore-print: Spore Print: White to pale yellow.
humaria-hemisphaerica.ecology: Saprobic, often found on well-decayed wood or forest floor rich in organic material.

hydnellum-aurantiacum.hymenium: Consists of spines or teeth, varying from pale yellow to orange.
hydnellum-aurantiacum.cap: 3-10 cm across, typically irregular or lobed, bright orange when young, fading with age.
hydnellum-aurantiacum.hymenium-attachment: Spines are decurrent along the stipe.
hydnellum-aurantiacum.stipe: 2-6 cm long, 0.5-1.5 cm thick; typically lighter than the cap, often covered in orange mycelium at the base.
hydnellum-aurantiacum.microscopy: Spores 4.5-6 x 3-4.5 µm, elliptical, with warts.

hydnellum-peckii.hymenium: Spines, whitish when young, becoming brown with age, 3–6 mm long, hanging down from the underside of the cap
hydnellum-peckii.cap: Irregularly shaped, and convex with a depressed center, surface is rough and covered with a white to pinkish crust that exudes blood-like droplets when young, color of the cap darkens to a brownish/tan as it matures
hydnellum-peckii.stipe: Off-center, cylindrical, and covered with a rough, fibrous surface that is similar in color to the cap
hydnellum-peckii.ecology: Mycorrhizal with coniferous trees (pines and spruces), on the ground, among moss and litter, solitary or in small groups from late summer to early autumn
hydnellum-peckii.edibility: Inedible due to its bitter taste and tough, fibrous texture
hydnellum-peckii.microscopy: Spores roughly spherical, 5–6 x 4–5 µm, covered with small spines, hyphae are monomitic, with clamp connections

hygrocybe-acutoconica.hymenium: Gills broad, moderately spaced; pale yellow to lemon-yellow, becoming yellow-orange with maturity
hygrocybe-acutoconica.cap: Sharply conical to conical-campanulate, later broadly conical with pointed umbo; smooth, viscid when moist; lemon-yellow, golden-yellow; margin translucent-striate and often splitting with age
hygrocybe-acutoconica.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, sometimes twisted or longitudinally grooved; yellow to orange with a whitish base; smooth to finely fibrillose; ring absent
hygrocybe-acutoconica.description: Symbiotic with higher plants and mosses; associated with unimproved nutrient-poor grasslands, meadows; neutral to calcareous soils; solitary or scattered; summer to late autumn
hygrocybe-acutoconica.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2–8(–13) cm long and ~0.3–1.2 cm thick
hygrocybe-acutoconica.flesh: Yellowish, thin and fragile, does not blacken
hygrocybe-acutoconica.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~9–12 × 5–7 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; hymenial cystidia absent; lamellar trama parallel; pileipellis an ixocutis

hygrocybe-coccinea.hymenium: Gills that are spaced moderately apart, white to pale cream, becoming more yellowish with age.
hygrocybe-coccinea.cap: Initially conical or bell-shaped, expanding to become broadly convex or almost flat; bright scarlet to red-orange, sometimes fading with age.
hygrocybe-coccinea.stipe: Cylindrical, often tapering towards the base; similarly colored to the cap or slightly paler, moist but not slimy.
hygrocybe-coccinea.description: Saprobic, found in grasslands, meadows, and other grassy areas, often after rains.
hygrocybe-coccinea.edibility: Edible, but not particularly sought after due to its small size and rarity.
hygrocybe-coccinea.microscopy: Spores 7-10 x 4-5 µm, ellipsoid, hyaline, smooth.
hygrocybe-coccinea.odour: Not particularly distinctive, sometimes faintly sweet or fragrant.

hygrocybe-conica.hymenium: Gills moderately close, initially pale yellow to orange-yellow, becoming orange and finally grey-black
hygrocybe-conica.cap: Sharply conical to bell-shaped, sometimes broadly conical with age; smooth, greasy to slightly viscid when moist, silky when dry; yellow, orange to scarlet-red
hygrocybe-conica.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, sometimes flattened or longitudinally grooved; yellow to orange-yellow, paler toward base; fragile, ring absent
hygrocybe-conica.ecology: Ecology uncertain; in unimproved nutrient-poor grasslands, meadows, lawns, churchyards, roadside verges and mossy turf; alone or gregariously; summer to late autumn
hygrocybe-conica.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–10 cm long and ~0.3–1 cm thick
hygrocybe-conica.flesh: Yellow to orange, thin and fragile, rapidly becoming grey-black to jet black when cut or bruised
hygrocybe-conica.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to oblong, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8–11.5 × 5–7.5 µm; basidia 2- or 4-spored; hymenial cystidia absent; lamellar trama parallel; pileipellis an ixocutis

hygrocybe-miniata.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, pale orange to reddish-orange, sometimes with a yellowish edge
hygrocybe-miniata.cap: Convex to flat, often with a small central depression, surface dry, finely scurfy or granular, bright scarlet to orange-red, fading to orange or yellowish with age
hygrocybe-miniata.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, dry, smooth or faintly fibrous, scarlet to reddish-orange, often paler towards the base, hollow
hygrocybe-miniata.description: Likely saprobic, in mossy grasslands, heaths, woodland edges, nutrient-poor or acidic soils, late summer to autumn
hygrocybe-miniata.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 3–6 cm long, 2–4 mm thick
hygrocybe-miniata.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid or constricted and subpyriform, smooth, 5–9 x 3–4.5 µm, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, basidia 35–45 µm, 4-sterigmate

hygrophorus-agathosmus.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, decurrent, white to pale gray, sometimes with a slight waxy appearance
hygrophorus-agathosmus.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming flat with age, smooth, viscid or slimy when wet, gray to grayish-brown, margin incurved when young
hygrophorus-agathosmus.stipe: Slender to thick, cylindrical, white to grayish, sometimes with a faint, slimy coating when young, becoming dry with age
hygrophorus-agathosmus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, found in association with conifers (spruces and pines), in coniferous and mixed forests, autumn
hygrophorus-agathosmus.edibility: Edible, with a mild taste and pleasant fragrance, though not widely consumed
hygrophorus-agathosmus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 4-8 cm long, 0.5-1.5 cm thick
hygrophorus-agathosmus.odour: Odour strong, pleasant, almond-like or marzipan-like scent
hygrophorus-agathosmus.microscopy: Ellipsoid, smooth, 7-10 x 4-5 µ, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, basidia 4-sterigmate, 45-60 µ long

hygrophorus-persoonii.hymenium: Gills broad, waxy and moderately distant; white to cream, sometimes developing faint ochraceous tones with age
hygrophorus-persoonii.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later to nearly flat; strongly glutinous; honey-brown, chestnut to ochraceous-brown, usually darker centrally and paler toward margin
hygrophorus-persoonii.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly clavate, strongly glutinous below; whitish and dry near apex, with ochraceous-brown to olive-brown bands or patches lower down; ring absent
hygrophorus-persoonii.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods, especially oak, also beech and hazel; deciduous forests and groves, on calcareous soil; scattered to gregariously; autumn to late autumn
hygrophorus-persoonii.edibility: Edible but modest; thick gluten often removed before cooking
hygrophorus-persoonii.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~5–12 cm long and ~0.5–1.5 cm thick
hygrophorus-persoonii.flesh: White, firm when young, becoming slightly spongy with age; unchanging when cut
hygrophorus-persoonii.chemical-reactions: NH₄OH greenish-blue on cap and stipe gluten; KOH dark blue-green on cap, reddish-orange toward stipe base
hygrophorus-persoonii.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8.1–10.8(–11.3) × 5.3–6.7 µm; basidia 4-spored, occasionally 2-spored; cystidia absent

hymenoscyphus-epiphyllus.hymenium: Smooth, pale yellow to egg-yellow, sometimes olive-yellow or ochraceous; becoming ochre-brown with age
hymenoscyphus-epiphyllus.apothecium: Cup- to shallow disc-shaped, later nearly flat; fleshy-waxy, pale yellow to yellow-orange; often slightly reddening when damaged
hymenoscyphus-epiphyllus.stipe: Very short to rudimentary, pale yellow to whitish; sometimes nearly sessile
hymenoscyphus-epiphyllus.description:
Saprobic on decaying broadleaf litter, especially fallen leaves of oak, beech, maple, hornbeam and birch; also petioles and other small plant debris; scattered to densely gregarious; late summer to late autumn
Paraphyses cylindrical with strongly refractive yellowish guttules
hymenoscyphus-epiphyllus.edibility: Inedible; tiny and without culinary value
hymenoscyphus-epiphyllus.fruit-body: Fruit body tiny; usually only a few millimetres tall
hymenoscyphus-epiphyllus.flesh: Pale yellow to whitish, thin and waxy; sometimes reddening slightly when damaged
hymenoscyphus-epiphyllus.microscopy: Ascospores asymmetric fusiform to narrowly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, usually ~15–23 × 3–5.5 µm, aseptate when young and occasionally septate when overmature, with several oil droplets; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~90–135 × 9–11 µm, apical pore amyloid

hymenoscyphus-fructigenus.hymenium: Smooth fertile disc, whitish to cream or pale yellow-ochre; flat to slightly concave, becoming flatter with maturity
hymenoscyphus-fructigenus.apothecium: Minute, cup- to disc-shaped, soft and waxy; outer surface whitish, smooth to minutely downy
hymenoscyphus-fructigenus.hymenium-attachment: Exposed on upper surface of the apothecium
hymenoscyphus-fructigenus.ecology: Saprobic on fallen acorns, acorn cupules and other decaying nut shells, especially Quercus; also reported from Fagus, Corylus and Carpinus fruits; usually in small groups; late summer to autumn
hymenoscyphus-fructigenus.fruit-body: Fruit body tiny; stipe ~0.5–10 mm long
hymenoscyphus-fructigenus.flesh: Whitish to cream, thin, soft and waxy, unchanging when cut
hymenoscyphus-fructigenus.microscopy: Ascospores fusiform-ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, ~13–21 × 3–5 µm, aseptate when young and sometimes 1-septate at maturity; asci cylindrical-clavate, 8-spored, ~80–140 × 7–10 µm, apical pore hemiamyloid; paraphyses filiform

hymenoscyphus-lutescens.hymenium: Smooth, exposed on the inner surface of the apothecium, pale yellow to cream in color
hymenoscyphus-lutescens.cap: Cup-shaped to saucer-shaped, pale yellow to ochre, thin and fragile
hymenoscyphus-lutescens.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Forms the interior surface of the cup)
hymenoscyphus-lutescens.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, translucent white to pale yellow
hymenoscyphus-lutescens.description: Saprobic, grows on decaying pine cones (Pinus sp.), in coniferous forests, in damp forest floors, late spring to early autumn
hymenoscyphus-lutescens.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 5–15 mm long, 0.5–1 mm thick
hymenoscyphus-lutescens.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to elliptical, smooth, 10–15 x 3–5 µm, hyaline, inamyloid, basidia 8-spored

hypholoma-capnoides.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially pale orangish-yellow, pale grey when mature, later darker purple/brown
hypholoma-capnoides.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming slightly flattened with age, honey-yellow to orange-brown, often paler at the margin, with a smooth and slightly sticky surface
hypholoma-capnoides.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, yellowish to orange-brown, darker towards the base, fibrous, with faint remnants of a cortina or veil
hypholoma-capnoides.ecology: Saprobic, found growing in clusters on decaying coniferous wood, especially stumps and logs, autumn
hypholoma-capnoides.edibility: Edible with mild taste, but can be confused with the poisonous Hypholoma fasciculare, so caution is advised
hypholoma-capnoides.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 5–10 cm long, 0.5–1.5 cm thick
hypholoma-capnoides.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 6–8 x 3.5–4.5 µm, basidia 4-spored

hypholoma-fasciculare.hymenium: Gills crowded, adnate; sulphur-yellow when young, becoming olive-green, then dark purplish-brown to blackish
hypholoma-fasciculare.cap: Convex to broadly convex or nearly flat; sulphur-greenish-yellow, darker orange-brown in centre; smooth, dry, sometimes with small veil fragments at margin
hypholoma-fasciculare.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, often curved; yellow to tawny, browner toward base; partial veil evanescent, sometimes leaving a faint fibrillose ring zone
hypholoma-fasciculare.ecology: Saprobic on dead wood, stumps, fallen trunks, buried roots and logs of hardwoods and conifers, often in dense clustered tufts, mainly summer to autumn
hypholoma-fasciculare.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, stipe ~3–12 cm long, ~0.4–1.0 cm thick
hypholoma-fasciculare.flesh: Flesh thin, sulphur-yellow, firm, unchanging when cut
hypholoma-fasciculare.chemical-reactions: KOH: No distinctive macroscopic field reaction documented; spores yellowish in KOH microscopically
hypholoma-fasciculare.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, thin-walled, with germ pore, ~5–8 × 3–4.5 µm; pleurochrysocystidia fusoid-ventricose to mucronate; pileipellis a cutis or ixocutis with encrusted elements

hypholoma-lateritium.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially yellowish or pale gray but turning dark gray to purple-brown as the spores mature
hypholoma-lateritium.cap: convex when young, flattening with age, and often with a broad, umbonate, brick-red to orange-red, sometimes fading toward the margin
hypholoma-lateritium.stipe: cylindrical, fibrous, yellowish to reddish-brown, lighter near the top and darker toward the base, with veil remnants of faint ring or fibrous zone
hypholoma-lateritium.ecology: Saprobic, grows in dense clusters on decaying hardwood logs, stumps, and buried wood, in deciduous forests, autumn, also in spring
hypholoma-lateritium.edibility: Edible (nutty-flavour), potential confusion with toxic species
hypholoma-lateritium.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 5–10 cm long and 0.5–1.5 cm thick
hypholoma-lateritium.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid, 6–7 x 4–5 µm, with prominent germ pore, basidia 4-spored, cheilocystidia are flask-shaped or clavate

hypomyces-chrysospermus.hymenium: Smooth in the early (white) stage, later becomes covered by golden-yellow or reddish-brown spore masses, final sexual stages produce perithecia giving it a crusted texture
hypomyces-chrysospermus.spore-print: Spore print white (early asexual stages), yellow when spore coating is abundant, sexual sporulation less visible for spore print
hypomyces-chrysospermus.ecology: Parasitic on bolete mushrooms (Boletaceae), begins infecting the pore surface and spreads over cap and stem, summer through autumn, more noticeable in wet seasons
hypomyces-chrysospermus.description:
Asexual: Ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline; ~ 8-12 × 3.5-5 µm.
Aleuriospores: Round, warty/spiny, yellow; ~ 9-20 µm diameter.
Ascospores (sexual): Fusiform to lanceolate, often bi-septate or bicellular, ~ 20-30 × 4-6 µm.
Initially appears as a white cottony or floccose coat, turning golden yellow then reddish-brown and crusty.
It produces multiple spore types in its lifecycle (two asexual, one sexual), progressively changing texture and coloration.

hypomyces-lateritius.hymenium: Perithecia immersed to partly exposed in the subiculum, dark amber to reddish-brown, appearing as minute pimples over the infected surface
hypomyces-lateritius.body: Dense coating covering and deforming the host hymenium; initially white to lemon-yellow, becoming buff, ochre, orange-brown and finally brick-red to reddish-brown
hypomyces-lateritius.description:
Spore mass hyaline; mature infected surface ochre to brick-red
Parasitized host becomes firm, deformed and partially mummified
hypomyces-lateritius.ecology: Fungicolous parasite mainly on Lactarius species, especially orange-milkcaps; covers undeveloped gills; summer to autumn
hypomyces-lateritius.edibility: Edibility depends on the correctly identified host mushroom
hypomyces-lateritius.fruit-body: Fruiting layer thin, spreading across substantial portions or nearly all of the host hymenium
hypomyces-lateritius.chemical-reactions: KOH subiculum negative; perithecia becoming yellowish
