hypomyces-lateritius.microscopy: Ascospores fusiform to lanceolate/naviculate, finely verrucose, aseptate, ~15–27 × 3.5–5.5 µm, with conspicuous acute apiculi at both ends; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~90–150 × 4–8 µm; anamorph forms subglobose aseptate conidia ~5–6.5 × 4.5–6 µm

hypomyces-luteovirens.ecology: Parasitic on the fruit bodies of mushrooms, particularly species of Russula and Lactarius.
hypomyces-luteovirens.edibility: Not typically consumed. While not known to be toxic, the altered texture and appearance due to the parasitic mold make it unappetizing.
hypomyces-luteovirens.fruit-body: Varies depending on the size of the host mushroom, but is completely transformed in appearance by the mold.
hypomyces-luteovirens.dimensions: Cap size varies depending on the host.

hypoxylon-fuscum.spore-print: Spore print dark brown to black
hypoxylon-fuscum.ecology: Saprobic, primarily found on dead or dying wood of hazel species (sometimes found on other hardwood species), contributes to wood decay and is commonly found on fallen branches and dead trunks in forests and woodland areas
hypoxylon-fuscum.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to fusiform, 8–12 x 3.5–5 µm, smooth, and feature a distinct germ slit that runs the length of the spore, perithecia are embedded within a dark brown to black stromatic tissue, which forms irregular crusts on the surface of the host wood

imleria-badia.hymenium: Pores, small and round, yellowish when young, turning olive to brown with age
imleria-badia.cap: Convex to flat with maturity, smooth, slightly sticky when wet, chestnut-brown to dark brown, often with a velvety sheen when dry.
imleria-badia.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly depressed around the stipe
imleria-badia.stipe: Slender to slightly bulbous, cylindrical, smooth or faintly wrinkled, pale brown to reddish-brown, lacking a ring or veil
imleria-badia.ecology: Mycorrhizal, associated with pines, spruces, and birches, grows in soil, mossy areas, leaf litter, summer to late autumn
imleria-badia.edibility: Edible and highly regarded, firm texture and pleasant nutty flavor
imleria-badia.fruit-body: Medium to large, cap 5–15 cm in diameter, stipe 4–12 cm long, 1–3 cm thick
imleria-badia.chemical-reactions: Flesh quickly blue when cut or bruised
imleria-badia.microscopy: Spores boletoid-fusiform, 11–15 x 4–6 µm, smooth, ochraceous in KOH, basidia 2- or 4-sterigmate

infundibulicybe-geotropa.hymenium: Gills crowded, broad; whitish to cream when young, pale buff to yellowish with age
infundibulicybe-geotropa.cap: Convex when young with a prominent central umbo, then flat to deeply funnel-shaped; smooth to finely felted; cream, buff, pale ochre to tan; margin strongly inrolled when young, then wavy
infundibulicybe-geotropa.stipe:
Tall, robust, solid to spongy with age, cylindrical to distinctly enlarged toward base; whitish to pale buff, finely fibrillose; white basal mycelium; ring absent
Good edible when young; stipe too fibrous and tough
infundibulicybe-geotropa.description: Saprobic in leaf and needle litter, humus and grassy woodland soils; woodland edges, parks and grasslands; often in large troops, arcs or impressive fairy rings; late summer to late autumn
infundibulicybe-geotropa.fruit-body: Fruit body large; stipe ~6–20 cm long and ~1.3–3 cm thick
infundibulicybe-geotropa.flesh: White, thick, firm and slightly elastic, unchanging when cut
infundibulicybe-geotropa.chemical-reactions: Guaiac slowly dark blue-green on flesh
infundibulicybe-geotropa.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid or sublacrymoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~6–9.5 × 5–7 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis; clamp connections present

infundibulicybe-gibba.hymenium: Gills narrow, close to crowded; white to cream, becoming pale buff with age
infundibulicybe-gibba.cap: Convex when young, later broadly depressed to deeply funnel-shaped, retaining a small central umbo; smooth; cream, pinkish-buff to pale ochre-brown; margin initially inrolled, later wavy
infundibulicybe-gibba.stipe: Cylindrical, tough and fibrous, cream to pale buff; slightly enlarged at base with conspicuous white cottony mycelium; becoming hollow with age; ring absent
infundibulicybe-gibba.ecology: Saprobic among leaf and needle litter and humus; scattered, gregarious; forests, woodland edges and heathland; summer to late autumn
infundibulicybe-gibba.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.5–1 cm thick
infundibulicybe-gibba.flesh: Whitish, thin, soft, unchanging when cut
infundibulicybe-gibba.chemical-reactions: KOH sometimes briefly pale green on fresh cap surface
infundibulicybe-gibba.microscopy: Spores lacrymoid to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–8 × 3–5 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent; pileipellis a cutis; clamp connections present

inocybe-cincinnata.hymenium: Gills, crowded, and start off pale or cream-colored, eventually becoming grayish-brown with maturity
inocybe-cincinnata.cap: The cap is conical to convex, sometimes becoming broadly umbonate with age, surface is fibrillose to scaly, color brownish, with a more reddish-brown center, margins are striate when moist
inocybe-cincinnata.stipe: 4–7 cm long, 0.5–1 cm thick, cylindrical, slightly enlarged at the base, surface is fibrillose, typically the same color as the cap or paler, sometimes with faint brownish fibrils, no ring
inocybe-cincinnata.ecology: Mycorrhizal with deciduous trees (beech, oak) and conifers, in mixed and coniferous woodlands, on the forest floor, in well-drained soils, in autumn
inocybe-cincinnata.edibility: Toxic, contains muscarine, poisonous if ingested (sweating, salivation, abdominal pain, vomiting diarrhea)
inocybe-cincinnata.fruit-body: Fruit Body: Medium-sized, stipe 4–7 cm tall
inocybe-cincinnata.microscopy: Spores smooth, amygdaliform, 7–10 x 4.5–6 µm, cystidia fusiform, have thick-walled structures, basidia 4-spored

inocybe-geophylla.hymenium: Gills that are crowded, adnexed to almost free; initially pale then becoming brownish as the spores mature.
inocybe-geophylla.cap: Conical to bell-shaped, often with a small umbo; smooth or with tiny fibrous scales; white or pale lilac in variety lilacina.
inocybe-geophylla.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, and often swollen at the base; fibrous, white or slightly lilac in variety lilacina, with a bulbous base.
inocybe-geophylla.ecology: Mycorrhizal with broad-leaved trees, especially in grassy areas and parks.
inocybe-geophylla.odour: Mild, sometimes with a slightly mealy scent.
inocybe-geophylla.edibility: Toxic; contains muscarine which can cause serious poisoning.
inocybe-geophylla.fruit-body: Cap diameter of 1.5-4 cm; stipe length of 4-6 cm.
inocybe-geophylla.microscopy: Spores are almond-shaped, 7-9 x 4-5 µm, smooth, and brown in mass.

inocybe-lilacina.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially pale then turning snuff-brown with age; edges whitish and often exhibiting a delicate cortina in youth
inocybe-lilacina.cap: convex to broadly convex with a persistent central bump; surface silky, somewhat sticky when fresh, then dry; often lilac in center fading toward margins
inocybe-lilacina.stipe: subequal or slightly swollen at base; surface silky, whitish above, lilac below, becoming hollow; basal mycelium white
inocybe-lilacina.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers, singly/in small groups in forested or woodland habitats, summer–autumn
inocybe-lilacina.fruit-body: Small, stipe 2–4 cm long, 2–4 mm thick
inocybe-lilacina.microscopy: Spores smooth, elliptic to subamygdaliform, ~10–12×4–5 µm; basidia ~20–23×5–7 µm, clavate, 4-sterigmate, cheilocystidia/pleurocystidia 40–65 × 10–15 µm lageniform

inosperma-erubescens.hymenium: Gills, adnexed to adnate, crowded, initially whitish, becoming pinkish-brown to reddish-brown with age.
inosperma-erubescens.cap: 2-7 cm in diameter, convex to bell-shaped, often with an umbo; smooth to fibrillose; color ranges from white to cream, often bruising reddish or pinkish.
inosperma-erubescens.stipe: Cylindrical, sometimes with a bulbous base; white to cream, bruising reddish; often fibrillose.
inosperma-erubescens.ecology: Ecology is mycorrhizal, forming symbiotic relationships with broadleaf trees such as beech and oak.
inosperma-erubescens.edibility: Toxic; contains muscarine and can cause serious poisoning.
inosperma-erubescens.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to oblong, 8-11 x 5-6 μm; cystidia present on gills, often thick-walled and encrusted.

ischnoderma-benzoinum.hymenium: Pores, creamy, bruising brown, in maturity dark brown and hard, 3–4 per mm, tubes 2–4 mm deep.
ischnoderma-benzoinum.cap: Semicircular to fan-shaped, dark brown to reddish-brown, velvety when young, becoming smooth and darker with age, margin paler and wavy
ischnoderma-benzoinum.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, directly attached to wood
ischnoderma-benzoinum.ecology: Saprobic, growing on dead coniferous wood, particularly spruce and fir, causing white rot, annual, late summer to autumn
ischnoderma-benzoinum.edibility: Inedible due to tough structure, reported edible at a young age
ischnoderma-benzoinum.chemical-reactions: KOH black on cap surface and flesh
ischnoderma-benzoinum.odour: Odour pleasant, reminiscent of anise or vanilla when fresh
ischnoderma-benzoinum.microscopy: Spores allantoid, smooth, 5–7 x 1–2 µm, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, cystidia not found

kretzschmaria-deusta.hymenium: Typically located on the irregular, crust-like surface of the fruiting body, dark gray to black, turning powdery or ash-like with age
kretzschmaria-deusta.cap: Lacks a true cap, forms as an encrusting, flattened mass that adheres closely to the substrate, often with a rough, cracked, or uneven texture, initially pale gray to dark gray, becoming black with age
kretzschmaria-deusta.ecology: Parasitic and saprobic, primarily on hardwoods, causes white rot decay in living trees, on dead wood or decayed sections of living trees, throughout the growing season
kretzschmaria-deusta.fruit-body: Fruiting body crust-like, spreading, often covering areas up to 10–30 cm in diameter
kretzschmaria-deusta.chemical-reactions: KOH negative, does not react visibly with common reagents
kretzschmaria-deusta.odour: Odour indistinct or slightly unpleasant when fresh
kretzschmaria-deusta.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 16–30 x 5–9 µm, black in mass, hyaline to slightly tinted individually

laccaria-laccata.hymenium: Gills thick, broad and moderately distant; pinkish-flesh to salmon or pale reddish-brown, becoming paler as spores mature
laccaria-laccata.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to flat or centrally depressed; smooth to finely fibrillose; orange-brown, reddish-brown to tan when moist, fading to almost whitish when dry
laccaria-laccata.stipe: Slender, tough and fibrous, cylindrical or tapering toward base; coloured similarly to cap, becoming paler when dry; finely hairy toward base with white basal mycelium; ring absent
laccaria-laccata.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods and conifers; alone, scattered or gregariously; forests, woodland edges and heathland; summer to late autumn
laccaria-laccata.edibility: Edible but modest; caps usable, stems tough and fibrous
laccaria-laccata.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2–10 cm long and ~1 cm thick
laccaria-laccata.flesh: Thin, pale orange-brown to buff, unchanging when cut
laccaria-laccata.microscopy: Spores globose to subglobose, strongly echinulate, ~7–10 µm, with spines ~1–2 µm tall; hyaline, inamyloid; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia filamentous to subclavate; pileipellis a cutis

lactarius-aquizonatus.hymenium: Gills, crowded, cream to pale yellow, often turning darker with age or when bruised
lactarius-aquizonatus.cap: Initially convex, becoming more flattened with a central depression as it matures, surface is smooth to slightly sticky, typically greyish-brown to ochre with concentric zones
lactarius-aquizonatus.stipe: Cylindrical, firm, smooth, and generally the same color as the cap, though slightly paler towards the base, hollow when mature
lactarius-aquizonatus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, often found in association with coniferous trees
lactarius-aquizonatus.description: Before pickling, it requires a long soaking (up to 2-3 days with repeated water changes) to remove the stinging milky juice,belongs to mushrooms of 4th category.
lactarius-aquizonatus.microscopy: Spores are broadly ellipsoid, with warts connected by fine ridges forming a partial reticulum, 6,1–8,4 × 4,1 µm

lactarius-aurantiacus.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; whitish to cream when young, becoming pinkish-buff to pale ochre
lactarius-aurantiacus.cap: Convex when young, later broadly flat to shallowly depressed; smooth, dry to slightly glossy; vivid orange, orange-red to orange-brown; unzoned, margin initially inrolled
lactarius-aurantiacus.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly clavate, smooth, orange-brown to yellow-orange, usually paler near apex; becoming hollow with age; ring absent
lactarius-aurantiacus.spore-print: Spore print ivory to pale cream
lactarius-aurantiacus.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce and pine, occasionally birch and other hardwoods; coniferous and mixed forests, often on acidic soils; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
lactarius-aurantiacus.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2.5–7 cm long and ~0.5–1.2 cm thick
lactarius-aurantiacus.flesh: Whitish to pale orange, brittle; abundant white latex unchanging, mild
lactarius-aurantiacus.chemical-reactions: Guaiac grey-green; FeSO₄ grey-green on flesh
lactarius-aurantiacus.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, ~7–9.5 × 6–7.5 µm, ornamented with low amyloid warts and connecting ridges; numerous fusoid cystidia

lactarius-azonites.hymenium: Gills crowded, narrow; whitish to cream when young, becoming cream-ochre to yellowish
lactarius-azonites.cap: Convex when young, later flat to centrally depressed; dry, matte, finely pruinose to velvety; pale ochre, grey-brown to smoky brown, often irregularly paler toward margin; unzoned
lactarius-azonites.stipe: Cylindrical, often tapering toward base; initially white to whitish, later cream-grey; smooth to finely pruinose; becoming hollow with age
lactarius-azonites.spore-print: Spore print pale cream to ochre, sometimes pinkish-buff
lactarius-azonites.ecology: Mycorrhizal with hardwoods, especially oak and chestnut, also beech; deciduous forests, parks and woodland edges, on calcareous soil; scattered to gregariously; summer to autumn
lactarius-azonites.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.5–1.5 cm thick
lactarius-azonites.flesh: Whitish to cream, brittle, turning salmon-pink to pink-orange within minutes when cut; abundant white latex also stains gills and flesh pink but remains white when isolated
lactarius-azonites.chemical-reactions: Guaiac rapidly blue-green; KOH negative on flesh and latex; FeSO₄ weak to nearly negative
lactarius-azonites.taste: Mild initially, then slightly bitter to acrid
lactarius-azonites.microscopy: Spores globose to subglobose, ~7–9 × 6–8.5 µm, ornamented with amyloid warts and ridges; basidia 4-spored; cheilomacrocystidia abundant, fusiform with elongated necks; pileipellis a trichoderm

lactarius-controversus.hymenium: Gills, white to pale cream, crowded, adnate to slightly decurrent
lactarius-controversus.cap: Convex when young, becoming flat or slightly depressed with age, surface is white to pale pinkish, often with concentric zones, sticky when wet
lactarius-controversus.stipe: Stout, cylindrical, and tapers slightly at the base, white to pale cream, slightly rough surface
lactarius-controversus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with poplars, willows, and birches, grows in moist, grassy wooded meadow areas, often in large groups
lactarius-controversus.edibility: Not favored due to its acrid taste, can be consumed after parboiling and soaking to remove bitterness
lactarius-controversus.microscopy: Spores are broadly elliptical to subglobose, 8–10 x 6–8 µm, reticulate surface, basidia four-spored

lactarius-deliciosus.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, crowded, initially pale orange, darkening with age
hymenium is lamellar
lactarius-deliciosus.cap: cap is convex, becoming depressed with age, orange with darker orange concentric zones, often with a slightly wrinkled surface
lactarius-deliciosus.stipe: stipe is cylindrical, hollow, orange with darker orange spots or streaks, exudes a carrot-colored latex when cut or broken
lactarius-deliciosus.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal, typically found in coniferous and mixed forests, often associated with pine trees

lactarius-deterrimus.hymenium: Gills, closely spaced, decurrent, pale orange to carrot-orange when young
lactarius-deterrimus.cap: convex to flat with a slight central depression, becoming funnel-shaped with age, surface is smooth and sticky when wet, orange to reddish-orange, often with concentric darker zones
lactarius-deterrimus.stipe: Cylindrical, often hollow with age, 4–8 cm long and 1–2 cm thick, colored similarly to the cap—orange to reddish-orange
lactarius-deterrimus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, growing in association with spruce (Picea spp.). Found in coniferous forests, from late summer to autumn, prefers acidic soils
lactarius-deterrimus.edibility: Edible, but not as highly regarded as its relative, Lactarius deliciosus
lactarius-deterrimus.odour: Fruity or slightly resinous, sometimes faint
lactarius-deterrimus.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid with ridged, reticulated ornamentation, 7.5–9 × 6–7 µm. Basidia are four-spored, 40–50 × 8–10 µm

lactarius-evosmus.hymenium: Gills that are adnate to slightly decurrent, close to moderately spaced, and cream-colored to pale ochre, they exude a white to slightly yellowish latex when damaged
lactarius-evosmus.cap: Convex when young, becoming more flattened or slightly depressed with age, surface is smooth, sticky when wet, sometimes zoned, color varies from pale yellowish to ochre
lactarius-evosmus.stipe: Cylindrical or slightly tapered towards the base, similar in color to the cap or paler, surface is smooth and dry
lactarius-evosmus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with deciduous trees (oak and aspen), prefers calcareous soils
lactarius-evosmus.edibility: Inedible, not considered toxic, has an acrid taste
lactarius-evosmus.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, 7–8 µm x 5–6.5 µm, reticulate surface, basidia four-spored, cystidia abundant on the gill edges, swollen at the apex

lactarius-helvus.hymenium: Gills, close to moderately spaced, pale cream to ochre-pink when young, darkening with age
lactarius-helvus.cap: Convex to funnel-shaped, often with a central depression, smooth, dry, and somewhat velvety, color from pinkish-buff to brownish, sometimes with grayish or reddish hues
lactarius-helvus.stipe: Cylindrical, often narrowing toward the base, typically the same color as the cap or paler, hollow and fragile with age
lactarius-helvus.spore-print: Spore print is pale cream to light ochre.
lactarius-helvus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in damp, mossy habitats, particularly in coniferous forests, often associated with pines and spruces, on acidic soils
lactarius-helvus.odour: Odour is strong and distinctive, resembling fenugreek, curry, which intensifies when the mushroom is dried
lactarius-helvus.microscopy: Spores are broadly elliptic with moderately prominent warts and partial reticulation, 6.5–9 x 5.5–7 µm, pleurocystidia are spindle-shaped to narrowly fusiform

lactarius-necator.hymenium: Gills that are crowded, slightly decurrent, pale cream becoming ochre with age.
lactarius-necator.cap: Initially convex, later flattening and developing a central depression, smooth, dark brown to blackish, sometimes with a slightly paler margin.
lactarius-necator.stipe: Cylindrical, often slightly swollen at the base, smooth, paler than the cap but still dark, with a zoned appearance.
lactarius-necator.spore-print: Spore Print: Cream to pale ochre.
lactarius-necator.ecology: Mycorrhizal, found predominantly under conifers, especially spruces.
lactarius-necator.description: Contains the mutagen necatorin. Choice mushroom in slavic culture for pickling (salted)
lactarius-necator.microscopy: Spores 7-9 x 6-8 µm, broadly elliptic, ornamented with warts and ridges.

lactarius-pubescens.hymenium: Gills crowded, narrow, and cream to pale pinkish-buff in color, staining brownish with age or when bruised
lactarius-pubescens.cap: convex when young, becoming flattened to slightly depressed with age, with an inrolled margin, surface is pubescent, cream to pale pinkish in color
lactarius-pubescens.stipe: cylindrical, hollow with age, concolorous with the cap or slightly paler, surface is dry and downy, with a faint pinkish hue
lactarius-pubescens.spore-print: Spore print cream to pale yellow
lactarius-pubescens.ecology: Mycorrhizal with birch, in damp areas, in mixed forests, in the vicinity of bogs and wet meadows, in groups or scattered, late summer to autumn
lactarius-pubescens.edibility: Edible as salted pickles, of low culinary value
lactarius-pubescens.fruit-body: Fruit body stipe 3–6 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
lactarius-pubescens.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, 7–9 x 6–8 µm, finely ornamented surface with low warts connected by thin ridges, basidia 4-spored

lactarius-pyrogalus.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced to distant; pale yellow to ochre-yellow when young, becoming orange-ochre with age
lactarius-pyrogalus.cap: Convex when young, later centrally depressed to funnel-shaped; smooth, slightly viscid when moist; grey, grey-brown to grey-ochre, sometimes with olive or lilac tints; weakly zoned
lactarius-pyrogalus.stipe: Cylindrical to slightly tapering toward base; pale grey-brown to buff, usually paler than cap; smooth, becoming hollow with age; ring absent
lactarius-pyrogalus.spore-print: Spore print pale ochre to yellowish-ochre
lactarius-pyrogalus.ecology: Mycorrhizal almost exclusively with hazel; deciduous and mixed woodland, coppices, hedgerows and woodland edges; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to autumn
lactarius-pyrogalus.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2.5–6.5 cm long and ~0.8–2 cm thick
lactarius-pyrogalus.flesh: Whitish to pale grey, brittle; abundant white latex, drying yellow-olive to grey-green on damaged gills
lactarius-pyrogalus.chemical-reactions: KOH turns latex yellow-orange to golden yellow; FeSO₄, NH₄OH and phenol negative
lactarius-pyrogalus.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, ~6.5–8 × 5–7 µm, ornamented with amyloid warts and broad connecting ridges forming an incomplete zebra-like network; basidia 4-spored; pleurocystidia fusiform to ventricose

lactarius-rufus.cap: 5-15 cm across. Convex, later becoming flattened or slightly depressed, with a wavy or curled margin. Its surface is rough and zoned with varying shades of reddish-brown.
lactarius-rufus.hymenium: Close to slightly distant gills that are adnate to slightly decurrent. Initially cream-colored, turning buff or pale ochre with age.
lactarius-rufus.stipe: Cylindrical, same color as the cap or a bit lighter, sometimes with darker spots or streaks, and is often hollow in mature specimens.
lactarius-rufus.spore-print: Spore Print: Cream to pale ochre.
lactarius-rufus.ecology: Ecology: Mycorrhizal, associating predominantly with conifers but also found with birch in some regions.
lactarius-rufus.edibility: Edible, but some may find it slightly acrid or peppery to taste.
lactarius-rufus.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid, 6-8 µm x 5-6 µm, with a slightly roughened surface.

lactarius-trivialis.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, crowded, cream-colored turning more brownish with age
hymenium is lamellar
lactarius-trivialis.cap: cap is convex to flat, often depressed in the center with age, light brown to olive-brown, sometimes with zones of different colors, often slightly sticky when wet
lactarius-trivialis.stipe: stipe is cylindrical, smooth, pale, with darker colorations or spots in some instances
lactarius-trivialis.spore-print: spore print is pale ochre to cream
lactarius-trivialis.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal, commonly associated with birch trees
lactarius-trivialis.edibility: edibility: edible but not highly prized due to its slightly acrid taste. Best when cooked thoroughly.

lactarius-uvidus.hymenium: Gills fairly crowded; whitish to pale cream when young, becoming pale buff with age
lactarius-uvidus.cap: Convex when young, later flat to shallowly depressed; smooth, viscid to slimy when fresh; pale violet-grey, lilac-grey to buff-brown, darkening with age; unzoned or faintly zoned
lactarius-uvidus.stipe: Cylindrical, pale cream to whitish, smooth, sometimes slightly viscid when young; becoming hollow with age; ring absent
lactarius-uvidus.spore-print: Spore print pale cream to pale yellowish
lactarius-uvidus.ecology: Mycorrhizal mainly with birch and willow; damp woodland, bog margins and mossy acidic soils; solitary to gregariously; summer to autumn
lactarius-uvidus.edibility: Not recommended; bitter, regarded as potentially poisonous
lactarius-uvidus.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.6–2.5 cm thick
lactarius-uvidus.flesh: Whitish to buff, firm and brittle; white latex and exposed flesh slowly stain lilac
lactarius-uvidus.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, ~7.5–11 × 6.5–8.5 µm, ornamented with amyloid broad ridges ~0.5–1 µm high forming an incomplete reticulum; pleuro- and cheilomacrocystidia fusiform to subventricose; pileipellis an ixocutis

laetiporus-sulphureus.hymenium:
pores on hymenium, small and round, bright yellow to orange
hymenium is tubular (composed of tubes instead of gills)
laetiporus-sulphureus.cap: cap is shelf-like, semicircular to fan-shaped, bright yellow to orange, often in overlapping clusters
laetiporus-sulphureus.stipe: stipe is not typically present, as this fungus grows directly from the wood in a shelf-like manner
laetiporus-sulphureus.spore-print: spore print is white to pale yellow
laetiporus-sulphureus.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic and sometimes parasitic, typically found on deciduous trees, especially oak, but sometimes also on conifers
laetiporus-sulphureus.edibility: tasty when young and tender, but becomes tough and inedible with age
laetiporus-sulphureus.fruit-body: individual shelves can be 5-40 cm across

leccinum-albostipitatum.hymenium: Pores, the pore surface is white to pale cream when young, becoming slightly darker with age, small and rounded, bruising brownish
leccinum-albostipitatum.cap: Convex when young, flattening out with age, color ranges from reddish-brown to orange-brown, often with a slightly dry, velvety texture
leccinum-albostipitatum.stipe: Distinctly white or pale cream throughout its length, with white or pale scales that darken slightly with age, base can have a slight bluish tinge when cut
leccinum-albostipitatum.ecology: Mycorrhizal, primarily associated with Populus sp, late summer to autumn, typically in mixed or deciduous woodlands
leccinum-albostipitatum.edibility: Edible, considered a good edible mushroom
leccinum-albostipitatum.microscopy: Spores fusiform to somewhat ellipsoid, 14–18 x 4–6 µm, smooth, basidia 4-spored, hyphal system is monomitic

leccinum-holopus.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, initially white then becoming greyish with age.
leccinum-holopus.cap: 5-10 cm across, convex becoming broadly convex with age. White to pale grey, smooth to slightly scaly.
leccinum-holopus.stipe: Cylindrical, 7-15 cm tall, 1-3 cm thick. Whitish with white to grey scales that become more prominent with age.
leccinum-holopus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, primarily associating with birch in damp, mossy, woodland areas.
leccinum-holopus.edibility: Edible but not of high culinary value.
leccinum-holopus.microscopy: Spores are oblong to ellipsoid, smooth, 13-17 x 4-5 µm.

leccinum-scabrum.hymenium: Pores small, round to irregular; whitish to cream when young, becoming greyish to brownish with age; bruising slowly brownish
leccinum-scabrum.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex; dry to slightly moist, finely velvety when young and smoother with age; various shades of brown, or grey or reddish tones
leccinum-scabrum.hymenium-attachment: Adnexed to slightly depressed around the stipe
leccinum-scabrum.stipe: Robust, cylindrical to slightly clavate, whitish to buff; densely covered with blackish scabers, coarser toward the base; ring absent
leccinum-scabrum.ecology: Mycorrhizal with birch; alone, scattered or gregariously; forests, woodland edges, parks and grassy places; summer to autumn
leccinum-scabrum.edibility: Edible after thorough cooking; young firm specimens preferred
leccinum-scabrum.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~7–20 cm long and ~1–3 cm thick
leccinum-scabrum.flesh: White, usually unchanging or slowly becoming faintly pinkish to greyish when cut; no rapid blue staining
leccinum-scabrum.chemical-reactions: KOH reddish-brown on cap and flesh; FeSO₄ bluish-slate on flesh; NH₄OH negative
leccinum-scabrum.microscopy: Spores narrowly ellipsoid to subfusiform, smooth, ~14–20 × 4.5–6 µm; basidia 4-spored; caulocystidia clavate to fusoid-ventricose; no clamp connections

leccinum-versipelle.hymenium: White to cream-colored pores that become grayish or brownish with age; may bruise dark brown.
leccinum-versipelle.cap: initially convex, becoming nearly flat with age; orange-red to orange-brown, dry, and slightly scaly.
leccinum-versipelle.hymenium-attachment: Attached directly to the stipe or slightly descending.
leccinum-versipelle.stipe: 10-25 cm long, 2-4 cm thick; white, covered with small black scab-like scales.
leccinum-versipelle.ecology: Mycorrhizal, commonly found under birch trees.
leccinum-versipelle.edibility: Edible but should be cooked well; some people may experience gastrointestinal distress.

leccinum-vulpinum.hymenium: Pores small, round, cream to whitish when young, later greyish-cream to yellowish-olive; tubes adnate to nearly free
leccinum-vulpinum.cap: Convex to broadly convex; dry, finely woolly-fibrillose; muted fox-red, reddish-brown to cocoa-brown, darker in the centre
leccinum-vulpinum.stipe: Stout, whitish to pale, slightly swollen toward base; covered with scabers that darken from whitish to reddish-brown, then dark brown or chocolate
leccinum-vulpinum.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with conifers, especially Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris), in dry pine woods, coniferous and mixed forests, often on sandy or acidic soils; summer to autumn
leccinum-vulpinum.edibility: Good, tasty and edible after cooking
leccinum-vulpinum.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large; stipe ~8–14 cm long, ~1–3 cm thick
leccinum-vulpinum.flesh: Flesh white to pale; cap flesh mostly unchanging, stipe flesh slowly pinkish to wine-coloured, sometimes blue-green near the base, later greyish or steel-blue in patches
leccinum-vulpinum.chemical-reactions: No distinctive KOH macroscopic field reaction
leccinum-vulpinum.microscopy: Spores fusiform to subfusiform, smooth, ~11–16.5 × 3–4.7 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia ventricose to fusiform

legaliana-badia.hymenium: Smooth to slightly glossy, olive-brown, chestnut-brown, becoming darker as it dries
legaliana-badia.apothecium: Deeply cup- or saucer-shaped when young, later spreading, irregularly lobed, undulating or split; outer surface reddish-brown to olivaceous-brown and finely furfuraceous, especially near the margin
legaliana-badia.stipe: Absent or represented by a very short, inconspicuous basal attachment
legaliana-badia.ecology: Saprobic on bare, compact, sandy or clay-rich soil in coniferous, deciduous and mixed woodland; often along paths, banks, ditches and disturbed ground; summer to late autumn
legaliana-badia.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; approximately 1.5–3.7 cm tall
legaliana-badia.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid, hyaline to faintly yellow-brown, usually biguttulate, ~17–20 × 8–11 µm, asci cylindrical, operculate, amyloid, 8-spored, approximately 300–350 × 12–15 µm; paraphyses cylindrical, septate and slightly enlarged at the apex

lentinellus-ursinus.hymenium: Gills radiating from point of attachment, close to nearly crowded, gill edges coarsely serrated or saw-toothed, often irregular and torn
lentinellus-ursinus.cap: Semi-circular to kidney-shaped, surface tomentose or velvety (especially toward center), darker brown at center fading toward margin, margin rolled under or lobed
lentinellus-ursinus.stipe: Absent, fruiting bodies sessile or lateral on wood substrate
lentinellus-ursinus.ecology: Saprobic on decaying hardwood or conifer wood, grows clustered, overlapping shelves on logs or stumps, summer through autumn
lentinellus-ursinus.edibility: Inedible, extremely bitter and acrid, not poisonous
lentinellus-ursinus.fruit-body: Fruit body size small to medium
lentinellus-ursinus.chemical-reactions: Fresh cap surface usually KOH negative, dried flesh strong amyloid reaction with Melzer’s reagent
lentinellus-ursinus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, 3–4 × 2–3 µm, sparsely, finely spiny, strongly amyloid, basidia 18–20 × 3–4 µm, clavate, 4-sterigmate, pleurocystidia 22–30 × 4–6 µm, fusiform or cylindric

lentinus-arcularius.hymenium: Pores large, angular to hexagonal, whitish to pale cream becoming light brown with age
lentinus-arcularius.cap: Convex to depressed center, surface dry, scaly to fibrillose, color from dark brown in youth to pale tan, margin with fine hairs/cilia
lentinus-arcularius.stipe: Central, matching or slightly paler than cap, dry and scaly, tough in texture
lentinus-arcularius.ecology:
Saprobic on deciduous hardwoods (fallen logs, stumps, branches), spring to autumn
Inedible, too small, tough, and insubstantial
lentinus-arcularius.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 2–6 cm × ~1.5–4.5 mm
lentinus-arcularius.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to narrowly ellipsoid, smooth, ~5.0–8.5×1.5–2.5µm, hyaline in KOH, basidia 2- to 4-sterigmate, no cystidia, pileipellis radial cutis of brown, clamped hyphae 4–7 µm wide, dimitic

lenzites-betulinus.hymenium: Gills (true lamellae, broad and tough), white or cream when young, later a pale buff
lenzites-betulinus.cap: Bracket- or shelf-shaped (sometimes semicircular or fan-shaped), attached laterally to wood, surface zoned in concentric rings of whitish, greyish-buff, brown tones, velvety/tomentose
lenzites-betulinus.hymenium-attachment: N/A (the gills are part of the underside of the bracket)
lenzites-betulinus.stipe: Absent — fruit body is sessile on wood
lenzites-betulinus.ecology:
Saprobic causing white-rot on dead or dying hardwood, especially birch, beech and other broadleaves, all year round
Inedible - tough and corky,
lenzites-betulinus.dimensions: Cap width up to ~10 cm or more, 2 cm thick
lenzites-betulinus.flesh: Flesh white, corky, unchanging when cut
lenzites-betulinus.chemical-reactions: KOH on surface or flesh negative to weak yellow
lenzites-betulinus.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to allantoid, smooth, hyaline, ~5–6×1.5–2.5 µm, hyphal system monomitic/trimitic with clamp connections

lepiota-cristata.hymenium: Gills crowded; white to cream, becoming slightly buff with age; numerous shorter lamellulae
lepiota-cristata.cap: Ovoid to convex when young, later broadly bell-shaped to flat; whitish background covered with concentrically arranged reddish-brown scales; centre darker and usually smooth
lepiota-cristata.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, whitish, often becoming pinkish-brown toward base; smooth to finely fibrillose; fragile white ring usually ephemeral and easily lost
lepiota-cristata.ecology: Saprobic in woodland, parks, gardens, lawns, paths and disturbed ground; solitary, scattered or gregariously; summer to autumn
lepiota-cristata.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~3–7 cm long and ~0.2–0.4 cm thick
lepiota-cristata.flesh: Whitish, thin, fragile, unchanging when cut
lepiota-cristata.chemical-reactions: KOH negative on pale cap areas, negative to yellowish on brown scales
lepiota-cristata.microscopy: Spores bullet-shaped to wedge-shaped, smooth, hyaline, dextrinoid, ~5–8 × 2.5–4(–5) µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia clavate to subclavate; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis hymeniform; clamp connections present

leptoporus-mollis.hymenium: Pores are white, small, and dense, becoming yellowish with age.
leptoporus-mollis.cap: Convex to flat, soft and spongy in texture, yellowish-white to pale orange.
leptoporus-mollis.stipe: Absent or rudimentary; the mushroom is often sessile.
leptoporus-mollis.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying coniferous wood, particularly on spruce.
leptoporus-mollis.edibility: Generally considered inedible due to its soft and insubstantial texture.
leptoporus-mollis.fruit-body: Fruit body: Up to 5-10 cm across.

leucoagaricus-leucothites.hymenium: Gills, free from the stipe, crowded, initially white, turning pinkish with age, and eventually brown
leucoagaricus-leucothites.cap: Initially bell-shaped or convex, becoming broadly convex to flat with age, smooth and white, sometimes with a faint buff center, surface may become slightly cracked or scaly with age
leucoagaricus-leucothites.stipe: Cylindrical, smooth, white, hollow, and somewhat fragile with a bulbous base, persistent, movable, thin ring near the upper part
leucoagaricus-leucothites.ecology: Saprobic, typically found growing in grasslands, meadows, lawns, and gardens, often in rich soil or compost
leucoagaricus-leucothites.edibility: Edible, though caution is advised due to its resemblance to toxic white Amanita species, especially A. virosa and A. ocreata
leucoagaricus-leucothites.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid, 8-11 x 5-6.5 µm, basidia are four-spored, cheilocystidia are present on the gill edges, typically clavate or flask-shaped

leucopaxillus-tricolor.hymenium: Gills, crowded, cream to pale yellow, staining reddish-brown or rust with age or damage
leucopaxillus-tricolor.cap: Convex to flat with a slightly depressed center, yellowish-brown to rusty-brown, often with reddish or orange tints, smooth and dry
leucopaxillus-tricolor.stipe: Stout, swollen in the middle, dry, bald, white, with prominent and copious white basal mycelium
leucopaxillus-tricolor.ecology: Saprobic, decomposing the litter of hardwoods, growing gregariously, summer and autumn
leucopaxillus-tricolor.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe 3–6 cm long, 2–4 cm thick
leucopaxillus-tricolor.odour: Odour strong and foul, reminiscent of coal tar
leucopaxillus-tricolor.chemical-reactions: Cap surface grayish to dull red with KOH
leucopaxillus-tricolor.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subamygdaliform (spines under 0.5 µm), 6–8 x 4–4.5 µm, amyloid, basidia 4-spored, cheilocystidia 35–75 x 2–3 µm

lichenomphalia-umbellifera.hymenium: Gills, pale yellowish to whitish, decurrent (running down the stem), distant, thick-waxy; may fork or form cross-links
lichenomphalia-umbellifera.cap: Convex to flat with a distinctly depressed center, dull yellowish to brownish-tan; thin, moist (lubricous), margin becomes wavy or pleated
lichenomphalia-umbellifera.stipe: slender, moist, smooth or with a fuzzy base, pale yellowish-brown to reddish at the apex
lichenomphalia-umbellifera.ecology: Ecology: Lichenized basidiomycete (basidiolichen) forming mutualism with green algae (Coccomyxa); grows on moist soil, moss, and rotting conifer wood, spring through fall
lichenomphalia-umbellifera.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe 1–3 cm long, 1–3 mm thick
lichenomphalia-umbellifera.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5–7 × 3–4 µm

lycogala-epidendrum.plasmodium-phase: The active, feeding phase consists of a gelatinous, amorphous mass that is translucent white to pale pink, moving slowly across decaying wood and consuming microorganisms
lycogala-epidendrum.fruiting-bodies: Initially spherical to cushion-shaped, bright pink or salmon, turning gray, reddish-brown, or black as they mature, surface smooth to slightly roughened, eventually breaking open to release spores
lycogala-epidendrum.description: Spore mass powdery and pinkish-gray to dark gray when mature.
lycogala-epidendrum.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying wood, bark, stumps in forests and woodlands, clusters or scattered groups, summer and autumn in moist, shaded areas
lycogala-epidendrum.fruit-body: Fruiting body 2–15 mm in diameter, with the surface often slightly wrinkled or cracked as it ages
lycogala-epidendrum.microscopy: Subglobose to slightly elongated, covered in fine warts, 6–9 µm, spore mass dispersed in a capillitium network

lycoperdon-excipuliforme.cap: 2-5 cm across. Initially round to pear-shaped, with a rough surface covered in small white spines. As it matures, spines may shed, revealing a brownish skin beneath. The apex ruptures to release spores.
lycoperdon-excipuliforme.stipe: Present in some mature specimens, elongated, and can be quite long relative to the size of the fruiting body. It's hollow and might have a reticulate surface towards the top.
lycoperdon-excipuliforme.ecology: Saprobic, found on the ground in grassy areas, heaths, and woodlands.
lycoperdon-excipuliforme.edibility: Edible when young and the gleba is still white, but becomes inedible as it matures and turns to spore dust.
lycoperdon-excipuliforme.microscopy: Spores are round, 3.5-4.5 µm in diameter, with a finely warted surface.

lycoperdon-umbrinum.hymenium: Initially solid, becoming powdery with maturity due to the transformation of the internal tissue into spores.
lycoperdon-umbrinum.fruit-body:
Globose to slightly pear-shaped puffball, smooth to finely granulated or spiny at a young age; spines, if present, often fall off with age, leaving a net-like pattern.
Fruit body: Up to 2-4 cm in diameter.
lycoperdon-umbrinum.color: Dark brown to olive-brown when mature.
lycoperdon-umbrinum.ecology: Grasslands, meadows, and forest clearings; often found growing in groups.
lycoperdon-umbrinum.edibility: Edible when young and the internal flesh is white and firm, but not considered a top choice.

lyophyllum-decastes.hymenium: Gills are close and white, but may take on a grayish hue as the mushroom ages. Darkening when pressed.
lyophyllum-decastes.cap: 5-12 cm in diameter. Initially convex, maturing to nearly flat, with a slightly inrolled margin. Smooth, and typically gray-brown to brown.
lyophyllum-decastes.stipe: Cylindrical, white, and typically smooth or slightly fibrous, with no ring.
lyophyllum-decastes.ecology: Saprobic; typically growing in dense clusters on disturbed ground, often near rotting wood or wood chips.
lyophyllum-decastes.edibility: Edible and said to be mild in flavor, but as always caution is advised.
lyophyllum-decastes.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, and hyaline.

marasmiellus-ramealis.hymenium: Gills are white to pale cream.
marasmiellus-ramealis.cap: Initially convex, becoming broadly convex to nearly flat with maturity, hygrophanous, pale tan to light brown, drying paler.
marasmiellus-ramealis.stipe: Cylindrical, slender, pale at the top and becoming darker brown towards the base.
marasmiellus-ramealis.spore-print: spore print: White to pale cream.
marasmiellus-ramealis.ecology: ecology: Saprobic, growing on fallen twigs and woody debris, primarily of broadleaf trees.
marasmiellus-ramealis.edibility: edibility: Inedible due to its small size and tough texture, but not known to be toxic.

marasmius-epiphyllus.hymenium: Gills very distant, few and narrow, often reduced to irregular vein-like folds, sometimes forked or interconnected; white to pale cream
marasmius-epiphyllus.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later flattened or shallowly depressed; extremely thin, dry, smooth to finely pruinose, becoming radially wrinkled; white to ivory; margin slightly wavy
marasmius-epiphyllus.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to shortly decurrent, sometimes forming a partial collar
marasmius-epiphyllus.stipe: Extremely slender, thread-like, tough and wiry; whitish near apex, dark reddish-brown toward base; finely pruinose to minutely hairy; ring absent
marasmius-epiphyllus.description: Saprobic on decaying hardwood leaves, petioles; deciduous and mixed forests, usually scattered to gregariously; summer to late autumn
marasmius-epiphyllus.fruit-body: Fruit body tiny; stipe ~0.5–3 cm long and ~0.1–0.5 mm thick
marasmius-epiphyllus.flesh: Whitish to pale cream, membranous, extremely thin and pliant; unchanging when cut; drying out and reviving with moisture
marasmius-epiphyllus.microscopy: Spores elongated-ellipsoid to lacrymoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~8.5–12.5 × 3–5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; cheilocystidia fusiform to lageniform, often with elongated necks; pleurocystidia scattered; pileipellis hymeniform; clamp connections present

marasmius-oreades.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, white to cream, widely spaced
hymenium is lamellar
marasmius-oreades.cap: cap is convex, becoming flat with a slight central depression and often a small umbo, smooth, pale tan to buff
marasmius-oreades.stipe: stipe is thin, tough, and wiry, same color as the cap or slightly paler
marasmius-oreades.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic, typically found in grassy areas such as lawns, pastures, and meadows
marasmius-oreades.edibility: edibility: choice, known for its excellent taste and texture, especially when dried

melampsora-ari-salicina.hymenium: Not formed as a cap-and-gill structure; spores produced in rust sori on infected willow leaves
melampsora-ari-salicina.body: Microscopic rust fungus forming yellow-orange uredinia, later dark brown to black telia on leaves of Salix species
melampsora-ari-salicina.hymenium-attachment: Not applicable; spore-producing sori erupt through or develop within host leaf tissue
melampsora-ari-salicina.ecology: Ecology obligate biotrophic parasite on willows (Salix spp.); uredinia reinfect willow leaves during the growing season, telia develop later in summer to autumn
melampsora-ari-salicina.fruit-body: Fruit body microscopic; visible only as small rust pustules or dark telial patches on leaves
melampsora-ari-salicina.dimensions: Sori usually minute, appearing as yellow-orange to brown-black spots or patches on willow leaves
melampsora-ari-salicina.flesh: No true flesh; infected leaf tissue may yellow, spot, brown or distort
melampsora-ari-salicina.microscopy: Urediniospores one-celled, yellowish, finely echinulate to spiny; teliospores formed in dark telia on willow leaves

melanoleuca-strictipes.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, white to cream sometimes slightly tinged pinkish
melanoleuca-strictipes.cap: Convex to broadly convex and slightly umbonate, smooth, dry, white to cream or pallid, slightly darker center, margin smooth or slightly wavy
melanoleuca-strictipes.stipe: Slender, tall, cylindrical, bulbous base, pale cream to tan, smooth, with a fibrous texture, without a ring
melanoleuca-strictipes.spore-print: Spore print white, cream or yellowish
melanoleuca-strictipes.description: Saprobic, growing in nutrient-rich soil or grassy areas, often found in meadows, gardens, and woodland clearings, spring to autumn
melanoleuca-strictipes.edibility: Said to be edible but little information exists and potential misidentification possible
melanoleuca-strictipes.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 8–14 cm long, 0.8–1.2 cm thick
melanoleuca-strictipes.odour: Odour mildly fragrant, sometimes slightly sweet
melanoleuca-strictipes.taste: Taste slight, smell strongly of meal
melanoleuca-strictipes.microscopy: Spores elliptic,minutely warted, amyloid, 8–9 x 4.5–5 µm, basidia 4-spored

melastiza-chateri.hymenium: Smooth to slightly uneven, vivid orange to orange-red or vermilion
melastiza-chateri.apothecium: Sessile, initially cup-shaped, later shallowly saucer- to disc-shaped; exterior paler orange to reddish-brown, finely pubescent; margin dotted with short inconspicuous brown hairs
melastiza-chateri.ecology: Saprobic on damp bare, mossy or sandy soil; forests, woodland tracks, roadsides and disturbed ground; scattered to gregarious; summer to autumn
melastiza-chateri.fruit-body: Fruit body very small; apothecia ~1–2 mm tall
melastiza-chateri.flesh: Orange-red, thin, waxy and brittle, unchanging when cut
melastiza-chateri.description: Paraphyses filiform with enlarged orange-pigmented apices; marginal hairs brown, blunt, septate, up to ~200 µm long
melastiza-chateri.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid, hyaline, biguttulate, ~16–20 × 9–11 µm excluding ornamentation; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~215–300 × 11–15 µm, inamyloid;

mollisia-cinerea.hymenium: Smooth, forms the inner surface of the apothecium, gray to gray-brown, sometimes darkening with age or when moist
mollisia-cinerea.cap: Disc- or cup-shaped, thin, often slightly depressed in the center, gray to grayish-brown, with a smooth or slightly roughened surface
mollisia-cinerea.hymenium-attachment: N/A (Forms the inner surface of the cup)
mollisia-cinerea.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood, plant debris, and sometimes on bark or fallen leaves, in damp, shaded areas, year-round
mollisia-cinerea.edibility: Inedible due to its small size and insubstantial flesh
mollisia-cinerea.microscopy: Spores fusiform, 7-12 x 2.5-3 µm, with an oil drop at each end, asci cylindrical, 40-65 x 4-5.5µm, 8 spores per ascus

morchella-elata.hymenium: hymenium is ribbed, forming a honeycomb-like pattern
morchella-elata.cap: cap is conical to oval, covered with a network of ridges and pits, dark brown to black, attached to the stipe at the base
morchella-elata.stipe: stipe is hollow, cylindrical, whitish to pale grayish-brown, smooth or slightly granular
morchella-elata.spore-print: spore print is cream to yellowish
morchella-elata.edibility: edibility: choice, but should be cooked thoroughly as raw morels can cause gastrointestinal upset

morchella-esculenta.hymenium: Fertile surface smooth, lining deep pits and honeycomb-like depressions; ridges sterile, pale cream to yellow-ochre, darkening slightly with age
morchella-esculenta.cap: Ovoid to broadly conical, hollow, attached to stipe at the lower margin; surface strongly pitted and ridged, yellowish, ochre, tan to pale brown
morchella-esculenta.hymenium-attachment: Apothecial, fused to the stipe along the lower cap margin
morchella-esculenta.stipe: Cylindrical to clavate, hollow, whitish to cream, finely granular or furfuraceous, sometimes broadened at the base
morchella-esculenta.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
morchella-esculenta.ecology: Facultatively mycorrhizal (hardwoods, conifers, grass plants), in woodlands, meadows, orchards, disturbed ground and calcareous soils
morchella-esculenta.edibility: Choice edible after thorough cooking, toxic raw/insufficiently cooked
morchella-esculenta.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe ~2–9 × 2–5 cm
morchella-esculenta.flesh: Thin, brittle, whitish to pale cream, hollow, unchanging when cut
morchella-esculenta.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, ~17–22 × 9–11 µm, asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~220–350 × 16–20 µm, paraphyses filiform to slightly enlarged apically

mucilago-crustacea.plasmodium: Pale yellow to whitish, slimy and mucilaginous when active, spreading across grass, leaves, or decaying organic matter
mucilago-crustacea.sporangia: Formed as a crust-like aethalium, irregularly shaped, often cushion-like, white to cream or pale yellow when fresh, turning grayish-brown or ochre as it matures. The surface is covered by a calcareous, powdery layer (peridium)
mucilago-crustacea.description:
Spore mass powdery, grayish-brown to dark brown
Saprotrophic, on decaying plant material, typically in meadows, gardens, or forest edges, late summer to autumn
mucilago-crustacea.fruit-body: Aethalium size variable, typically 2–10 cm across and up to 1 cm thick
mucilago-crustacea.chemical-reactions: Peridium dissolves in KOH, revealing spores, plasmodium may react faintly yellow in ammonia
mucilago-crustacea.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, warted, 6–9 µm, loose capillitium network

mucor-mucedo.sporangia: Terminal, globose, non-apophysate; white to yellowish when immature, becoming grey-brown to dark grey at maturity; borne on tall, erect sporangiophores with prominent columellae
mucor-mucedo.colony: Rapidly growing, cottony to fluffy, initially white, later grey
mucor-mucedo.description: Spore mass Grey-brown to dark grey or nearly black at maturity
mucor-mucedo.ecology: Saprobic on soil, dung, compost, decaying plant matter, stored grain, fruit and other moist organic substrates; widespread and often appearing under cool, humid conditions
mucor-mucedo.fruit-body: Microscopic mould colony, often growing several centimetres high
mucor-mucedo.microscopy: Hyphae broad, coenocytic or sparsely septate; sporangiophores tall, simple or occasionally branched, lacking basal rhizoids; sporangia globose with a prominent columella and residual collarette; sporangiospores smooth, globose to slightly elongated, approximately 4–8 µm; heterothallic, producing dark, thick-walled, ornamented zygospores when compatible mating types meet

mycena-epipterygia.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; white to cream when young, becoming faintly pinkish with age; edges sometimes gelatinous
mycena-epipterygia.cap: Conical to bell-shaped when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat; smooth, strongly viscid when moist, with a separable gelatinous pellicle; pale yellowish-grey; margin distinctly translucent-striate
mycena-epipterygia.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly decurrent, often with a short decurrent tooth
mycena-epipterygia.stipe: Very slender, cylindrical, hollow and fragile; lemon-greenish-yellow; smooth, viscid, covered with a separable gelatinous layer; ring absent
mycena-epipterygia.spore-print: Spore print white to very pale cream
mycena-epipterygia.ecology: Saprobic on conifer needle litter, moss, decaying twigs, woody debris; mainly spruce and pine forests, also mixed woodland, damp grassland and heathland; scattered to gregariously; late summer to autumn
mycena-epipterygia.edibility: Not recommended; tiny, fragile and insubstantial
mycena-epipterygia.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~3–8 cm long and ~0.1–0.3 cm thick
mycena-epipterygia.flesh: Flesh whitish, pale yellowish, very thin and fragile, unchanging when cut
mycena-epipterygia.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to cylindrical, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~8–11 × 4–6 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia irregularly clavate with numerous finger-like projections; pleurocystidia absent; pileipellis an ixocutis

mycena-galericulata.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced; white to pale grey when young, often becoming pinkish-grey with age; short lamellulae frequent, cross-veins often developing between mature gills
mycena-galericulata.cap: Conical to bell-shaped when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat with a persistent low umbo; smooth to slightly rugose, translucent-striate toward margin; grey-brown, darker centrally and paler toward margin
mycena-galericulata.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to emarginate, sometimes with a short decurrent tooth
mycena-galericulata.stipe: Slender, hollow, tough and elastic; whitish near apex, grey-brown to dark brown below; base with coarse white fibrils, rooting into decayed wood; ring absent
mycena-galericulata.ecology: Saprobic on well-decayed hardwood logs, stumps, fallen branches and buried wood; solitary to densely clustered; late spring to late autumn
mycena-galericulata.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~4.5–11(–18) cm long and ~0.15–0.6 cm thick
mycena-galericulata.flesh: Whitish to pale grey, thin and fragile, unchanging when cut
mycena-galericulata.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to pip-shaped, smooth, amyloid, ~9–12 × 6–8 µm; basidia 2- or 4-spored; pleurocystidia absent; clamp connections present in 4-spored forms

mycena-galopus-var-leucogala.hymenium: Gills, adnate to slightly decurrent, moderately spaced, whitish to pale gray, darkening slightly with age
mycena-galopus-var-leucogala.cap: Conical to bell-shaped, becoming broadly conical with age, smooth, moist, grayish-brown to pale brown, darker at the center, translucent when moist
mycena-galopus-var-leucogala.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, fragile, whitish to gray, exuding a white, milky latex when damaged, particularly near the base
mycena-galopus-var-leucogala.ecology: Saprobic, found in coniferous and mixed forests, growing on decaying leaf litter, wood, and soil, often in groups or scattered, late summer to autumn
mycena-galopus-var-leucogala.edibility: Inedible, not considered poisonous but too small and insubstantial to be of culinary value
mycena-galopus-var-leucogala.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 4–8 cm long, 0.2–0.5 cm thick
mycena-galopus-var-leucogala.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 7–9 x 4–5 µm, inamyloid

mycena-haematopus.hymenium: Gills whitish to pale grey or pinkish, sometimes developing reddish-brown stains; edges usually concolorous but occasionally darker
mycena-haematopus.cap: Conical to bell-shaped, later broadly convex; hygrophanous, finely pruinose when young and translucent-striate when moist; reddish-brown, fading to pale pinkish-grey
mycena-haematopus.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to adnexed, sometimes decurrent with a small tooth
mycena-haematopus.stipe: Slender, hollow and fragile; reddish-brown, darker below, with white basal fibrils
mycena-haematopus.ecology: Saprobic, usually growing in tufts or clusters on well-decayed hardwood logs, stumps and fallen branches; summer to late autumn
mycena-haematopus.edibility: Insubstantial and of poor culinary value
mycena-haematopus.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~4–8 cm long and ~0.1–0.3 cm thick
mycena-haematopus.flesh: Flesh very thin, pale to vinaceous
mycena-haematopus.description: Exudes dark blood-red liquid when cut
mycena-haematopus.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to pip-shaped, smooth, amyloid, ~8–11 × 5–7 µm; basidia clavate, predominantly 4-sterigmate; cheilocystidia fusiform with elongated narrow apices; pleurocystidia similar when present; clamp connections abundant

mycena-sanguinolenta.hymenium: Gills, well-spaced, initially sordid reddish to grayish, with even, dark-red-brown edges
mycena-sanguinolenta.cap: Conical to broadly convex or bell-shaped, starting moist with whitish-grayish bloom that soon disappears, revealing a smooth, reddish-brown cap
mycena-sanguinolenta.hymenium-attachment: Hymenium attachment adnate to slightly decurrent
mycena-sanguinolenta.stipe: Fragile, same color as cap, smooth to polished above, base with coarse stiff white hairs, exudes dark reddish-purple sap when broken
mycena-sanguinolenta.ecology: Ecology saprotrophic, growing in groups on leaf-litter, moss beds, acidic soils in conifer and deciduous forests, spring to autumn
mycena-sanguinolenta.edibility: Unknown; too insubstantial for culinary use
mycena-sanguinolenta.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 2–6 cm × 1–1.5 mm
mycena-sanguinolenta.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, weakly amyloid, 8–10 × 4–5 µm; basidia 4-spored, abundant pleuro- and cheilocystidia filled with red pigment

mycena-viridimarginata.hymenium: Gills, crowded, narrow, color whitish to pale gray initially, gill edges distinctly green-tinged
mycena-viridimarginata.cap: Starts conical to campanulate, flattening with age, surface pruinose when young, then glabrescent, hygrophanous and radiately striate when moist, colors olivaceous-grayish-greenish-brown, margins paler
mycena-viridimarginata.hymenium-attachment: Narrowly adnate to adnate, occasionally with a short decurrent tooth
mycena-viridimarginata.stipe: Hollow, fragile; smooth to pruinose above, glabrous below, coloration yellowish-brown, darkening toward base, apex pale, base covered in whitish fibrils
mycena-viridimarginata.ecology: Saprotrophic, growing on decaying wood of coniferous trees, summer to autumn
mycena-viridimarginata.fruit-body: Fruit body size medium, stipe 20–70 × 1–3 mm
mycena-viridimarginata.flesh: No notable color change when cut
mycena-viridimarginata.microscopy: Spores broadly subellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, amyloid; ~ 9–11.8 × 6–7.5 µm, Basidia 25–32 × 8–10 µm, slender-clavate, 4-spored, sterigmata 5–8 µm, cheilocystidia 23–70 × 7–18 (–29) µm

mycetinis-scorodonius.hymenium: Gills whitish, close to almost distant, narrowly attached to the stipe
mycetinis-scorodonius.cap: Convex to broadly convex or bell-shaped, often with a small central depression or bump; dry, smooth to slightly wrinkled; reddish-brown when young, fading to buff or pale tan
mycetinis-scorodonius.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to adnexed, sometimes almost free
mycetinis-scorodonius.stipe: Very slender, tough, wiry, shiny and mostly smooth; pale near apex, reddish-dark-brown-blackish toward base
mycetinis-scorodonius.ecology: Saprobic on fallen conifer needles, twigs, bark, leaf litter, grass stems and woody debris; scattered to gregarious, summer to late autumn
mycetinis-scorodonius.edibility: Edible, dried and used for strong garlic flavouring
mycetinis-scorodonius.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe up to ~6 cm long, ~0.5–3 mm thick
mycetinis-scorodonius.flesh: Flesh very thin, pale, insubstantial, unchanging when cut
mycetinis-scorodonius.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to pip-shaped, inamyloid, ~6–10(–11) × 3–5 µm; pleurocystidia absent; cheilocystidia clavate to cylindrical or irregular, lobed, with knob-rod-like projections

nectriopsis-rubefaciens.hymenium: Perithecia with ostioles—reddish-orange, globose to subglobose, surface often with scattered glandular hairs around the ostiole
nectriopsis-rubefaciens.cap: N/A (does not form a cap; perithecial fungus)
nectriopsis-rubefaciens.spore-print: Spore Print: N/A (minute ascomycete; no macroscopic spore print)
nectriopsis-rubefaciens.description:
Lichenicolous (parasitic on lichens), especially crustose and foliose lichens (Aspicilia, Parmeliaceae hosts), grows on the thalli of host lichens in damp forest habitats
Ascospores: Hyaline, oblong–cylindrical, 8 per ascus (8-spored asci)
Paraphyses: Absent
Perithecial hairs: Gland-like hairs surrounding ostioles, fine cellular in texture

neoantrodia-serialis.hymenium: Pores rounded, white to buff, fairly thick-walled, about 2–4 per mm
neoantrodia-serialis.cap: Reflexed to nearly resupinate, often imbricate or arranged in rows; small tough brownish brackets with ochraceous to pale cinnamon, faintly zoned, finely tomentose upper surface
neoantrodia-serialis.ecology:
Saprobic and brown heart-rot causing polypore, mainly on dead conifer wood, fallen trunks, stumps, logs and processed timber, common in boreal conifer forests
Inedible — tough, corky and crust-like
neoantrodia-serialis.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium, often forming fused rows or overlapping patches
neoantrodia-serialis.dimensions: Bracketed portions usually small; resupinate patches may extend along wood
neoantrodia-serialis.flesh: Flesh white, tough, corky, thin, unchanging when cut
neoantrodia-serialis.chemical-reactions: No distinctive KOH field reaction documented
neoantrodia-serialis.microscopy: Spores subfusiform to cylindrical, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, about 6.3–8 × 2.2–3.3 µm; hyphal system dimitic, with skeletal hyphae; cystidia absent or not prominent

neobarya-parasitica.hymenium: Perithecioid (ostiolate perithecia), densely agglomerated, greenish-yellow to olivaceous, seated on a whitish–yellow subiculum representing an abundant asexual state
neobarya-parasitica.spore-print: N/A (minute perithecioid ascomycete; no practical spore print)
neobarya-parasitica.ecology: Mycoparasitic on the pyrenomycete Bertia moriformis (on dead hardwood), gregarious on host stromata
neobarya-parasitica.microscopy:
Inedible (microscopic)
Asci (8-spored) (100)120–140(150) × (5)5.5–8(9) µm, cylindrical to narrowly clavate, with distinct thickened apical cap, ascospores filiform, hyaline, 150–200 × 3–4.5 µm
neobarya-parasitica.fruit-body: Perithecia 0.35–0.50 mm tall × 0.20–0.30 mm wide; gregarious, often in groups up to ~20

neolentinus-cyathiformis.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, decurrent, crowded, white to pale yellow
hymenium is lamellar
neolentinus-cyathiformis.cap: cap is funnel-shaped with an incurved margin, grayish-brown to dark brown, scaly or fibrillose
neolentinus-cyathiformis.stipe: stipe is central, cylindrical, sometimes curved, white to pale grayish-brown, scaly or fibrillose
neolentinus-cyathiformis.edibility: edibility: edible, but caution is advised due to similarity to poisonous species

orbilia-xanthostigma.hymenium:
Smooth under the disc, producing asci in thin hymenial layer, apothecial disc shows a glassy, translucent surface
Asci: Typical operculate asci within the hymenium (standard for Orbiliaceae)
orbilia-xanthostigma.apothecium: Small, disc/cup-shaped apothecia, yellow to ochre, semi-transparent, shining, waxy texture
orbilia-xanthostigma.stipe: Absent or extremely reduced, discs typically borne directly on wood or substrate
orbilia-xanthostigma.ecology: Saprobic on decaying hardwood (often with e.g. Mollisia and Nemania spp.), in moist shaded woodland, spring through autumn
orbilia-xanthostigma.description:
Ascospores: Ellipsoid to kidney-shaped, hyaline, size ~ 1–2 × 3–4 µm.
Paraphyses: Present (intermixed among asci)

otidea-alutacea.hymenium: Smooth, yellowish-brown, tan to clay-brown, usually slightly darker than the outer surface
otidea-alutacea.apothecium: Cup- to ear-shaped, typically split along one side; pale yellowish-brown to brown, margin wavy or irregular; outer surface paler and finely furfuraceous
otidea-alutacea.hymenium-attachment: Exposed on inner surface of the apothecium
otidea-alutacea.stipe: Usually absent or rudimentary; base narrowed with whitish tomentum
otidea-alutacea.ecology: Terrestrial on rich, neutral to calcareous woodland soil and humus under deciduous trees; scattered to gregarious; summer to autumn
otidea-alutacea.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; ~1.5–7 cm tall
otidea-alutacea.flesh: Flesh pale yellowish to cream, thin, waxy and brittle, unchanging when cut
otidea-alutacea.microscopy: Spores narrowly ellipsoid to oblong, smooth, hyaline, typically biguttulate, ~14.5–16.5(–17.5) × 6.5–7.5(–8) µm; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, inamyloid;

otidea-leporina.cap: 2-5 cm in diameter. Split and ear-shaped, typically with one side curled or folded, color varying from yellow-brown to pinkish or orange-brown, inner surface smooth to slightly wrinkled.
otidea-leporina.hymenium: Smooth, located on the inner side of the split cap, pale yellowish to tan.
otidea-leporina.stipe: Generally absent or reduced to a small stub-like base.
otidea-leporina.spore-print: Spore Print: Yellowish to light brown.
otidea-leporina.ecology: Saprobic; found on the ground monstly in coniferous forests, especially among leaf litter and rotting wood.
otidea-leporina.edibility: Inedible. Contains toxins which may cause serious gastric upset.
otidea-leporina.fruit-body: Fruit body: Up to 4-8 cm tall.
otidea-leporina.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, 15-18 x 7-9 µm.

oxyporus-populinus.hymenium: Features a smooth, white to cream underside where the spores are produced, unique among polypores for being soft and leathery rather than hard or woody.
oxyporus-populinus.cap: 5-15 cm in diameter. Flat to slightly convex, soft, and typically pale to medium orange or salmon pink, with a velvety to slightly fuzzy texture.
oxyporus-populinus.hymenium-attachment: Attached directly to the wood substrate, often appearing as a lateral extension with no distinct stipe.
oxyporus-populinus.stipe: Absent or rudimentary, not distinct from the cap.
oxyporus-populinus.ecology: Saprobic, growing exclusively on dead or dying wood of mapple trees (Acer spp.).
oxyporus-populinus.edibility: Inedible due to its tough and leathery texture.
oxyporus-populinus.fruit-body: Typically 5-15 cm across and 1-3 cm thick.
oxyporus-populinus.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical to allantoid, smooth, 3-5 x 1-1.5 µm.

panaeolina-foenisecii.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, brownish, closely spaced
hymenium is lamellar
panaeolina-foenisecii.cap: cap is convex, becoming broadly convex to flat, smooth, brown, often with a slightly darker center
panaeolina-foenisecii.stipe: stipe is cylindrical, smooth, white, often with a slight brownish tint
panaeolina-foenisecii.ecology: ecology is saprotrophic, commonly found in lawns, grassy areas, and pastures
panaeolina-foenisecii.edibility: edibility: inedible - contains small amounts of the hallucinogenic compound psilocin and can cause gastric upset

parasola-plicatilis.hymenium: Gills whitish at first, becoming grey and finally black, shrivelling rather than deliquescing into ink
parasola-plicatilis.cap: Very thin, strongly pleated, ovoid when young, then convex to bell-shaped and finally flat; brownish when young, becoming pale grey with a tawny-brown central disc
parasola-plicatilis.hymenium-attachment: Free to remote from the stipe, often appearing joined to a collar
parasola-plicatilis.stipe: Very slender, fragile, hollow, white to dingy cream, slightly swollen at base, without ring
parasola-plicatilis.ecology: Saprobic in short grass, lawns, parks, meadows, woodland edges and sometimes leaf litter or woodchip; appears rapidly after rain, often short-lived within a day; late spring to autumn
parasola-plicatilis.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~6–10 cm long, 1-2 mm thick
parasola-plicatilis.microscopy: Spores angular-ovoid to limoniform, smooth, ~10–15 × 8–11 µm, eccentric germ pore; basidia 4-sterigmate; pleurocystidia utriform to broadly cylindrical; cheilocystidia utriform to broadly fusoid-ventricose; clamp connections present

paxillus-ammoniavirescens.hymenium: Gills, decurrent and often forking, initially pale, aging to rusty-brown or vinaceous tones
paxillus-ammoniavirescens.cap: Depressed to funnel-shaped, initially velvety or tomentose (especially at margin), later smoother, brownish-vinaceous, margin often inrolled for an extended period
paxillus-ammoniavirescens.stipe: Central, short, stout; color similar to cap (brownish tones), with preserved basal mycelium and rhizomorphs
paxillus-ammoniavirescens.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with Tilia, Populus, Carpinus, on rich soil in parks, churchyards, open forests, summer to autumn
paxillus-ammoniavirescens.chemical-reactions: Greenish reaction on the cap when exposed to ammonia (NH₄OH) vapor

paxillus-involutus.hymenium:
gills on hymenium
hymenium is decurrent

paxillus-rubicundulus.hymenium: Gills that are decurrent, close, yellowish to orange-brown, and bruising reddish-brown upon handling or aging
paxillus-rubicundulus.cap: Convex, often with a depressed center and an inrolled margin when young, smooth to slightly velvety, with colors ranging from reddish-brown to rusty-brown
paxillus-rubicundulus.stipe: Cylindrical, tapering towards the base, and of a similar or paler color than the cap, bruises reddish or brown when handled
paxillus-rubicundulus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, most commonly associated with broadleaved trees, especially alders, it grows in mixed and broadleaf forests, favoring acidic soils
paxillus-rubicundulus.edibility: Toxic. Similar to other species in the genus, it is poisonous and can cause gastrointestinal symptoms
paxillus-rubicundulus.odour: Odour is earthy or slightly fruity
paxillus-rubicundulus.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid, 7–9 x 3–5 µm, basidia are four-spored

penicillium-camemberti.body: Fast-growing, dense, white, floccose to cottony mould forming the characteristic bloomy rind of soft cheeses; colonies remain predominantly white
penicillium-camemberti.description:
Spore mass white to very pale cream
Domesticated saprobic fungus specialised for cheese surfaces, especially Camembert, Brie and other bloomy-rind cheeses; grows well in cool, protein- and lipid-rich environments
Deliberately cultivated to form the rind and contribute characteristic flavour, aroma and texture
penicillium-camemberti.fruit-body: Microscopic filamentous mould forming visible white colonies that may cover the entire cheese surface
penicillium-camemberti.dimensions: Colony size variable with substrate and culture conditions; typically forms a continuous felt-like rind rather than discrete fruit bodies
penicillium-camemberti.odour: Mushroom-like, creamy, fatty to mildly ammoniacal during advanced cheese ripening
penicillium-camemberti.taste: Mild, mushroomy, creamy and characteristic when growing as an intended cheese-ripening culture
penicillium-camemberti.microscopy: Conidiophores typically terverticillate with rough-walled stipes; conidia smooth, ellipsoid to subglobose, ~3–5×2.5–4.5 µm, produced in chains

penicillium-glaucum.body: Filamentous mould forming dense white mycelium that develops sage-green, blue-green to grey-green coloration as conidia mature; colonies may be velvety, powdery or floccose depending on substrate and conditions
penicillium-glaucum.description:
Spore mass sage-green to blue-green or grey-green
Saprobic; domesticated strains are deliberately cultivated inside blue-veined cheeses (Gorgonzola, Bleu de Gex, Rochebaron, Bleu d'Auvergne)
Selected cultures historically called P. glaucum have been used in some blue cheeses
penicillium-glaucum.fruit-body: Microscopic filamentous mould forming visible spreading colonies, sometimes covering many centimetres of substrate
penicillium-glaucum.dimensions: Colony variable according to substrate, temperature and culture medium; no discrete macroscopic fruit body
penicillium-glaucum.odour: Strong, mouldy and characteristic; during cheese ripening contributes to the distinctive pungent blue-cheese aroma
penicillium-glaucum.taste: Characteristically mild and piquant when present as a food-grade culture in ripened blue cheese
penicillium-glaucum.microscopy: Branched conidiophores up to ~200–400 µm long, bearing brush-like groups of phialides; conidia globose, smooth, ~2.5 µm, in long chains

penicillium-roqueforti.body: Rapidly growing, dense, velvety to fasciculate mould; mycelium whitish but colonies become blue-green, grey-green to dark olive-green from abundant conidia, often with a paler margin and occasional clear exudate droplets
penicillium-roqueforti.description:
Spore mass: Blue-green, grey-green to dark green
Saprobic; domesticated strains are deliberately cultivated inside blue-veined cheeses such as Roquefort, Stilton and Danablu
penicillium-roqueforti.edibility: Edible when used as an intentionally selected food-grade culture in properly produced blue cheese
penicillium-roqueforti.fruit-body: Microscopic filamentous mould forming visible colonies and characteristic blue-green veins or cavities throughout ripening cheese
penicillium-roqueforti.dimensions: Colony rapid-growing; laboratory colonies commonly reach ~4–7 cm across within about 1–2 weeks, depending strongly on strain and growth medium
penicillium-roqueforti.odour: Strong, mouldy and characteristic; during cheese ripening contributes to the distinctive pungent blue-cheese aroma
penicillium-roqueforti.taste: Characteristically sharp and piquant when present as a food-grade culture in ripened blue cheese
penicillium-roqueforti.microscopy: Conidiophore stipes rough-walled, ~100–200 µm; terminal penicilli predominantly terverticillate, sometimes quaterverticillate and rarely biverticillate; phialides flask-shaped; conidia spherical, smooth, dark green, ⌀ ~3–4.5 µm, in loose chains

phaeoclavulina-eumorpha.fruit-body:
Coral-like, repeatedly dichotomously branched, compact to moderately open; branches ochre-yellow when young, becoming dull honey-brown to clay-coloured; tips initially buff-yellow to cream, usually pointed
Fruit body small to medium; ~2.5–7 cm tall and ~1.5–4 cm wide
phaeoclavulina-eumorpha.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the branches
phaeoclavulina-eumorpha.stipe: Short, distinct, whitish to pale yellow; base surrounded by conspicuous white to cream tomentum and whitish-yellow rhizomorphs
phaeoclavulina-eumorpha.spore-print: Spore print ochre-yellow to pale brown
phaeoclavulina-eumorpha.ecology: Probably saprobic on conifer needle litter, humus and occasionally woody debris; mainly coniferous forests; scattered, gregarious or in rows; summer to autumn
phaeoclavulina-eumorpha.flesh: Whitish to pale yellow, tough and leathery, unchanging when cut
phaeoclavulina-eumorpha.chemical-reactions: 15% KOH briefly bright yellow on rhizomorphs
phaeoclavulina-eumorpha.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to oblong-ellipsoid, yellowish, ornamented with numerous cyanophilous warts, ~6–10 × 3.3–5 µm; spines up to ~1–1.5 µm; basidia clavate, 4-spored with basal clamps

phaeolepiota-aurea.hymenium: Gills crowded; pale yellowwhen young, becoming yellow-brown with maturity
phaeolepiota-aurea.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat with a low umbo; dry, densely granular to finely scaly; golden-yellow; margin often fringed with veil remnants
phaeolepiota-aurea.hymenium-attachment: Adnate, often with a short decurrent tooth
phaeolepiota-aurea.stipe: Robust, clavate toward base; golden-ochre, densely granular below the ring, smoother and paler above; large membranous flaring ring, later pendulous and skirt-like
phaeolepiota-aurea.spore-print: Spore print pale yellow-brown to orange-buff
phaeolepiota-aurea.ecology: Saprobic on rich humus, leaf litter, compost and disturbed nutrient-rich soil; often associated with nettles; gregarious or clustered; late summer to autumn
phaeolepiota-aurea.edibility: Edible after cooking but not recommended
phaeolepiota-aurea.description: May accumulate high concentrations of cadmium and other heavy metals
phaeolepiota-aurea.fruit-body: Fruit body large; stipe ~10–20(–25) cm long and ~2–5 cm thick
phaeolepiota-aurea.flesh: Pale yellow to whitish, thick and firm; stipe flesh slowly darkening when cut
phaeolepiota-aurea.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth to minutely ornamented, pale yellow-brown, ~10–14 × 5–6 µm, without a germ pore; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia absent; pleurocystidia absent or rare; clamp connections present

phaeolus-schweinitzii.hymenium: Pores, initially yellow, maturing to brown or olive-brown, pores angular, 1–3 per mm
phaeolus-schweinitzii.cap: Typically fan-shaped or semicircular, surface velvety to woolly, ranging from yellow-brown to dark brown, often zoned with concentric bands of different colors
phaeolus-schweinitzii.stipe: Short, thick, and off-center, or sometimes absent; when present, the stipe is brown to dark brown and covered with a velvety texture similar to the cap
phaeolus-schweinitzii.ecology: Parasitic and saprobic, primarily found on the roots, lower trunks, and stumps of conifers, causes a brown cubical rot, late summer to autumn

phaeotremella-frondosa.hymenium: Smooth, covering the exposed surfaces of the gelatinous lobes
phaeotremella-frondosa.fruit-body:
Densely clustered, leaf- to seaweed-like, composed of thin undulating and folded lobes arising from a common base; ochre-brown, amber-brown to reddish-brown
Fruit body medium; ~1–5 cm tall, often several lobes fused together
phaeotremella-frondosa.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the lobes
phaeotremella-frondosa.stipe: Absent; lobes arise from a common basal attachment
phaeotremella-frondosa.ecology: Fungicolous parasite of Stereum hirsutum; grows on dead hardwood colonized by the host fungus; parasite attacks Stereum hyphae within the wood; mainly autumn
phaeotremella-frondosa.flesh: Brownish, soft, rubbery and gelatinous when fresh; shrinking to a thin dark horny crust when dry
phaeotremella-frondosa.chemical-reactions: KOH negative; FeSO₄ negative on surface
phaeotremella-frondosa.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline to faintly brownish, ~6.5–10.5 × 5–9 µm; basidia tremelloid, 4-celled, ovoid to subglobose, ~13–18 × 12–16 µm;

phellodon-melaleucus.hymenium: Small, spiky tooth-like structures on the underside.
