phellodon-melaleucus.cap: Somewhat irregular, flat to slightly convex or depressed at the center; surface is smooth, gray to bluish-black or black.
phellodon-melaleucus.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, as the spines run down onto the stem.
phellodon-melaleucus.stipe: Central or slightly off-center, cylindrical, sometimes with a swollen base, colored similarly to the cap.
phellodon-melaleucus.spore-print: Spore print: White to pale cream.
phellodon-melaleucus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, commonly found under conifers, especially pine trees.
phellodon-melaleucus.edibility: Inedible, tough and woody in texture.
phellodon-melaleucus.fruit-body: Cap measures 3-7 cm in diameter, while the stipe is 3-6 cm long.
phellodon-melaleucus.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, from 3.5-4.5 x 2.5-3 µm.

phellodon-tomentosus.hymenium: Spines, the spines are short, conical, and dense, usually white to pale grey, darkening with age to brown or grey
phellodon-tomentosus.cap: irregularly circular, often fused with adjacent fruit bodies, surface is densely tomentose, particularly when young, color ranges from brown to dark grey or black, with zoned patterns
phellodon-tomentosus.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, with the spines extending slightly down the stipe
phellodon-tomentosus.stipe: cylindrical, sometimes tapered towards the base, surface is fibrous and grey to black, blending with the cap
phellodon-tomentosus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, in coniferous forests in association with spruces and pines, on the ground, on mossy or acidic soils, late summer to autumn
phellodon-tomentosus.edibility: Inedible due to its tough texture and bitter taste
phellodon-tomentosus.fruit-body: Fruit body: 2–8 cm wide, 5–10 cm tall, 2–5 cm long, 0.5–1 cm thick
phellodon-tomentosus.microscopy: Spores subglobose, 4–5.5 x 3.5–4.5 µm, smooth and hyaline, basidia four-spored, hyphae brownish, lacks clamp connections

pholiota-gummosa.hymenium: Gills crowded, narrow; cream to pale yellow when young, becoming ochre-brown with maturity, sometimes with olive tones; edges often whitish
pholiota-gummosa.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat, with a low umbo; sticky to viscid when moist; cream-yellow, straw-yellow to pale ochre with olive-greenish tints; margin fringed with veil remnants
pholiota-gummosa.stipe: Cylindrical, cream to pale yellowish, becoming brownish toward base; finely pruinose near apex, covered with whitish to yellow-brown fibrils or small scales below; partial veil leaving a fragile ring or indistinct ring zone
pholiota-gummosa.ecology: Saprobic on decaying hardwood, especially buried roots, stumps and woody debris; in grass, parks, gardens and woodland paths; solitary, scattered or clustered; summer to late autumn
pholiota-gummosa.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~3–10 cm long and ~0.5–1 cm thick
pholiota-gummosa.flesh: Whitish to pale yellowish, thin, unchanging when cut
pholiota-gummosa.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to oblong or slightly bean-shaped, smooth, yellow-brown, ~5.5–8 × 3.5–4.5 µm; basidia predominantly 4-spored; cheilocystidia cylindrical to lageniform; pileipellis an ixocutis

pholiota-spumosa.hymenium: Gills are adnate to subdecurrent, close, and yellowish, turning brownish with age.
pholiota-spumosa.cap: Up to 10 cm in diameter.Convex to flat, with a somewhat slimy, scaly surface; yellow-brown to dark brown.
pholiota-spumosa.stipe: Cylindrical, yellowish at the top and brownish toward the base, sometimes with a ring.
pholiota-spumosa.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood or on wood chips and sometimes on the ground.
pholiota-spumosa.microscopy: Microscopic Features: Spores are elliptical, smooth, and measure approximately 6-8 x 4-5 µm.

pholiota-squarrosa.hymenium: Gills, close to crowded, whitish to yellowish when young, becoming greenish-yellow then cinnamon-brown
pholiota-squarrosa.cap: convex to broadly convex, surface dry, yellow-ochre underneath buff to tawny, overlaid with upturned, coarse, brownish, recurved scales
pholiota-squarrosa.stipe: cylindrical, dry, yellowish and covered in tawny scales below the ring zone; bears a persistent woolly or fibrous ring formed from the partial veil
pholiota-squarrosa.ecology: Saprobic, opportunistically parasitic, clusters on living (weakened) or decaying wood, at tree bases, summer to late autumn
pholiota-squarrosa.edibility: Not recommended, sever cases of poisoning (with alcohol)
pholiota-squarrosa.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 4–12 cm long, ~1.5 cm thick
pholiota-squarrosa.flesh: Flesh is white to pale yellow, no staining
pholiota-squarrosa.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, ~6–8×4–5 µm, distinct apical pore, pleurocystidia clavate to subfusiform, ~45×14 µm, cheilocystidia subfusiform to fusoid-ventricose, ~43×15 µm

physarum-rubiginosum.plasmodium-phase: The active feeding phase is a slimy, shapeless mass, typically yellow, orange in color, crawling over decaying plant material and feeding on microorganisms
physarum-rubiginosum.fruiting-bodies: Forms scattered to grouped sporangia, spherical to slightly flattened, supported by short, delicate stalks, surface is powdery, rusty-brown, with a metallic sheen as they mature
physarum-rubiginosum.description: Spore mass powdery, rusty-brown in mature fruiting bodies
physarum-rubiginosum.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying leaves, wood, bark on soil, in moist, shaded areas of forests or gardens, spring to autumn
physarum-rubiginosum.fruit-body: Individual sporangia are 0.3–1 mm in diameter, clusters may cover several centimeters of substrate
physarum-rubiginosum.chemical-reactions: Peridium dissolves in KOH, plasmodium may stain substrates with orange pigment
physarum-rubiginosum.microscopy: Spores spherical, warted or spiny, 8–11 µm, dense, branching capillitium network

pleurotus-ostreatus.hymenium: Gills, crowded, initially white to cream, becoming more pale-yellow or buff with age
pleurotus-ostreatus.cap: Fan- to oyster-shaped, sometimes broadly convex or nearly flat in crowded clusters, margin lobed or wavy, surface smooth, velvety when fresh, colour white/grey/tan
pleurotus-ostreatus.stipe: Often short, lateral or eccentric, sometimes almost absent, white to pale, solid, may be offset or thin
pleurotus-ostreatus.ecology: Saprobic on dead or dying wood of hardwoods (logs, stumps, trunks), shelf-like clusters, year-round
pleurotus-ostreatus.edibility: Choice edible, widely cultivated and culinary valued
pleurotus-ostreatus.flesh: Flesh white, firm, unchanging in colour when cut
pleurotus-ostreatus.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, ~8–12 × 3–4 µm, basidia 4-sterigmate, clamp connections present

pleurotus-pulmonarius.hymenium: Gills that are white to pale yellowish, running down the stipe
pleurotus-pulmonarius.cap: Oyster-shaped or fan-shaped, ranging from pale grayish when young to brownish with age
pleurotus-pulmonarius.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, extending down the length of the stipe
pleurotus-pulmonarius.stipe: Typically off-center or even lateral, often short or sometimes even absent
pleurotus-pulmonarius.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid, smooth, and hyaline, typically measuring 7-9 x 3-4 µm
pleurotus-pulmonarius.odour: Pleasant, typically mushroomy, sometimes with subtle anise-like or seafood undertones
pleurotus-pulmonarius.ecology: Saprobic; grows on dead and decaying wood, especially hardwoods
pleurotus-pulmonarius.edibility: Edible and choice; has a mild, pleasant taste and is often used in culinary dishes
pleurotus-pulmonarius.fruit-body: Fruit body: Cap can reach up to 5-15 cm in diameter
pleurotus-pulmonarius.dimensions: Cap: Up to 5-15 cm in diameter and 2-5 cm deep

plicaturopsis-crispa.hymenium: Lamellae (gills) are deeply wrinkled or folded, giving them a distinctive 'crisped' appearance.
plicaturopsis-crispa.description: Convex to flat, often with a depressed center, and smooth to slightly wrinkled surface. Cap color ranges from pale to dark brown.
plicaturopsis-crispa.stipe: Central or slightly off-center, cylindrical, and often with a tapering base. Stipe surface is smooth and colored similar to the cap.
plicaturopsis-crispa.ecology: Saprobic, initiating wood decay. Typically found on decaying wood, particularly in forests.
plicaturopsis-crispa.edibility: Considered inedible due to its tough and leathery texture.
plicaturopsis-crispa.fruit-body: Cap diameter ranges from 3-10 cm, while the stipe can be 4-12 cm tall and 0.5-1 cm thick.
plicaturopsis-crispa.microscopy: Spores are elliptical to spindle-shaped, smooth, 5-7 x 3-4 µm.

pluteus-cervinus.hymenium: Gills free, crowded, white at first, becoming pink to salmon-pink as spores mature
pluteus-cervinus.cap: Bell-shaped to convex, later broadly convex or nearly flat; brown, darker in centre, smooth to silky, sometimes radially streaked or fibrillose
pluteus-cervinus.hymenium-attachment: Free, not attached to the stipe
pluteus-cervinus.stipe: Central, cylindrical, whitish to pale, with brown vertical fibrils; slightly enlarged at base; no ring
pluteus-cervinus.spore-print: Spore print pale pink to salmon-pink
pluteus-cervinus.ecology: Saprobic on decaying wood, stumps, fallen branches, buried wood, sawdust and wood chips, on hardwood, spring to autumn
pluteus-cervinus.edibility: Edible but mediocre, not highly prized
pluteus-cervinus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe ~5–12 cm long, ~0.5–2 cm thick
pluteus-cervinus.chemical-reactions: Flesh without KOH reaction, spores hyaline to faintly ochraceous in KOH
pluteus-cervinus.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid, ~6–8 × 4.5–6 µm, cheilocystidia abundant, pleurocystidia thick-walled, fusiform to utriform, with 2–5 apical hooks, clamp connections absent

podosphaera-mors-uvae.hymenium: No exposed macroscopic hymenium; sexual spores develop within asci enclosed in globose chasmothecia, while the conspicuous white powdery coating consists mainly of superficial mycelium, conidiophores and chains of conidia
podosphaera-mors-uvae.body: White, flour-like superficial colonies on leaves, young shoots and fruits, initially patchy but often becoming confluent; ageing colonies turn greyish, brown to dark brown, with minute dark chasmothecia developing later in the season
podosphaera-mors-uvae.description: Spore mass white, powdery conidial mass; mature chasmothecia dark brown to black
podosphaera-mors-uvae.ecology: Obligate biotrophic parasite of Ribes species; infects leaves, young shoots and berries; conidia spread infections through the growing season while chasmothecia may overwinter and release ascospores in spring
podosphaera-mors-uvae.microscopy: Hyphae ~4–7 µm wide; conidiophores erect, cylindrical, ~92–165 × 9–11 µm; conidia produced in chains, broadly ellipsoid-ovoid to doliiform, ~22–31 × 14–22 µm, containing conspicuous fibrosin bodies; chasmothecia globose, ~92–104 µm, with few mycelioid appendages; each chasmothecium contains a single 8-spored ascus ~80–96 × 60–72 µm; ascospores ellipsoid-ovoid to subcylindrical, ~20–26 × 10–14 µm

postia-tephroleuca.cap: Semi-circular to fan-shaped, surface smooth to slightly rough, white to greyish or pale brown.
postia-tephroleuca.ecology: Saprobic; grows on dead conifer wood, particularly pine and spruce.
postia-tephroleuca.fruit-body: Fruit Body is ip to 10 cm wide and 3 cm thick
postia-tephroleuca.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical to ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, 3.5-5 x 1.5-2 μm.

psilocybe-coronilla.hymenium: Gills close to moderately spaced; pale grey when young, becoming purplish-grey to dark grey-brown or nearly black with maturity; edges often whitish
psilocybe-coronilla.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex to flat; smooth, slightly sticky when fresh, soon dry; golden-yellow, ochre-yellow to brownish-yellow; young margin may retain white veil fragments
psilocybe-coronilla.hymenium-attachment: Adnate, sometimes with a slight decurrent tooth
psilocybe-coronilla.stipe: Short, cylindrical, white to cream, sometimes yellowish below; smooth to finely fibrillose; base slightly tapered with white mycelial threads; membranous white ring persistent to fragile, characteristically grooved above and darkened by deposited spores
psilocybe-coronilla.spore-print: Spore print dark purple-brown to blackish
psilocybe-coronilla.description: Saprobic in lawns, meadows, pastures, parks, gardens; especially nutrient-rich soils; alone, scattered or gregariously; summer to late autumn
psilocybe-coronilla.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe ~2–6 cm long and ~0.4–1 cm thick
psilocybe-coronilla.microscopy: Spores amygdaliform to ellipsoid, smooth, thick-walled, ~7–10 × 4–5.5 µm, with a small germ pore; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia clavate to broadly cylindrical; clamp connections

puccinia-recondita.hymenium: Rhe­emata of rust pustules on host leaves (uredinia, telia) with sori breaking through the epidermis; internal hyphae intercellular, forming haustoria in host tissues
puccinia-recondita.morphology: No cap; symptoms appear as yellowish to brown spots or pustules (rust sori) on leaves; pustules may be brownish and powdery
puccinia-recondita.ecology: Obligate plant pathogen; heteroecious (requires alternate hosts), macrocyclic (has all typical rust life cycle stages: pycniospores, aeciospores, urediniospores, teliospores, basidiospores), primary hosts are cereals (wheat, rye) and some grasses
puccinia-recondita.dimensions: Sorus size: pustules generally small—visible on leaves
puccinia-recondita.description:
Germination of urediniospores requires free moisture
Aeciospores: 21-26 × 17-22 µm, broadly ellipsoid to spherical, hyaline.
Urediniospores: 24-32 × 20-25 µm, yellow to cinnamon-brown, often finely echinulate (spiny) walls.
Teliospores: Two-celled, long clavate when mature, 40-58 × 17-25 µm, brown.

ramaria-eumorpha.hymenium: Branched coral-like structures, cream to yellowish when young, becoming tan or brownish with age.
ramaria-eumorpha.cap: Not applicable, as this species has coral-like fruit bodies rather than distinct caps.
ramaria-eumorpha.hymenium-attachment: Coral-like branches emerge directly from the base or substrate.
ramaria-eumorpha.stipe: Not distinctly separate due to its coral-like form, base is typically whitish to cream.
ramaria-eumorpha.ecology: Saprobic, found primarily on decaying wood and forest litter.
ramaria-eumorpha.fruit-body: fruit body: Up to 15 cm tall.

ramaria-stricta.cap: N/A (Coral-like branches instead of a cap)
ramaria-stricta.stipe: Short, often branched at the base, whitish to pale yellow.
ramaria-stricta.ecology: Saprobic; grows on decaying wood and forest litter.
ramaria-stricta.fruit-body: Fruit Body is up to 10 cm tall and 5 cm wide
ramaria-stricta.microscopy: Spores are broadly ellipsoid to roughly spherical, with finely warted surfaces, 7-10 x 3-4.5 μm.

ramariopsis-kunzei.hymenium: Smooth, covering most of the outer branch surfaces; white to cream, becoming pale yellowish or ochre with age
ramariopsis-kunzei.fruit-body:
Coral-like, repeatedly and irregularly branched from a common base; branches slender, crowded to somewhat spreading; tips forked, pointed to blunt
Fruit body small to medium; ~3–10 cm tall
ramariopsis-kunzei.hymenium-attachment: Fertile surface continuous over the branches
ramariopsis-kunzei.stipe: Short, rudimentary basal trunk, white to cream, often dividing rapidly into numerous branches
ramariopsis-kunzei.ecology: Presumed saprobic on soil among moss and grass, especially unimproved grasslands, pastures, dunes, banks and woodland clearings; occasionally in litter or on very decayed wood; solitary to clustered; summer to autumn
ramariopsis-kunzei.edibility: Edibility uncertain; insubstantial and of little culinary value
ramariopsis-kunzei.flesh: White to cream, thin, fragile to somewhat pliant, unchanging when cut
ramariopsis-kunzei.microscopy: Spores subglobose to ellipsoid, finely echinulate to verrucose, hyaline, ~3.5–5.5 × 3–4.5 µm, slightly dextrinoid; basidia 2–4-spored; cystidia absent; hyphae with clamp connections

rhizopogon-luteolus.hymenium: Enclosed within a chambered, labyrinthine gleba; basidia line the internal cavities
rhizopogon-luteolus.fruit-body: Subglobose, ellipsoid to irregularly potato-shaped, hypogeous to partly emerging; whitish when young, becoming honey-yellow, ochre to olive-brown; surface fibrillose to rugose
rhizopogon-luteolus.peridium: Thick, tough and leathery, initially whitish, becoming yellow-brown to ochraceous; drying very hard
rhizopogon-luteolus.stipe: Absent; attached to substrate by numerous branching rhizomorphs
rhizopogon-luteolus.description: Spore mass creamy-white to yellowish; gleba becoming olive-yellow to olive-brown at maturity
rhizopogon-luteolus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines; sandy, acidic pine forests and plantations, often beside tracks; solitary or in small groups; late summer to autumn
rhizopogon-luteolus.dimensions: Fruit body small to medium, ∅ ~1.5–5(–6) cm
rhizopogon-luteolus.flesh: Gleba white and soft when young, firmer and powdery with maturity; no characteristic reddening
rhizopogon-luteolus.chemical-reactions: FeSO₄ slightly olive on surface; KOH negative
rhizopogon-luteolus.odour: Mild when young, becoming unpleasant to garlicky with age
rhizopogon-luteolus.microscopy: Spores narrowly ellipsoid to oblong, smooth, hyaline becoming pale olive-brown, ~5.5–9 × 2.5–3.5 µm, often biguttulate; basidia lageniform, usually 4–6-spored; clamp connections absent

rhytisma-acerinum.hymenium: Developing inside elongated apothecial ascomata embedded within black stromata
rhytisma-acerinum.body: Initially yellow-green leaf spots, developing into slightly raised, glossy tar-black stromata; irregularly circular, often surrounded by a narrow yellow to brownish margin
rhytisma-acerinum.hymenium-attachment: Ascomata embedded beneath the surface of the stroma
rhytisma-acerinum.description:
Spore mass hyaline to whitish
Biotrophic parasite on living maple leaves, especially sycamore and Norway maple; stromata mature on fallen overwintered leaves, releasing ascospores in spring to infect newly emerging foliage
rhytisma-acerinum.flesh: Black stromatic tissue embedded within infected leaf tissue
rhytisma-acerinum.microscopy: Ascospores very slender, cylindrical to filiform, smooth, hyaline, aseptate, ~60–80 × 1.5–2.5 µm, with a small apical gelatinous appendage; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~105–130 × 9–12 µm; paraphyses hyaline, septate, often curved or branched apically; conidia cylindrical, ~6–10 × 1 µm

ripartites-tricholoma.hymenium: Gills, white to pale cream, turning brownish with age.
ripartites-tricholoma.cap: Convex to somewhat flattened with age, pale brown or beige, often with darker central regions.
ripartites-tricholoma.stipe: Cylindrical, usually paler than the cap, fibrous, often enlarging toward the base.
ripartites-tricholoma.dimensions: Cap: Ranging from 2-7 cm in diameter.
ripartites-tricholoma.spore-print: Spore Print: White to pale cream.
ripartites-tricholoma.ecology: Saprotrophic, found on rotting wood, especially coniferous wood.
ripartites-tricholoma.edibility: Not recommended for consumption, as its edibility status remains uncertain.

rubroboletus-satanas.hymenium: Pores, small, round, initially yellow, turning orange-blood-red, blue when bruised
rubroboletus-satanas.cap: Convex when young, flattening with age, surface smooth and velvety, pale grey to light beige, margin curved inward in young specimens
rubroboletus-satanas.stipe: Robust, bulbous to clavate, yellow at the top, transitioning to red or reddish-orange with a dense, fine red reticulation
rubroboletus-satanas.ecology: Mycorrhizal with broad-leaved trees such as oak, beech, and birch in calcareous soils, late spring to early autumn
rubroboletus-satanas.edibility: Highly toxic when raw, causing severe gastrointestinal distress, toxicity is not eliminated by cooking
rubroboletus-satanas.fruit-body: Large, cap 10–25 cm in diameter, stipe 5–12 cm long, 3–7 cm thick
rubroboletus-satanas.chemical-reactions: Flesh stains blue when cut, KOH on cap surface produces a dark red reaction
rubroboletus-satanas.odour: Unpleasant, reminiscent of decaying food or carrion
rubroboletus-satanas.microscopy: Ellipsoid to fusiform, smooth, 11–16 × 4–6 µm, basidia 4-spored

russula-adusta.hymenium: Gills that are closely spaced, white to cream-colored, often with reddish-brown spots in age.
russula-adusta.cap: Convex when young, flattening with age and often developing a central depression, smooth, dry, and matte; color varies from reddish-brown to dark brown or almost black.
russula-adusta.stipe: Cylindrical, white or with reddish discolorations, and firm.
russula-adusta.spore-print: Spore Print: Creamy white to pale yellow.
russula-adusta.ecology: Mycorrhizal, commonly found in coniferous forests.
russula-adusta.microscopy: Spores 7-9 x 6-7 µm, broadly ellipsoid, with warts connected by thin ridges.

russula-chloroides.hymenium: Gills, adnate to slightly decurrent, white or pale cream, often with a distinctive blue-green tinge near the stipe
russula-chloroides.cap: Convex when young, later flattening or becoming slightly depressed in the center, pale cream to pale greenish-blue, smooth
russula-chloroides.stipe: Cylindrical, white or slightly tinged with blue, firm, often with a bluish-green tinge at the base
russula-chloroides.ecology: Mycorrhizal with broadleaved trees, especially oak and beech, deciduous and mixed forests, calcareous soils
russula-chloroides.edibility: Considered of low culinary value due to its bitter taste
russula-chloroides.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to ovoid, 8–11 x 7–9 µm, and are ornamented with fine warts that connect to form ridges, basidia typically four-spored

russula-claroflava.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, white to pale cream, closely spaced
hymenium is lamellar
russula-claroflava.cap: cap is convex, becoming flat with a slight depression, smooth, yellow or ochre
russula-claroflava.spore-print: spore print is white to cream
russula-claroflava.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal, often found in coniferous and deciduous forests
russula-claroflava.edibility: edibility: edible, and considered quite good. It has a mild, nutty flavor.

russula-decolorans.hymenium: Gills, closely spaced, initially pale cream to ochre, often turning grayish-orange or reddish upon bruising or aging
russula-decolorans.cap: Convex to flattened, sometimes slightly depressed at the center with a smooth, somewhat sticky surface when wet, color ranges from orange to yellowish-orange, fading and becoming blotchy with age, cuticle can be peeled off
russula-decolorans.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, white at first but turns orange, reddish, or grayish when handled or with age
russula-decolorans.ecology: Mycorrhizal, forms symbiotic associations with conifers(pines and spruces), commonly found in boreal and temperate forests in acidic, mossy areas
russula-decolorans.edibility: Edible, but only after proper cooking, firm texture and mild flavor
russula-decolorans.microscopy: Spores elliptic to broadly elliptic with reticulate ornamentation, 7–9 x 6–8 µm, cystidia are fusiform and present, basidia are tetrasporic

russula-delica.hymenium:
gills on hymenium, white, closely spaced, brittle
hymenium is lamellar
russula-delica.cap: cap is convex, becoming flat and then depressed with age, white, can be slightly yellowish or grayish, often with a peeling cuticle
russula-delica.stipe: stipe is cylindrical, smooth, white, often stout and robust
russula-delica.spore-print: spore print is white to cream
russula-delica.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal, often found in association with deciduous and coniferous trees
russula-delica.edibility: edibility: edible, but of little culinary value due to its mild flavor and occasional bitterness

russula-fragilis.hymenium: Gills are adnate to free, quite brittle, white to cream in color.
russula-fragilis.cap: 2-6 cm in diameter, initially convex, flattening out with age; can be variable in color but generally red to purplish-red.
russula-fragilis.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to almost free from the stipe.
russula-fragilis.stipe: 3-8 cm long, 1-2 cm thick; white, often developing reddish spots or zones.
russula-fragilis.ecology: Mycorrhizal, most commonly found in coniferous and mixed forests.
russula-fragilis.edibility: Inedible; known to cause gastrointestinal distress.
russula-fragilis.microscopy: Spores 6-9 x 5-7 µm, elliptical, with warts.

russula-integra.hymenium: Gills, cream to pale yellow when young, turning ochre with age
russula-integra.cap: Convex to broadly convex, sometimes slightly depressed in the center with age, surface smooth, sticky when wet, color ranges from dark brown to chestnut or reddish-brown, margin often striate
russula-integra.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, and smooth, white to cream-colored, occasionally with faint brownish tones towards the base, often slightly broader at the base
russula-integra.spore-print: Spore print is ochre to deep yellow
russula-integra.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in mixed forests, particularly with conifers such as spruce and pine, but also associates with deciduous trees like beech
russula-integra.description: Considered good, with a mild taste
russula-integra.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, 7–10 × 6–8 µm, with fine warts and a partial reticulum. The basidia are typically four-spored and clavate. Pileipellisis an ixotrichoderm, consisting of gelatinized hyphae, which contributes to the sticky cap surface.

russula-roseipes.hymenium: Adnate, closely spaced gills, often white or cream-colored.
russula-roseipes.cap: 5-12 cm in diameter. Convex to flat, reddish to pinkish-brown, smooth surface.
russula-roseipes.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly adnexed to the stipe.
russula-roseipes.stipe: Cylindrical, usually white, sometimes flushed with pinkish tones.
russula-roseipes.ecology: Mycorrhizal, associated with broadleaf and coniferous trees, including pines and spruces.

russula-sanguinea.hymenium: Gills, the gills are adnexed to slightly adnate, crowded, and pale cream, turning brownish with age
russula-sanguinea.cap: convex at first, later flattening, sometimes with a central depression, surface is dry, smooth, blood-red color, sometimes with spots or patches of yellow
russula-sanguinea.stipe: cylindrical, white to slightly pink, smooth, and solid, often becoming hollow with age
russula-sanguinea.spore-print: Spore print pale cream to ochre
russula-sanguinea.ecology: Mycorrhizal with coniferous trees, pines, in acidic soils, found in mixed and coniferous forests, in late summer and autumn
russula-sanguinea.edibility: Inedible, known for its extremely acrid taste
russula-sanguinea.fruit-body: Fruit body 5–10 cm wide, stipe 4–8 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
russula-sanguinea.microscopy: Spores broadly elliptical to subglobose, 8–10 x 6.5–7.5 µm, with warts and partial reticulation, basidia tetrasporic, cystidia fusiform, hyphal system is monomitic

russula-xerampelina.hymenium: Gills, adnate to slightly decurrent, crowded, cream to pale yellow, later becoming ochre
russula-xerampelina.cap: convex when young, becoming flat or slightly depressed with age, surface is sticky or viscid when wet, colour is variable, most commonly purple to wine-red, margin is often slightly striate
russula-xerampelina.stipe: 4–10 cm long, 1.5–3 cm thick, stout, white to cream, often with reddish or pinkish tints towards the base, firm, but becoming hollow with age
russula-xerampelina.spore-print: Spore print is pale ochre to cream
russula-xerampelina.ecology: Mycorrhizal, commonly found in association with conifers, it thrives in coniferous and mixed forests, from late summer to autumn
russula-xerampelina.edibility: Edible and highly regarded by some for its seafood-like flavor
russula-xerampelina.odour: Odour is distinct, fishy or shrimp-like
russula-xerampelina.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, ornamented with warts and ridges forming a partial reticulum, 8–10 × 7–8 µm, basidia four-spored, measuring 35–45 × 10–12 µm

sarcodon-imbricatus.hymenium: Teeth, the spore-bearing surface is composed of downward-facing, brittle spines (teeth), 3–7 mm long, which are pale gray to brown in color
sarcodon-imbricatus.cap: Large and fleshy, broadly convex to flat with age, surface is covered in coarse, dark brown scales that resemble shingles or tiles, color is typically grayish-brown to dark brown
sarcodon-imbricatus.stipe: robust and often tapering toward the base, color is lighter than the cap, often pale brown or grayish
sarcodon-imbricatus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with spruces, appears solitary or in scattered groups on the forest floor in coniferous woodlands, late summer to autumn, in poor, sandy soils
sarcodon-imbricatus.edibility: Edible when young, a bit bitter flavor, used in some regions as a seasoning after being dried
sarcodon-imbricatus.fruit-body: Fruit body: Large, stipe 3–8 cm long, 2–5 cm thick
sarcodon-imbricatus.microscopy: Spores smooth, roughly spherical to ellipsoid, 5–7.5 x 3.5–5 µm, basidia 4-spored

sarcodon-squamosus.hymenium: Spines, long, grayish to brownish, becoming darker with age, 2-8 mm long
sarcodon-squamosus.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming depressed with age, covered with coarse, dark brown to blackish-brown scales that are more prominent towards the center, margin wavy and sometimes lobed
sarcodon-squamosus.stipe: Thick, short, cylindrical, concolorous with the cap or paler, covered with small scales, often swollen or club-shaped at the base
sarcodon-squamosus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with coniferous trees (pines), growing alone or or gregariously, summer to autumn
sarcodon-squamosus.fruit-body: Fruit body large-sized, 4-10 cm long, 1-2.5 cm thick
sarcodon-squamosus.chemical-reactions: Flesh and cap surface at first green with KOH, then resolving to gray
sarcodon-squamosus.microscopy: Spores irregularly globose to subglobose, nodulose, 5-7.5 µ

sarcoscypha-austriaca.hymenium:
Smooth, forming the inner surface of the cup (apothecium), bright scarlet to deep red in color
Hymenium forms the entire inner surface of the cup
sarcoscypha-austriaca.cap: Lacks a distinct cap, the fruiting body is cup-shaped, thin and smooth, often slightly translucent when moist, vivid scarlet color and sometimes a slightly wrinkled margin
sarcoscypha-austriaca.description:
Fruiting body is sessile and attached directly to the substrate by a minimal basal area
Ascospores are produced internally within the cup
sarcoscypha-austriaca.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying wood, bark, or leaf litter in damp, shaded forest environment, in spring to early summer
sarcoscypha-austriaca.edibility: Inedible, due to its small size and insubstantial flesh
sarcoscypha-austriaca.fruit-body: Fruit body small, cup-shaped, typically 1–6 cm in diameter
sarcoscypha-austriaca.microscopy: Spores 25-37 x 9.5-15 µ, ellipsoid to nearly football-shaped, with rounded or, not infrequently, flattened ends, asci are 8-spored

sawadaea-bicornis.hymenium: No exposed macroscopic hymenium; asci develop inside dark chasmothecia, while white powdery colonies produce chains of conidia
sawadaea-bicornis.body: Thin white powdery patches on living maple leaves, often predominantly on the underside; colonies may become extensive, with minute dark brown to black chasmothecia appearing at maturity
sawadaea-bicornis.description:
Spore mass white from conidia; mature chasmothecia dark brown to black
Obligate biotrophic parasite on living leaves of maples (Acer spp.), including field, Norway, sycamore and other maples; white colonies may occur alone or merge across leaf surfaces; summer to autumn
sawadaea-bicornis.fruit-body: Fruit body microscopic; powdery colonies may cover large areas of infected leaves
sawadaea-bicornis.flesh: No true flesh; composed of superficial white septate mycelium on host tissues
sawadaea-bicornis.microscopy: Macroconidia cylindrical-ellipsoid, hyaline, ~25–35 × 13–18 µm, with fibrosin bodies; microconidia ~12–18 × 5–12 µm; chasmothecial appendages hyaline, repeatedly dichotomously or occasionally trichotomously branched with curved to coiled tips; asci 6–12, 8-spored; ascospores hyaline, ~23–27 × 12.5–14 µm

schizophyllum-commune.hymenium: Gills are split longitudinally, whitish to pale gray, and quite unique in their appearance.
schizophyllum-commune.cap: 1-4 cm in diameter. Fan-shaped to nearly circular, wavy, and whitish to grayish.
schizophyllum-commune.stipe: Generally absent or very short, when present.
schizophyllum-commune.ecology: Saprobic; grows on decaying wood and logs in a variety of environments, from forests to urban settings.
schizophyllum-commune.edibility: Inedible due to its tough, woody texture.
schizophyllum-commune.microscopy: Spores are cylindrical to ellipsoidal, smooth, and hyaline.

schizothyrium-pomi.hymenium: Ascomata, black, rounded to slightly flattened, often embedded in the host surface, forming minute black dots
schizothyrium-pomi.cap: Lacking, the fruiting structure is composed of tiny, circular, shield-like ascomata (fruiting bodies) on the substrate
schizothyrium-pomi.description: Not applicable, spores are released directly from the ascomata
schizothyrium-pomi.ecology: Parasitic or saprobic, primarily affecting leaves, twigs, fruit surfaces of Malus, Pyrus, in humid environments, from spring to autumn
schizothyrium-pomi.fruit-body: Fruit body size individual ascomata are very small, 0.05–0.1 mm in diameter
schizothyrium-pomi.chemical-reactions: No significant reactions with common reagents
schizothyrium-pomi.microscopy: Ellipsoid to oblong, smooth, hyaline, measuring 7–10 × 2–3 µm, asci 8-spored

scleroderma-areolatum.hymenium: Internal gleba: initial whitish-flesh, turning dark violet-black or olive-brown and powdery at maturity, ruptures irregularly at the apex
scleroderma-areolatum.cap: No cap; fruit bodies globose to subglobose, peridium thin (<1mm), yellowish-cream turning ochre brown, with distinctly small brown scales
scleroderma-areolatum.stipe: With a short whitish pseudostipe with white rhizomorphs present, base often root-like
scleroderma-areolatum.spore-print: Spore print dark purplish-black to olive-brown through maturation
scleroderma-areolatum.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with oaks, on damp, clay-rich soils in mixed woodlands, garden edges, mossy margins, open woodland litter, in small groups from summer through autumn
scleroderma-areolatum.edibility: Poisonous—may cause vomiting, profuse sweating, collapse, and fainting
scleroderma-areolatum.fruit-body: Fruit body 1-5 cm across, pseudostipe ≤2cm when present
scleroderma-areolatum.chemical-reactions: Surface turns red to reddish-brown or dark red upon application of 5% KOH
scleroderma-areolatum.microscopy: Globose to subglobose, dense spines (1-2µm), 11-15µm diameter, not reticulate, inamyloid, pale yellow-brown in KOH

scleroderma-bovista.fruit-body:
Subglobose to flattened, pale straw-yellow, ochre, yellow-brown to reddish-brown, often granular and becoming finely cracked with age
Fruit body small, usually ~1.5–6 cm across
scleroderma-bovista.peridium: Thin, leathery and relatively fragile, ~0.5–2 mm thick; opens irregularly at the apex to release spores
scleroderma-bovista.stipe: Absent, with conspicuous bundle of whitish mycelial cords
scleroderma-bovista.description: Spore mass grey-brown, dark brown to nearly black at maturity
scleroderma-bovista.ecology: Ecology ectomycorrhizal, growing partly buried in sandy, grassy or disturbed soil beneath broadleaved and coniferous trees (oak, pine); solitary, scattered or gregarious; late summer to autumn
scleroderma-bovista.flesh: Flesh immature gleba whitish and firm, later marbled grey-brown to blackish and finally powdery, outer surface often bruising pinkish
scleroderma-bovista.microscopy: Spores globose, dark brown, strongly echinulate and partly reticulate-crested, ∅ ~9–16 µm, with projections up to ~2 µm high; basidia subglobose, 4-sterigmate and rapidly collapsing; true capillitium absent

scleroderma-citrinum.hymenium: Gleba, marbled with white veins when young, eventually powdery and (dark purple to black) when mature
scleroderma-citrinum.cap: No cap, instead, it has a peridium that is rough and yellowish-brown, resembling pigskin
scleroderma-citrinum.hymenium-attachment: spores are formed inside the body
scleroderma-citrinum.stipe: lacks a stem or has a very rudimentary base, almost sessile on the ground
scleroderma-citrinum.spore-print: Spore print is brownish-black to purplish-black
scleroderma-citrinum.ecology: Mycorrhizal; commonly found in forests, particularly under broad-leaved and coniferous trees, frequently found in sandy soils, grassy areas, and heathlands
scleroderma-citrinum.edibility: Poisonous, can cause gastrointestinal distress if ingested
scleroderma-citrinum.fruit-body: Fruit Body is 3–10 cm wide, globular to irregularly shaped.
scleroderma-citrinum.odour: Odour is mild to unpleasant, often described as earthy or rubbery
scleroderma-citrinum.microscopy: Spores spherical, thick-walled, and covered with spiny projections, 8–13 µm

sowerbyella-imperialis.hymenium: Smooth, bright sulphur-yellow to golden-yellow or yellow-orange, sometimes becoming slightly more orange when dry
sowerbyella-imperialis.apothecium: Cup- to saucer-shaped, often irregular and split along one side; margin initially incurved, later wavy; outer surface concolorous to paler, finely pruinose-tomentose
sowerbyella-imperialis.hymenium-attachment: Exposed on inner surface of the apothecium
sowerbyella-imperialis.stipe: Distinct, short and relatively thick, often narrowed toward apex; yellow-orange to reddish-orange, finely felted, sometimes shallowly grooved or lacunose
sowerbyella-imperialis.ecology: Terrestrial in coniferous and mixed forests, often among needle litter on calcareous soil; scattered to gregariously; late summer to autumn
sowerbyella-imperialis.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; stipe usually ~0.8–2 cm tall
sowerbyella-imperialis.flesh: Yellowish to pale orange, thin, brittle, unchanging when cut
sowerbyella-imperialis.description: Paraphyses cylindrical to slightly clavate with yellow intracellular pigment
sowerbyella-imperialis.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid, hyaline, usually biguttulate, ~11.5–14 × 6–7.5 µm, ornamented with low isolated warts; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, inamyloid

spathularia-flavida.hymenium: Smooth; found on the flattened, spathulate upper surface of the fruiting body
spathularia-flavida.cap: No traditional cap, but the upper part of the fruit body is flattened, spoon- or spatula-shaped, bright yellow to pale yellow in color, surface is smooth and fleshy
spathularia-flavida.stipe: slender, cylindrical, and whitish to pale yellow, smooth, slightly translucent, merges seamlessly with the flattened upper part of the fruit body
spathularia-flavida.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
spathularia-flavida.ecology: Saprobic, growing on mossy or decaying wood, usually in coniferous or mixed forests, moist, shady areas, appearing after rain, late summer and autumn
spathularia-flavida.edibility: Inedible due to small size and gelatinous texture, not known to be toxic
spathularia-flavida.fruit-body: Fruit body 3–7 cm height, stipe 2–6 cm long
spathularia-flavida.microscopy: Spores long and cylindrical, 12–18 x 3–5 µm, smooth, colorless, hyaline in KOH, asci long, narrow, containing 8 spores, paraphyses unbranched, hyaline, septate

stereum-hirsutum.hymenium: Smooth, without pores or gills; yellow, ochre-yellow to yellow-brown or grey-brown, sometimes bruising darker yellow
stereum-hirsutum.cap: Fan- to semicircular, thin and leathery, often fused laterally into overlapping tiers; concentrically zoned yellow, orange, buff to brown; densely velvety to hirsute when young, becoming smoother with age; margin thin and wavy
stereum-hirsutum.hymenium-attachment: Smooth fertile surface covers the underside
stereum-hirsutum.ecology:
Saprobic, causing white rot on dead hardwood; fallen branches, trunks, stumps and standing dead wood; densely gregarious and often fused; persistent year-round
Inedible; tough, leathery and tasteless
stereum-hirsutum.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; flesh ~0.5–1 mm thick
stereum-hirsutum.flesh: Whitish to pale ochraceous, very thin, tough and leathery, unchanging when cut
stereum-hirsutum.chemical-reactions: KOH red, often becoming black on cap and hymenium
stereum-hirsutum.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to narrowly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~5–8 × 2–3.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; hyphidia with rounded to subacute tips; acanthohyphidia absent; clamp connections absent

stereum-subtomentosum.hymenium: Smooth, without pores or gills; pale cream, buff to ochraceous; fresh surface characteristically stains bright yellow when scratched or bruised
stereum-subtomentosum.cap: Fan- to semicircular, thin and leathery, overlapping in tiers; concentrically zoned grey-yellow, ochre, buff to pale brown; finely velvety to tomentose, sometimes greenish from algae with age; margin thin and wavy
stereum-subtomentosum.hymenium-attachment: Smooth fertile surface covers the underside
stereum-subtomentosum.stipe: Absent; usually attached by a relatively narrow lateral base
stereum-subtomentosum.spore-print: Spore print white to very pale brown
stereum-subtomentosum.ecology:
Saprobic, causing white rot on dead hardwood trunks and branches; overlapping clusters; fruit bodies persistent year-round, sporulating summer to autumn
Inedible; tough, leathery and tasteless
stereum-subtomentosum.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; flesh ~1–2 mm thick
stereum-subtomentosum.flesh: Beige to ochraceous, thin, tough and leathery; fertile surface bruises distinctly yellow
stereum-subtomentosum.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to narrowly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~5.5–8 × 2–3 µm; basidia 4-spored; thick-walled pseudocystidia present;

stilbella-byssiseda.cap:
N/A; this is a conidial (asexual) fungus and does not form a typical mushroom cap.
N/A
stilbella-byssiseda.ecology: Parasitic, grows parasitically on the fruiting bodies (sporangia) of slime molds in the genus Cribaria, found in moist, forested environments where slime molds occur, invades and consumes the slime molds, often appearing as fine, hair-like mycelium covering their sporangia
stilbella-byssiseda.fruit-body: Stilbella byssiseda does not form typical mushroom fruit bodies. Instead, it produces minute, thread-like structures (conidiophores) that emerge on the surface of parasitized slime molds.
stilbella-byssiseda.microscopy: Conidiophores are filamentous, septate, bear cylindrical conidia, 6–12 x 2–3 µm

stropharia-aeruginosa.hymenium: Gills, initially pale gray, becoming dark purple-brown with age, edged with white
stropharia-aeruginosa.cap: Convex to bell-shaped when young, flattening with age, sticky, bright bluish-green to greenish with a slimy surface, often fading with age, adorned with white veil remnants on the margin
stropharia-aeruginosa.stipe: Cylindrical, pale bluish-green to whitish, covered in small white scales, with a fragile, membranous ring near the top
stropharia-aeruginosa.ecology: Saprobic, grows on decaying wood, wood chips, or in nutrient-rich soil, in grasslands and woodlands, late summer to autumn
stropharia-aeruginosa.edibility: Inedible, effect of poisoning is little known and toxic constituents unknown
stropharia-aeruginosa.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 5–10 cm long, 0.5–1.5 cm thick
stropharia-aeruginosa.microscopy: Elliptical, smooth, 7–10 x 4–5 µm, basidia 4-spored, cheilocystidia bottle-shaped

stropharia-caerulea.hymenium: Gills, crowded and initially pale purplish-brown, maturing to deeper brown as spores develop
stropharia-caerulea.cap: Conical to convex when young, then broadly convex to flat, surface greenish-blue to blue-green when fresh, often sticky/glutinous, with white veil-flecks around the margin
stropharia-caerulea.stipe: Cylindrical, pale above the ring zone, green-bluish below; faint ring zone, lower stem with white-scaly fibres.
stropharia-caerulea.description:
Saprobic, in meadows, roadsides, gardens, and woodchip mulch, on alkaline and humus-rich soils, July to November
Unknown, possible gastric upset
stropharia-caerulea.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stem ~5–12 cm tall
stropharia-caerulea.flesh: Flesh pale bluish-tinged, unchanging when cut
stropharia-caerulea.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to ovoid, smooth, ~ 8.0-9.0×4.0-5.5 µm, basidia broadly club-shaped, 4-sterigmate, ~ 24–40 × 7–12 µm

suillellus-luridus.hymenium: Pores, initially yellowish-orange, maturing to orange-red
suillellus-luridus.cap: Convex becoming flat, surface initially finely tomentose, later smooth, color olive-yellow-brown, reddish-purplish flushes
suillellus-luridus.stipe: Sturdy, cylindrical, bright yellow with a prominent red-orange reticulate pattern
suillellus-luridus.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal, found in calcareous mixed and broadleaf woodlands with beech, oak, birch, late summer to autumn
suillellus-luridus.edibility: Edible when thoroughly cooked, when undercooked causes gastrointestinal upset, alcohol may worsen effects
suillellus-luridus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, cap 5-20 cm, stipe 6-15 x 2-5 cm
suillellus-luridus.description: Rapidly and intensely turning blue-black when bruised or cut
suillellus-luridus.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface → blackish-red, flesh → orange-yellow
suillellus-luridus.microscopy: Spores smooth, subfusiform to broadly ellipsoid, 11-15 x 4.5-6.5 µm, brownish in KOH

suillus-bovinus.hymenium: Gills, moderately spaced, pale yellow ochre when young, turning brown as spores mature, slight blueing reaction
suillus-bovinus.cap: Convex when young, becoming broadly convex or flat with age, surface smooth and sticky when wet, typically brownish with a slightly darker center, and with a striate margin
suillus-bovinus.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, with a scabrous to reticulate surface in the upper portion, pale to brownish, sometimes with a slightly bulbous base
suillus-bovinus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with pine trees (Pinus spp.) in coniferous and mixed woodlands, late summer to autumn
suillus-bovinus.edibility: Edible and not the best choice
suillus-bovinus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 7–15 cm long and 1.5–3 cm thick.
suillus-bovinus.microscopy: Ellipsoid, smooth, typically measuring 8–11 × 4–5 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-spored.

suillus-collinitus.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, with yellow to olive pores.
suillus-collinitus.cap: 5-12 cm in diameter. Convex to flat, slimy when wet, and shiny when dry. The cap is typically yellow to olive-brown.
suillus-collinitus.stipe: Cylindrical, sometimes swollen at the base, yellow with a reddish-brown scabers towards the base.
suillus-collinitus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, predominantly found in association with Aleppo pine trees, particularly in sandy soils.
suillus-collinitus.edibility: Edible, but the slimy cap skin should be removed before consumption.
suillus-collinitus.microscopy: Spores are elliptical, smooth, 8-10 x 3-4 µm.

suillus-granulatus.hymenium: Pores small, round to slightly angular; pale yellow to lemon-yellow, becoming ochre-yellow with age; young pores characteristically exude milky-white droplets that dry brownish
suillus-granulatus.cap: Hemispherical to convex when young, later broadly convex; smooth, strongly viscid and sticky when moist; cinnamon-brown, orange-brown to yellow-brown, often paler toward margin
suillus-granulatus.stipe: Cylindrical, solid, pale yellow to straw-coloured; covered with fine yellowish to brown glandular granules; ring absent; basal mycelium white
suillus-granulatus.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pines, especially two-needled pines such as Scots pine; alone, scattered or gregariously; coniferous forests, parks and grassy places beneath pines; summer to late autumn
suillus-granulatus.edibility: Edible after thorough cooking; mediocre quality, cap skin often removed
suillus-granulatus.fruit-body: Fruit body medium; stipe ~4–10 cm long and ~1–2 cm thick
suillus-granulatus.flesh: Pale whitish-yellow, soft, unchanging when cut
suillus-granulatus.chemical-reactions: KOH olive-grey on cap, pink to reddish-lilac on flesh; FeSO₄ bluish-grey on cap and olive-grey on flesh
suillus-granulatus.microscopy: Spores boletoid-fusiform to elongated-ellipsoid, smooth, ~7–10 × 2.5–3.5 µm; basidia 4-spored; clamp connections absent

suillus-grevillei.hymenium: Pores that are initially yellow, aging to a deeper orange or reddish hue; can bruise brownish.
suillus-grevillei.cap: convex to nearly flat in maturity; sticky when wet, smooth; yellow to orange-yellow, often with reddish-brown tones in the center.
suillus-grevillei.hymenium-attachment: Attached directly to the stipe, sometimes slightly descending.
suillus-grevillei.stipe: 4-10 cm long, 1-2.5 cm thick; yellow at the top, reddening towards the base; may have a ring-like, reticulation on the upper part.
suillus-grevillei.edibility: Edible and considered good by many, though some recommend peeling the sticky skin off the cap before cooking.

suillus-luteus.hymenium: Pores, large, angular, yellow, turning brown with age, exude a milky liquid when fresh
suillus-luteus.cap: convex to flattened as it matures, with a very slimy or viscid surface when wet, color is brown to chestnut, darkening with age
suillus-luteus.stipe: cylindrical, yellowish with a slimy, brown ring that may disappear in older specimens, base is often covered in white mycelium
suillus-luteus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with pine trees, found in coniferous forests, on sandy soil, late summer to autumn, often in large numbers
suillus-luteus.edibility: Edible and widely collected, slimy cuticle of the cap removed before cooking
suillus-luteus.fruit-body: Fruit body 7–12 cm tall, stipe 5–10 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
suillus-luteus.microscopy: Spores smooth, spindle-shaped to ellipsoid, 7.5–10.5 x 3–4.5 µm, basidia tetrasporic, hyphal structure lacks clamp connections

suillus-variegatus.description: tubes under the cap instead of gills, yellow to olive, becoming brownish with age
suillus-variegatus.cap: cap is convex, becoming broadly convex to nearly flat in age, smooth to finely velvet, reddish-brown with a variegated pattern
suillus-variegatus.hymenium-attachment: hymenium attachment is adnate to decurrent
suillus-variegatus.stipe: stipe is cylindrical, yellowish at the top, reddish-brown towards the base, may have a ring
suillus-variegatus.ecology: ecology is mycorrhizal, often found in association with pine trees
suillus-variegatus.edibility: edibility: edible, but should be peeled before consumption due to a potentially indigestible cuticle on the cap

taphrina-padi.hymenium: Naked whitish pale grey ascus layer developing on swollen fruits
taphrina-padi.body: Forms elongated, hollow, bladder- or tongue-shaped galls replacing normal fruits of bird cherry, initially pale green, later yellowish-reddish-brown
taphrina-padi.hymenium-attachment: Exposed ascus layer on the surface of infected plant tissue
taphrina-padi.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
taphrina-padi.ecology: iotrophic plant parasite on Prunus padus and related bird cherries, causing tongue-like fruit galls, spring to early summer
taphrina-padi.edibility: Inedible, infected fruits distorted, hollow and stone-less
taphrina-padi.fruit-body: Microscopic fungus, host deformations up to ~1–3 cm long
taphrina-padi.flesh: Gall tissue soft, spongy, pale green to yellowish, becoming brownish with age
taphrina-padi.microscopy: Asci cylindrical to clavate, ~50–60 × 25–52 µm, ascospores globose to subglobose, ~4–5 µm, budding within asci, no true ascomata

tapinella-atrotomentosa.hymenium: Gills, decurrent, thick and widely spaced, color ranges from pale yellow to brownish as the mushroom matures
tapinella-atrotomentosa.cap: Initially convex, becoming flat to slightly funnel-shaped with age, often wavy at the edges, surface is dry and velvety, brown to dark brown, sometimes with a slight olive tinge
tapinella-atrotomentosa.hymenium-attachment: Decurrent, with gills running down the stipe
tapinella-atrotomentosa.stipe: Short, thick, and cylindrical, velvety to the touch, and covered with dark brown to nearly black tomentum
tapinella-atrotomentosa.spore-print: Spore print is brown to rusty-brown
tapinella-atrotomentosa.ecology: Saprobic, growing on decaying coniferous wood, often on stumps, fallen logs, or woody debris, coniferous and mixed forests
tapinella-atrotomentosa.edibility: Inedible, consumption is not recommended due to potential gastrointestinal upset
tapinella-atrotomentosa.microscopy: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to almond-shaped, 6–9 x 4–5.5 µm, gill edges fertile, with basidia two- or four-spored

tapinella-panuoides.hymenium: Gills, thick, irregularly spaced, pale yellow to tan, darkening to ochre-brown as the fungus ages
tapinella-panuoides.cap: Fan-shaped to semicircular, velvety to smooth, pale yellowish-brown to dark brown, often wavy and irregular at the margin, surface becomes dry and cracked with age
tapinella-panuoides.stipe: Often absent, when present, short and off-center, blending into the cap, pale brown to ochre
tapinella-panuoides.ecology: Saprobic, typically growing on decaying wood, especially on coniferous logs, stumps, and wood piles, late summer to autumn
tapinella-panuoides.edibility: Inedible, known to cause digestive discomfort if consumed
tapinella-panuoides.description: Characterises first enzymes in atromentin biosynthesis
tapinella-panuoides.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe up to 1–2 cm long
tapinella-panuoides.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 6–8 x 3–5 µm, basidia 4-spored

thelephora-caryophyllea.hymenium: Smooth to longitudinally wrinkled or striate, brown to purplish-brown, covering the lower/inner surface of the fan- or funnel-like fruit body
thelephora-caryophyllea.cap: Thin, leathery, rosette- to funnel-shaped, often centrally split or lobed; brown to purplish-brown with paler, frilled, fringed or carnation-like margins
thelephora-caryophyllea.hymenium-attachment: Not gilled; hymenium spread over the wrinkled underside/inner surface
thelephora-caryophyllea.stipe: Present, central to slightly eccentric, short, tough, brownish, merging into the funnel-shaped cap
thelephora-caryophyllea.ecology:
Ectomycorrhizal, growing on sandy soil, mossy ground or needle litter in coniferous and deciduous woodland; solitary or in small groups; summer to late autumn
Inedible, thin, tough and leathery
thelephora-caryophyllea.flesh: Thin, brown, coriaceous/leathery, unchanging when cut
thelephora-caryophyllea.microscopy: Spores angular to irregularly lobed, warted or tuberculate, brownish to umber-purple, ~6–10 × 5–8 µm; basidia usually 2–4-sterigmate; hyphae with clamp connections

thelephora-palmata.hymenium: Wrinkled to irregularly ridged, covering surfaces of coral-like branches, initially pale pinkish, becoming dark brown with age
thelephora-palmata.cap: Lacks a true cap, fruiting body is fan-shaped, with densely clustered, flattened branches that are rosette-shaped, surface often appears velvety or fibrous
thelephora-palmata.stipe: Lacking or poorly defined; sometimes with a short, fused base connecting multiple branches
thelephora-palmata.spore-print: Spore print brown to dark brown
thelephora-palmata.ecology: Mycorrhizal with conifers, on the ground, in moss or leaf litter, dense clusters, late summer to autumn
thelephora-palmata.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, clusters may reach up to 10 cm wide and 6–8 cm tall
thelephora-palmata.dimensions: Branches (Lobes) each branch is 0.5–3 cm wide and 2–6 cm tall
thelephora-palmata.chemical-reactions: Spores brownish in KOH. KOH instantly black on all surfaces and flesh. Flesh unchanging when sliced.
thelephora-palmata.microscopy: Spores vaguely ellipsoid to more or less subglobose—occasionally slightly lobed, 8–11 x 6–8 µm, spines 1 µm wide, 0.5–1 µm high, basidia 40–70 x 6–10 µm, clavate to widely cylindric; 4-sterigmate

thelephora-terrestris.hymenium: Irregular, lobed or flattened branches which are split at their ends, giving them a fringed appearance.
thelephora-terrestris.cap: Not clearly differentiated, as the fruiting body is more of a lobed or fringed mass rather than the typical mushroom cap.
thelephora-terrestris.hymenium-attachment: N/A for this species due to its unique fruit body structure.
thelephora-terrestris.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found associated with coniferous trees, particularly pines.
thelephora-terrestris.edibility: Edibility: Inedible, with a tough and woody consistency.
thelephora-terrestris.fruit-body: The entire structure can range from 3-10 cm across and up to 5 cm tall.
thelephora-terrestris.microscopy: Microscopic features: Spores are ellipsoid, 9-12 x 6-7 µm.

tolypocladium-ophioglossoides.stipe: Elongated, club-shaped structure (stroma) which is dark brown to black, emerging from the parasitized host fungus.
tolypocladium-ophioglossoides.ecology: Parasitic on truffle-like fungi, especially species of Elaphomyces.
tolypocladium-ophioglossoides.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid and smooth, 3-4 µm x 1.5-2 µm.

tomentella-crinalis.hymenium: Smooth, resupinate, covering the surface of the substrate
tomentella-crinalis.cap: N/A (Forms a crust-like fruit body without a defined cap)
tomentella-crinalis.hymenium-attachment: Adnate, fully attached and spreading flat across the substrate
tomentella-crinalis.stipe: N/A (Lacks a stipe as it is a crust fungus)
tomentella-crinalis.spore-print: Spore print pale brown to rusty-brown
tomentella-crinalis.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal, on decaying wood or forest litter in coniferous and deciduous forests, late summer to autumn
tomentella-crinalis.edibility: Inedible, due to its tough, crust-like structure
tomentella-crinalis.fruit-body: Fruit body thin, spreading crust on wood, covering large areas of substrate, up to 10–20 cm in patches
tomentella-crinalis.dimensions: Crust thickness less than 1 mm thick
tomentella-crinalis.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, 7–10 x 5–6.5 µm, basidia 4-spored

trametes-ochracea.hymenium: Pores round to slightly angular, cream to pale ochre; ~3–4 per mm
trametes-ochracea.cap: Semicircular to shell-shaped, often overlapping in tiers; concentrically zoned ochre, buff, orange-brown to grey-brown; alternating finely tomentose, velvety and smoother zones; margin thin and paler
trametes-ochracea.hymenium-attachment: Pore surface covers the underside of the bracket
trametes-ochracea.ecology:
Saprobic, causing white rot on dead hardwood, especially beech and oak; fallen trunks, branches, stumps and standing dead wood; overlapping clusters; annual but persistent, visible year-round
Inedible; tough, leathery and corky
trametes-ochracea.fruit-body: Fruit body small to medium; often forming much larger overlapping masses
trametes-ochracea.flesh: White to cream, tough-fibrous and corky, unchanging when cut
trametes-ochracea.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to slightly curved/allantoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, ~5.5–8 × 2–3 µm; basidia 4-spored; cystidia absent

trametes-velutina.hymenium: Pores, small and round (4–6 per mm), white to cream when young, becoming yellowish with age
trametes-velutina.cap: Shelflike, semicircular to fan-shaped, velvety to tomentose surface when young, often zoned, margin often wavy
trametes-velutina.stipe: Lacking, fruiting body is attached laterally to the substrate
trametes-velutina.spore-print: Spore print white to pale cream
trametes-velutina.ecology: Saprobic, grows on decaying hardwoods, often found on logs, stumps, or fallen branches, year-round
trametes-velutina.edibility: Inedible due to tough, woody texture
trametes-velutina.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, caps measure 5–15 cm wide and 1–3 cm thick
trametes-velutina.chemical-reactions: Yellowish to reddish-brown KOH on cap surface
trametes-velutina.microscopy: Spores cylindrical to slightly curved, smooth, hyaline in KOH, 5–7 x 2–3 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-sterigmate

tremella-mesenterica.hymenium: Gelatinous, irregularly lobed or brain-like in appearance, bright yellow to orange in color.
tremella-mesenterica.cap: Absent, as this species forms gelatinous fruiting bodies.
tremella-mesenterica.stipe: Absent, as this species forms gelatinous fruiting bodies.
tremella-mesenterica.ecology: Saprobic, commonly found on decaying wood, particularly on fallen branches and logs in forested habitats.
tremella-mesenterica.edibility: Generally considered edible and used in culinary dishes in some cultures.
tremella-mesenterica.fruit-body: Size varies, typically ranging from a few centimeters to several decimeters across.
tremella-mesenterica.microscopy: This species does not produce conventional spores.

tricholoma-album.hymenium: Gills that are crowded and white, often with a slightly serrated edge.
tricholoma-album.cap: Convex to flattened with age, smooth, and pure white; sometimes with a slight umbo at the center.
tricholoma-album.stipe: Cylindrical, solid, and white; it can be somewhat swollen at the base.
tricholoma-album.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in association with deciduous and coniferous trees.
tricholoma-album.edibility: Edible but not particularly sought after due to its bland taste. Caution is advised as it can be confused with other toxic white mushrooms.
tricholoma-album.fruit-body: Cap diameter of 5-10 cm; stipe length of 6-12 cm.

tricholoma-equestre.hymenium: Gills, crowded, emarginate to adnate, bright yellow, turning ochre with age
tricholoma-equestre.cap: Convex to flat, slightly depressed in the center, with a dry, fibrillose to scaly surface, color is typically yellow to greenish, with darker brownish scales concentrated in the center
tricholoma-equestre.stipe: Cylindrical, robust, slightly tapered at the base, bright yellow, with faint longitudinal fibrils
tricholoma-equestre.ecology: Mycorrhizal with pine trees, often found in sandy soils in coniferous forests, appears in late summer to autumn
tricholoma-equestre.edibility: Historically consumed, some populations are reported to rhabdomyolysis with repeated consumption
tricholoma-equestre.microscopy: Spores elliptical, smooth, 7–9 x 4–5 µm, and inamyloid, basidia four-spored

tricholoma-fulvum.hymenium: Gills that are white to cream, adnate to emarginate, not particularly crowded.
tricholoma-fulvum.cap: 4-8 cm in diameter. Convex becoming broadly convex to nearly flat in age, dry and slightly scaly, colors ranging from yellow-brown to reddish-brown.
tricholoma-fulvum.stipe: Cylindrical, firm, usually lighter at the top and darkening towards the base, often with white to off-white fibrils.
tricholoma-fulvum.ecology: Mycorrhizal, growing exclusively under birch in deciduous and mixed forests.
tricholoma-fulvum.edibility: Edible, but not highly regarded. Some caution advised as it can be confused with toxic species.

tricholoma-imbricatum.hymenium: Gills, crowded, pale to light brown, sometimes with a slightly pinkish hue, not staining when bruised
tricholoma-imbricatum.cap: Convex to broadly convex, becoming flat or slightly depressed with age, with dark brown, fibrous scales, margin wavy, inrolled when young
tricholoma-imbricatum.stipe: Cylindrical, firm, brown to reddish-brown, with a fibrillose surface, base slightly swollen, basal mycelium white
tricholoma-imbricatum.ecology: Mycorrhizal with coniferous trees (pines), growing alone, scattered, gregariously, late summer to autumn
tricholoma-imbricatum.edibility: Reported edible, but has bitter taste and tough texture
tricholoma-imbricatum.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 3–8 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
tricholoma-imbricatum.chemical-reactions: KOH negative or red on cap surface.
tricholoma-imbricatum.odour: Odour sweetish, slightly mealy, or not distinctive
tricholoma-imbricatum.taste: Taste not distinctive, or slightly bitter and farinaceous
tricholoma-imbricatum.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid or occasionally subglobose, smooth, 4–8 x 4–6 µm, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, basidia 4-spored

tricholoma-inamoenum.hymenium: Gills, white to cream, becoming slightly yellowish with age
tricholoma-inamoenum.cap: Convex to flat, sometimes with a shallow depression in the center, smooth and dry, white to pale cream in color, sometimes with a yellowish tint at the center
tricholoma-inamoenum.stipe: Cylindrical, often tapering toward the base, white or pale cream in color, with a smooth to slightly fibrous surface
tricholoma-inamoenum.ecology: Mycorrhizal, typically found in coniferous forests, associated with pines and other conifers, it grows solitary or in small groups among moss and needles
tricholoma-inamoenum.odour: Odour is unpleasant, reminiscent of coal gas or rotten rubber
tricholoma-inamoenum.microscopy: Spores smooth, elliptical, 8.1-13.0 × 5.5-8.2 µm, basidia typically 4-spored, 40-55 × 9-12 µm

tricholoma-scalpturatum.hymenium: Gills, crowded, white to pale cream, sometimes becoming grayish with age, edges slightly scalloped, not staining when bruised
tricholoma-scalpturatum.cap: Convex to broadly convex, flattening with age, surface smooth to finely fibrillose, adorned with fine scales, grayish-white with a slightly darker center, margin inrolled when young
tricholoma-scalpturatum.stipe: Cylindrical, firm, white to pale gray, slightly fibrillose, may develop grayish discoloration at the base, no ring or veil
tricholoma-scalpturatum.ecology: Mycorrhizal with broadleaf trees (e.g., beech, oak) and conifers, in sandy soils or grassy areas, late summer to autumn
tricholoma-scalpturatum.edibility: Edible, but considered of mediocre quality
tricholoma-scalpturatum.fruit-body: Fruit body Medium-sized, stipe 4–8 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
tricholoma-scalpturatum.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, inamyloid, 5–7 × 3–4.5 µm, basidia 4-spored

tricholoma-terreum.hymenium: Gills, moderately crowded, whitish to pale gray, becoming stained darker with age
tricholoma-terreum.cap: Convex to flat, sometimes slightly depressed, covered with fine gray to dark gray fibrillose scales on a lighter gray background, margin inrolled when young, becoming wavy with age
tricholoma-terreum.stipe: Cylindrical, whitish to pale gray, fibrillose, smooth to finely scaly, lighter than cap, without a ring, base slightly thickened
tricholoma-terreum.ecology: Ectomycorrhizal with pines, in sandy or well-drained soils, growing in large groups or troops, late summer to late autumn
tricholoma-terreum.edibility: Traditionally considered edible but now discouraged (rhabdomyolysis in high consumption reported)
tricholoma-terreum.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 4–8 cm long, 0.5–1.5 cm thick
tricholoma-terreum.chemical-reactions: KOH and FeSO₄ reactions negative on cap and stipe surfaces
tricholoma-terreum.microscopy: Ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, inamyloid, 5–7 × 3–4.5 µm, basidia 4-spored, cystidia absent

tricholoma-vaccinum.hymenium: Gills, crowded, pale cream to light brown, often becoming darker with age
tricholoma-vaccinum.cap: Initially convex, becoming broadly convex to flat with age, reddish-brown to cinnamon-brown, covered in coarse, fibrous scales
tricholoma-vaccinum.stipe: Cylindrical, somewhat fibrous, reddish-brown to pale brown, covered with fine fibrils, base slightly bulbous, lacking a ring
tricholoma-vaccinum.ecology: Mycorrhizal, with spruces (rarely with other conifers), in coniferous woodlands, alone, scattered, or gregariously, autumn
tricholoma-vaccinum.edibility: Inedible, due to its bitter taste
tricholoma-vaccinum.fruit-body: Fruit body medium-sized, stipe 4–10 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
tricholoma-vaccinum.chemical-reactions: KOH negative, gray, purplish, or reddish to brown on cap surface
tricholoma-vaccinum.odour: Odour mealy, sometimes fruity and sweet
tricholoma-vaccinum.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid, smooth, 5–8 x 4–5.5 µm, inamyloid, basidia 4-sterigmate

tricholomopsis-decora.hymenium: Gills, close to crowded, yellow, gleaming when fresh
tricholomopsis-decora.cap: Convex at first, becoming broadly convex, nearly flat or shallowly depressed with uplifted margin, golden yellow background with fine grey-brown to fibrils concentrated toward the center
tricholomopsis-decora.stipe: Cylindrical, pale yellow; smooth to faintly fibrillose, hollow in mature specimens, base with whitish basal mycelium, no ring
tricholomopsis-decora.ecology: Saprobic on decaying wood of conifers, alone, scattered, in groups, summer to fall
tricholomopsis-decora.fruit-body: Fruit body medium, stipe 2-5 cm long, 3-10 mm thick
tricholomopsis-decora.flesh: Flesh does not change much when cut
tricholomopsis-decora.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface yields a red to pink or orange reaction
tricholomopsis-decora.microscopy: Spores broadly ellipsoid to subglobose, smooth, hyaline in KOH, ~4-8×4-6 µm; inamyloid, cheilocystidia 50-62.5×10-15 µm, cylindric to subclavate

tricholomopsis-rutilans.hymenium: Gills, crowded, bright yellow, becoming darker with age, not staining when bruised
tricholomopsis-rutilans.cap: Convex to broadly convex, flattening with age, covered in purplish scales on a yellow background, giving a fibrous appearance, margin sometimes slightly wavy
tricholomopsis-rutilans.stipe: Cylindrical, bright yellow with reddish to purplish fibrils, fibrous texture, often hollow or slightly swollen at the base, no ring or veil
tricholomopsis-rutilans.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying conifer wood, in clusters or scattered groups, summer to autumn
tricholomopsis-rutilans.edibility: Conditionally edible mushroom of low quality, only at a young age, mature become bitter
tricholomopsis-rutilans.fruit-body: Fruit body medium to large, stipe 5–10 cm long, 1–2.5 cm thick
tricholomopsis-rutilans.chemical-reactions: KOH red on cap surface, flesh yellow to pale yellow
tricholomopsis-rutilans.microscopy: Spores subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline in KOH, inamyloid, 3–5 x 2.5–5 µm, basidia 4-spored

tubaria-furfuracea.hymenium: Short-gills frequent, pale brownish to brownish yellow at first, becoming darker brown, edges faintly whitish at maturity
tubaria-furfuracea.cap: Convex at first, becoming broadly convex or nearly flat, brown to cinnamon brown, fading to nearly buff, mostly bald, when fresh with whitish partial veil remnants
tubaria-furfuracea.hymenium-attachment: Broadly attached to the stem, close or nearly distant
tubaria-furfuracea.stipe: Slightly fibrillose to fibrillose-scaly, whitish to brownish, poorly defined, ephemeral ring zone but without a true ring, basal mycelium white
tubaria-furfuracea.spore-print: Spore print brownish yellow to cinnamon brown
tubaria-furfuracea.ecology: Saprobic, on decaying wood, grass / leaf litter, soil in parks, woodlands and forest clearings, (mild late winter), early spring
tubaria-furfuracea.fruit-body: Fruit body small, stipe 2–5 cm long and 1–4 mm thick
tubaria-furfuracea.chemical-reactions: KOH on cap surface negative or grayish
tubaria-furfuracea.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 6.5–9.5 x 4–5.5 µm, inamyloid, basidia 25–35 x 4–6 µm, clavate, 4-sterigmate

tubifera-ferruginosa.plasmodium-phase: The active, feeding phase appears as a moist, slimy, gelatinous mass, usually pale pink to reddish, slowly moving across decaying wood and consuming microorganisms
tubifera-ferruginosa.fruiting-bodies: Forms dense, crowded, cushion-shaped to cylindrical sporangia, initially bright pink to red, transitioning to orange, rust-red, or dark brown as they mature, with a dry, granular surface
tubifera-ferruginosa.description: Spore mass powdery and rusty-brown in mature fruiting bodies
tubifera-ferruginosa.ecology: Saprobic, found on decaying logs, stumps, and wood debris, late spring to autumn, favoring moist, shaded environments
tubifera-ferruginosa.fruit-body: Fruiting body individual sporangia are 2–20 mm long and 1–2 mm wide, entire clusters may span several centimeters across
tubifera-ferruginosa.microscopy: Spores spherical, finely warted, 6–8 µm, interconnected by a capillitium network

tylopilus-felleus.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, pinkish-brown to brown.
tylopilus-felleus.cap: Convex to flat as it matures, brown with a velvety or slightly rough texture.
tylopilus-felleus.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly depressed around the stipe.
tylopilus-felleus.stipe: Cylindrical, paler than the cap, often swollen or bulbous at the base, adorned with a fine white netting (reticulation) near the top.
tylopilus-felleus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, found under broadleaf trees and conifers.
tylopilus-felleus.edibility: Technically edible but not recommended due to its extremely bitter taste.
tylopilus-felleus.fruit-body: Fruit body: Up to 10-15 cm tall.

xerocomellus-chrysenteron.hymenium: Pores, small and angular, yellow to olive-yellow when young, becoming olive-brown with age
xerocomellus-chrysenteron.cap: Convex, becoming flat with age, dry and velvety, cracked with a reddish flesh, color reddish-brown
xerocomellus-chrysenteron.hymenium-attachment: Adnate to slightly depressed around the stipe
xerocomellus-chrysenteron.stipe: Slender, cylindrical, often tapering at the base, yellowish with reddish streaks, surface smooth or slightly reticulate near the top, no ring or veil
xerocomellus-chrysenteron.ecology: Mycorrhizal with oaks, beeches, and pines, found on acidic soils, late summer to autumn
xerocomellus-chrysenteron.edibility: Edible but of mediocre quality, has slimy texture
xerocomellus-chrysenteron.fruit-body: Medium, cap 3–8 cm in diameter, stipe 4–10 cm long, 0.5–2 cm thick
xerocomellus-chrysenteron.chemical-reactions: Ammonia negative to brownish on cap, negative on flesh, KOH negative to brownish on cap, orangish on flesh, iron salts olive on cap, negative on flesh
xerocomellus-chrysenteron.microscopy: Spores boletoid-fusiform, smooth, 10–14 x 3–4 µm, yellowish to golden in KOH, inamyloid

xerocomus-subtomentosus.hymenium: Tubular or poroid, with fine, yellowish to olive-brown pores.
xerocomus-subtomentosus.cap: 4-10 cm in diameter. Convex, becoming more flattened with age; yellow-brown, olive-brown, or sometimes reddish-brown, often with a slightly downy or felty surface.
xerocomus-subtomentosus.hymenium-attachment: Adnate or slightly descending the stipe.
xerocomus-subtomentosus.stipe: Cylindrical, often with a slightly swollen base; pale yellow or yellow-brown, sometimes with a net-like (reticulated) pattern near the top.
xerocomus-subtomentosus.ecology: Mycorrhizal, associating primarily with broadleaf trees and occasionally with conifers, in woods, parks, and forests.
xerocomus-subtomentosus.edibility: Edible, but not highly regarded due to its somewhat bland taste.
xerocomus-subtomentosus.microscopy: Spores are ellipsoid and smooth, 11-14 x 4-5 µm.

xeromphalina-cauticinalis.hymenium: Gills moderately spaced, interveined; pale yellow to yellow-ochre, becoming slightly orange-ochre with age
xeromphalina-cauticinalis.cap: Convex when young, later broadly convex to nearly flat with a shallow central depression or umbilicus; smooth, hygrophanous, slightly viscid when moist; yellow-ochre, orange-brown, usually darker centrally
xeromphalina-cauticinalis.stipe: Very slender, tough and wiry; yellow-ochre near apex, dark reddish-brown to chestnut below; finely tomentose, with ochre to tawny basal mycelium; ring absent
xeromphalina-cauticinalis.ecology: Saprobic on conifer needle litter, twigs and woody debris; coniferous and mixed forests; scattered to densely gregarious; summer to autumn
xeromphalina-cauticinalis.fruit-body: Fruit body small; stipe ~2.5–8 cm long and ~0.1–0.25 cm thick
xeromphalina-cauticinalis.flesh: Yellowish to orange-brown, very thin and pliant, unchanging when cut
xeromphalina-cauticinalis.odour: Distinctive and pleasant scent reminiscent of Moneses uniflora
xeromphalina-cauticinalis.microscopy: Spores ellipsoid to broadly ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, amyloid, ~5.5–8 × 3–4 µm; basidia 4-spored; cheilocystidia abundant, fusoid to clavate; caulocystidia present; clamp connections present

xylaria-hypoxylon.hymenium: Perithecia embedded in the black stromatic surface, appearing as minute pimple-like bumps with ostioles; white powdery conidia produced externally during the asexual stage
xylaria-hypoxylon.fruit-body:
Erect, slender, cylindrical to flattened, often forked or antler-like; black, finely hairy near base, with conspicuous white powdery tips when young; becoming entirely charcoal-black and minutely roughened at maturity
Fruit body small to medium; ~2–8 cm tall and ~2–8 mm thick
xylaria-hypoxylon.stipe: Short to elongated, black, tough and wiry, sometimes longitudinally grooved; base broadened and covered with dark brown to black tomentum
xylaria-hypoxylon.description: Spore mass white from asexual conidia, dark brown to black from mature ascospores
xylaria-hypoxylon.ecology:
Saprobic, causing soft rot on decaying hardwood; fallen branches, stumps, logs and buried woody debris; scattered to densely clustered; year-round
Inedible; tough, rubbery and insubstantial
xylaria-hypoxylon.flesh: White to cream internally, solid, tough and elastic, unchanging when cut
xylaria-hypoxylon.chemical-reactions: Amyloid apical ring turning blue in Melzer's reagent
xylaria-hypoxylon.microscopy: Ascospores ellipsoid to bean-shaped, inequilateral, smooth, brown, ~9.5–13.5 × 4.5–6 µm; asci cylindrical, 8-spored, ~140–220 µm long; conidia hyaline, smooth, narrowly fusiform-clavate, ~8.5–12 × 3.5–4 µm
